text: # Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler
Keywords: Copper electroplating Leveler Microvia filling

An organic additive, Diazine Black (DB), was employed as a leveler for microvia filling using copper electroplating. DB is a derivative of Janus Green B (JGB), which is a common leveler used for copper fill of submicron or micron circuit metallization in electronic products. This study determined the optimal DB concentration for achieving the best filling performance. The electrochemical behavior of DB and its interaction with other additives, such as a suppressor and an accelerator were characterized using galvanostatic measurements. These electrochemical analyses helped explaining the filling mechanism of the plating formula containing the DB. Various surface morphologies and the crystalline orientation of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations were characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. The corresponding chemical activity of the surface atoms of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations was characterized using a test of etching rate.

Recently, multifunction and portable electronic products have become part of the mainstream of consumer electronic products. Not only the motherboard of electronic products but also the packaging substrates of integrated circuit (IC) chips need a high-density interconnection (HDI) made by a process using stacked microvias [1,2]. For example, the motherboard of cellular phones uses HDI to integrate more functions.

Because the diameter of the microvia has shrunk to less than 65 -m, and even as low as 50 -m, several metallization technologies such as filling with resin and conductive paste have not met the demands of process integration [1,2]. Instead, researchers believe that a more promising technology is to fill microvia using copper electroplating because this filling technique has been employed successfully to fabricate the interconnections of IC chips, such as via and trench metallization [3–13]. The microvia filling technology using copper electroplating is implemented using a specific plating formula that contains a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler [14–17]. The suppressor and the accelerator are basic additives for the microvia filling; the addition of a leveler can significantly improve the filling yield and extend the operative range of the accelerator concentration [16,17].

Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion. It preferentially adsorbs at the protrusion to inhibit the copper deposition rate because of the selective adsorption of the quaternary ammonium cation [18]. Therefore, a proper addition of JGB results in a copper deposit with a mirror-like surface. It is an effective reagent for carrying out a void-free filling in dual damascene metallization [4,5,7,8,10]. With regard to the electrochemical and adsorptive behaviors of JGB on the copper electrodeposition, Li et al. [18] and Bozzini et al. [19] presented detailed results using various instruments to identify the molecular structures of adsorbed JGB and the byproduct thereof. In addition, JGB can interact with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to form a composite suppressor whose adsorptive behavior is strongly convection dependent [16,17]. Hence, the addition of JGB can significantly enhance the filling performance of a plating formula because the forced convection acting on the board surface is always stronger than that at the bottom of the microvia during electroplating [20,21]. The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23].

Recently, many new levelers have been evaluated to determine their effectiveness as additives to copper electroplating for submicron via filling [11–13,24]. These new levelers also have the quaternary ammonium cations, except for polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) [13]. A preliminary evaluation of filling performance using the CDA metrology has shown that the derivative of JGB, namely, Diazine Black (DB), can compete with JGB in filling performance [17]. However, except for a patent [25] which claimed that DB is an effective leveler for copper fill, no detailed research has been undertaken to study DB as a leveler for the microvia filling. Therefore, in this study, we investigated the use of DB as a leveler, including the filling performance of the plating formula, the chemical interactions among the additives, the surface morphology of the copper deposit, and the influence of DB on the crystalline structure. In PCB fabrication, the etching process for patterning circuits is a subsequent step after copper plating. In this study, the influence of the DB concentration on the etching rate of the plated copper film was examined using an etching solution composed of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$
## 2.1. Electroplating

The electroplating conditions, procedures, and pretreatment methods have been detailed elsewhere [16,17]. PCB fragments with microvias formed by ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { 2 }$ laser ablation were used as test samples for filling plating. The size of the PCB fragment was $1 0 \times 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ The via density was 500 in array of $2 0 \times 2 5$ . The distance between two microvias was $2 2 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ or $3 2 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ (from center to center), depending on the diameter of the microvia. The specification of the microvias was described in the caption of cross-section images of these microvias. Before metallization, the microvias were conducted through a so-called desmear process to remove the smear that was formed by laser ablation on the microvia bottom. The desmear process can thoroughly clean copper surface of the via bottom to make sure of good conductivity at the interface between the filled copper and the inner copper pad after plating. Following the desmear process, electroless copper plating was used for sidewall metallization of the microvia. Following that, a plated copper layer with a thickness of $^ { 2 - 3 }$ -m was deposited on the sidewall to increase the thickness of the copper seed layer for the prevention of oxidation.

The PCB fragment was plated at a current density of $1 9 . 4 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ for 70 min. Two phosphorus-containing copper slices were used as anodes and directly placed in the plating bath with a working volume of 1500 mL. Constant agitation was performed by continuous air bubble flow with a flow rate of $2 . 5 \mathrm { L h } ^ { - 1 }$ during electroplating. The composition of the base electrolyte used for all plating tests was 0.88 M $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } }$ (Riedel-de Haën, ACS) and 0.54 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ (Merck, 96%, Ultrapure). The additives used herein were PEG with a molecular weight of 8000 (Fluka), NaCl (Fisher, Certified ACS), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) (Raschig GmbH, Germany), and DB (Aldrich). They were individually added to the plating bath through dilution from stock solutions that were prepared with properly concentrated contents. The temperature ofthe plating solution was maintained at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ The filling performance of a plating formula was examined through an image of the microvia cross-section obtained from an optical microscope (OM) (Olympus BX51).

The GM of the additive injection was performed using the Cu-RDE at a current density of 19.4 mA cm−<sup>2</sup>. At the beginning of the GM, the glass vessel contained only the base electrolyte. After the GM was performed for a period, one additive with a given content was injected into the glass vessel to achieve the desired concentration. The potential variation ofthe Cu-RDE could clearly indicate the electrochemical effect of these additives on copper deposition. The GM was carried out twice. One was carried out using the Cu-RDE at 100 rpm, and the other was carried out at 1000 rpm. A potential difference, $\Delta \eta ,$ defined by $\Delta \eta = \eta$ (average at 100 rpm)  (average at 1000 rpm), was evaluated from the GM. This value is a good indicator offilling performance [17,22,23]. Ifthe value is positive, it means that strong convection results in less copper deposition; thus, the plating solution may be effective for bottom-up filling (BUF) of microvia, whereas it is ineffective for BUF when the $\Delta \eta$ value is zero or negative. This approach was also adopted for this study to characterize the electrochemical behavior of these additives, providing further information for the BUF mechanism.

The etching rate ofthe copper deposits was obtained by measur ing the weight loss of a copper foil $( 3 \mathsf { c m } \times 5 \mathsf { c m } )$ after immersing the copper foil in an etching solution that was composed of4% $\scriptstyle ( \mathbf { v } / \mathbf { v } )$ $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $1 0 \% \left( \mathrm { v / v } \right) \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S } 0 _ { 4 }$ . The temperature ofthe etching solution was maintained at $2 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ . The copper foil with a thickness of 50 -m was formed by plating on a stainless steel plate using the required copper plating formula. It was then peeled off from the stainless steel plate. The etching solution contacted only one side ofthe copper foil that did not attach the surface of the stainless steel plate. The other side of the copper foil that was directly attached to the surface of the stainless steel plate was stuck tightly with tape to prevent corrosion. The etching time was 60 min. Each etching rate was measured three times to minimize the possibility of error.

Fig. 1 shows the molecular structures of DB and JGB. They are very similar, except for that DB has a functional alcohol group. Alcohol may be oxidized by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ or by anodic current to be a carboxyl group, which forms a chelating complex with metallic ions and has the ability to form hydrogen bonds with each other or with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } .$ Hence, small amounts of precipitate always appear in the plating solution after electroplating. Table 1 lists the plating results obtained from various plating formulas, showing that only two formulas resulted in BUF of microvia. One formula had 0.3 ppm SPS and no DB, and the other formula had 1 ppm SPS and 1 ppm DB. The rest of these formulas did not led to BUF but to conformal deposition. PEG–Cl is a well-known suppressor, and SPS–Cl has been confirmed to be an accelerator for copper electrodeposition [5,7,8,10,26–52]. Hence, the results listed in Table 1 indicate that the BUF behavior is caused by a synergistic interaction between the suppressor and the accelerator and that when the accelerator concentration is high, a leveler is an indispensable additive for achieving BUF.

The SPS concentration must be low for the BUF of microvia when DB is absent in the plating solution. Considering the function of SPS–Cl, the failure in the microvia filling caused by the high SPS concentration is attributable to the loss of synergy between suppression and acceleration; that is, the ratio of acceleration to inhibition is too high to effectively inhibit copper deposition on the board surface. This is also the reason why the surface appearance of the copper deposit is not bright and smooth but matte and rough.

The representative OM images ofthe cross-section and top view of the filled microvias are shown in Fig. 2. The formula of case 3, as shown in Fig. 2a and b, led to superfilling, namely, a hemispheric bump was formed on top of the filled microvia. When the

SPS concentration was increased from 0.3 to 1.0 ppm, the filling performance correspondingly decreased, especially in the case of a big microvia, as shown in Fig. 2c and d. The surface ofthe copper deposit also became more uneven than that ofcase 3. Many hill-like copper deposits were formed on the surface and a doughnut-like copper deposit was formed around the opening of the filled microvia. This result implies that the accelerator dominates copper deposition under this condition. Therefore, copper was preferentially deposited around the opening of the microvia due to a protrusive structure and the locally high current density. These negative results can be overcome by adding 1 ppm DB into the plating solution. A mirror-like copper surface as well as an excellent filling performance was obtained in case 8, as shown in Fig. 2e and f. The addition of 1 ppm DB could not only enhance the filling performance of the plating formula with 1 ppm SPS, but it could also flatten the plated Cu surface thoroughly. In addition, adding DB reduced the extent of overplating on the filled microvia. In particular, the doughnut-like copper deposit completely disappeared due to the addition of DB. This result strongly suggests that the good performance stems from the interaction among PEG, SPS, DB, and chloride ions.

However, when SPS was absent and DB was present in the plating solution, a conformal deposition occurred, as shown in Fig. 2g and h. An extremely rough copper surface is seen in Fig. 2g and h, although the doughnut-like copper deposit around the opening of the microvia does not appear. This result implies that the interaction between the inhibitor and the accelerator must exist such that equal deposition rates in a locally vertical and lateral direction can function well. This outcome also suggests that the leveling effect does not result from the leveler itselfbut from the interaction among the suppressor, leveler, and accelerator.

Fig. 3B shows that the cathodic potential was not significantly changed after SPS injection, implying that there was no significant interaction among DB, chloride ion, and SPS at the low potential. The CDA behavior (i.e., - > 0) only occurred after PEG was also present in the plating solution. To further clarify the interaction of these additives, the injective sequence was changed again, as shown in Fig. 4. There was no potential difference (i.e., $\Delta \eta = 0 )$ until SPS was injected into the plating solution, showing that copper deposition is not diffusion-controlled in the presence of PEG–Cl–DB. This result, combining with that of Fig. 3, also strongly suggests that the CDA behavior, which leads to BUF, is caused by the interaction of these four additives. This synergy ofadditives results in a slow copper deposition on the board surface and a relatively rapid copper deposition at the bottom of the microvia, which is characterized by the positive $\Delta \eta$ shown in Figs. 3 and 4. Fig. 4 also shows that DB does not enhance the inhibiting effect of PEG–Cl on copper deposition, which is different from that ofJGB [16]. The synergy of these additives stems from the adsorptive and transport characteristics of chloride ions and from the competitive interaction between the suppressor, accelerator, and leveler [5,7,8,10,26–52]. All the organic additives need to interact with chloride ion to exert individual function on copper deposition [5,7,8,10,26–52]. The establishment ofthe synergistic interaction between these additives reflects the positive $\Delta \eta .$

Fig. 5 shows the influence of DB concentration on filling performance. The filling performance of a plating solution is defined by a ratio percentage of two heights, $\mathrm { i . e . , } \left( h _ { 2 } / h _ { 1 } \right) \times 1 0 0 \% ,$ , where h is the copper thickness plated inside the microvia and $h _ { 1 }$ is the thickness ofdielectric layer plus the thickness ofcopper plated on the top surface of PCB [37]. A small amount of DB could markedly improve the filling performance of the plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, and 1 ppm SPS. The optimal DB concentration causing the best filling performance ranged from 0.5 to 1 ppm, depending on the diameter of the microvias. Similar results were also obtained from the system usingJGB as a leveler [17]. When the DB concentration was higher than 1 ppm, the filling performance declined with the DB concentration, particularly in the big microvia. This result is attributed to the CDA behavior [16,17,23,26] caused by the synergy of these additives, which is characterized by the $\Delta \eta$ values recorded by curve (c) shown in Fig. 5. Three representative - values were evaluated from Fig. 6.

The trend of the $\Delta \eta$ value with the increased DB concentration varies with the variation in filling performance. The positive value of $\Delta \eta$ implies that that the rate ofthe copper deposition is inversely proportional to the strength of forced convection [16,17,23,26], which leads to a slow copper deposition on the board surface and a relatively rapid copper deposition at the bottom of the microvia. Hence, the larger the $\Delta \eta$ value, the better will be the filling performance. These results also reveal that $\Delta \eta$ defined in this study is a useful indicator to evaluate the filling performance ofa plating solution employed for microvia filling. However, this evaluation tool is conditional, that is, a leveler must be present in the plating solution [26]. If there is no leveler in the plating solution, a poor filling performance may be obtained, even though a positive $\Delta \eta$ value is correspondingly obtained, as confirmed in Fig. 2c and d. It is notable that the positive $\Delta \eta$ value was obtained at lower cathodic potential because of the leveler-free plating solution, as recorded by curves (a) and (b) shown in Fig. 6. A significant continuous depolarization was observed in the case ofthe leveler-free solution. In other words, this plating solution was accelerator dominated. Hence, copper was preferentially deposited on the board surface, such that a conformal deposition occurred, as shown in Fig. 2d.

The crystalline orientation ofthe copper deposits was characterized by XRD, as plotted in Fig. 9. Not only the surface morphology but also the crystalline orientation was subject to the addition of DB. The intensity of[1 1 1] and [2 0 0] orientation peaks significantly decreased after DB was added in the plating solution. On the other hand, the intensity of [2 2 0] orientation peak obviously increased due to the addition of DB. A similar result was also found in other copper plating systems [54–56]. Honma et al. [54] reported that the addition of a leveler in a plating bath causes the [2 2 0] orientation to be dominant. After annealing at 120 ◦C for 1 h, the [1 1 1] orientation rather than the [2 2 0] orientation becomes dominant [54]. The change in the preferential orientation will lead to a change in the chemical activity of the surface copper atoms, which can be characterized by an etching test.

As can be seen from Fig. 10, the etching rate ofthe copper deposit decreased with an increased DB concentration in the plating solution. However, when the DB concentration was higher than 4 ppm, the etching rate did not vary with the DB concentration. The results are attributable to the difference in the atomic densities ofdifferent orientation and to the change in the preferential orientation ofthese copper films caused by DB addition. The grain size of [2 2 0], which was determined using Scherrer equation [57,58], also decreased with the DB concentration. A significant drop occurred at 1 ppm DB, indicating that DB is refining agent, that can lead to fine grains. A leveler, namely DB, employed for microvia filling was tested in this study. An excellent filling performance is obtained from a copper plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, 1 ppm SPS, and 1 ppm DB. This plating formula not only results in BUF of microvias but also leads to a mirror-like copper surface. According to electrochemical analyses, the root cause for achieving BUF in the plating solution was attributed to the CDA behavior ofthis formula.
# Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating
Keywords: Electroplating additives Levelers Microvia filling Copper electroplating

Leveler is one of the most important additives for super-conformal copper electroplating, which has been widely applied in the fabrication of nanoscale (or microscale) interconnect features in integrated circuits (ICs) and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. In this study, a series of triphenylmethane-based (TPM-based) molecules with different nitrogen-containing groups have been designed, synthesized, and investigated as novel levelers for superconformal copper electroplating. Their structure-property relationships are investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It is found that the steric hindrance and the type of the nitrogen-containing groups (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) in a leveler not only affect its adsorption ratio and strength on the copper interface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different copper crystalline plane. In combination with Cl−, polyethylene glycol (PEG, suppressor), and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS, accelerator), all TPM-based levelers show excellent microvia filling performances in copper electroplating and their effective concentrations are related to their antagonistic ability against the accelerator SPS.

Copper electrochemical deposition (ECD) for trench and microvia filling as interconnects in integrated circuits (ICs) or printed circuit boards (PCBs) is one of the most important techniques in modern electronic manufacturing industry [1,2]. For better stability and reliability, the ECD copper in these nanoscale and microscale interconnect features are required to be void-free. Therefore, a technology named “super-conformal” or “bottom-up” copper electroplating has been developed and widely applied in industrial practice. The electroplating process was carried out in an acid copper electrolyte, which was composed of copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, chloride, and trace organic additives. Though the organic additives’ amounts in the electrolytes are very small (generally at several parts per million), the additives play a crucial role in the super-conformal electroplating. The competitive adsorption and differential distribution of the additives on the cathode surface are the origination for the realization of “bottom-up” copper filling electroplating.

According to the additives’ different electrochemical effects in the electroplating, the additives were categorized as accelerators, suppressors, and levelers, respectively. Bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [3,4] and its reduced monomer sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [5,6] are most widely used accelerators. In electroplating, the accelerators can reduce the cathodic polarization and facilitate the copper reduction [7,8]. The suppressors are usually polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [9,10], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [11,12], or their copolymers [13,14]. In contrast to the accelerators, the suppressors synergistically work with chloride ions to increase the cathodic polarization and thus suppress the copper reduction. Leveler is another important additive used in the electrolyte to fulfill the super-conformal electroplating, which usually are nitrogencontaining molecules and positively charged in the acid electroplating solution. As reported, the levelers can adsorb at the highdensity charge region of the cathode to inhibit the copper deposition and level the copper surface [15]. In addition, the use of a leveler in the microvia filling electroplating solution can greatly expand the application concentration range of accelerators [16].

Currently, most of the reported levelers are nitrogen-containing dyes, such as the Janus Green B (JGB) [17], Alcian Blue (ABPV) [18,19], and Diazine Black (DB)[16] etc., or non-dye heterocyclic aromatic molecules, such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT)[20] and 2-mercaptopyridine (2-MP)[21,22] etc. Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear yet, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. More and more research groups began to purposefully design and synthesize various nitrogen-containing levelers to study their structureproperty relationship [23–27]. In our previous study, we reported a triphenylmethane-based leveler TPM-1, in which three pyrrolidine rings (nitrogen-containing functional groups) were linked by a triphenylmethane (TPM) backbone [28]. It was found that the small molecule with three saturated tertiary amines already be able to show strong inhibition effect and promising microvia filling performance in the copper electroplating experiments.

To further investigate the structural influence of nitrogencontaining groups on their electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance, a series of novel TPM-based molecules with different nitrogen-containing functional groups were designed and synthesized. As shown in Fig. 1, TPM-1 and TPM-3 are tertiary amines with pyrrolidine and piperidine as the nitrogen-containing groups, respectively. TPM-2, TPM-4, and TPM-5 are quaternary ammoniums, in which TPM-2 and TPM-5 were methylated base on TPM-1 with I− and Cl− as the counter anions, respectively, and TPM-4 was methylated from TPM-3. In this study, the TPM-based molecules were used as levelers in the super-conformal copper electroplating and their structure-property relationship were carefully investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments.

All electrochemical measurements were carried out using an electrochemical workstation (CHI 760E) with a three-electrode system. A platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE, PINE) with a diameter of 5 mm was employed as the working electrode. The counter electrode and the reference electrode were Pt bar and saturated mercury-mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE), respectively. The volume of the electroplating solution was 50 ml and the temperature were controlled at $2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathsf C .$

Before the galvanostatic measurements (GMs), a thin copper layer was deposited on the Pt-RDE (10 mA/cm<sup>2</sup>, 900 s) in the base electroplating solution to prepare a Cu-RDE. The composition of the base electroplating solution was 0.88 mol/L $\mathrm { C u S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } 0$ (JHD, analytical reagent, recrystallized from ultrapure water before use) and 0.54 mol/L $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ . The GMs were carried out with the current density of 20 mA/cm<sup>2</sup>. The rotating speed of the working electrode was controlled at 100 rpm or 1000 rpm to simulate the forced convection at the bottom of microvia and on the copper surface, respectively. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was carried out by a negative sweep from -0.4 to 0.75 V and then back from 0.75 to -0.4 V with a scan rate of 0.01 $\mathsf { V } / \mathsf { s }$
## 2.4. Electroplating measurements

Printed circuit boards $( 6 \times 8 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ with many microvias formed by ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ laser ablation were used as test samples for filling plating experiments. The diameter and depth of the microvias were 75 and $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ , respectively. Two phosphorus-containing copper slices $( 6 0 \times 1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 } )$ were used as anode and placed in the electroplating solution with a 1000 mL working volume. The electroplating solution was constantly agitated by air bubbles during electroplating to ensure suficiently convection. The composition of the electrolyte for microvia filling plating was 0.88 mol/L $\mathrm { C u S O } _ { 4 } { \bullet } \mathrm { S H } _ { 2 } 0$ 0.54 mol/L $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ , 200 ppm PEG (MW6000), 40 ppm Cl− (added as NaCl), 2 ppm SPS and various TPMs. The current density was controlled at 1.8 $\mathsf { A } / \mathsf { d } \mathsf { m } ^ { 2 }$ (ASD) for 45 min. The surface morphologies and crystalline structures of the copper deposits were characterized by a field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, Hitach SU8220) and an $\mathbf { X } { \mathrm { - } } \mathbf { I } \mathbf { a } \mathbf { y }$ diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 AD-VANCE), resepctively. The microvia filling performances were examined by cross-sectional imaging with optical microscopy (OM).

Fig. 2. Galvanostatic measurements with different injection orders of additives at 1000 rpm. The concentration of I− is 4.452 μmol/L. The electroplating solution is composed of 0.88 mol/L CuSO •5H O, 0.54 mol/L $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ . The molar ratio of TPMand TPM-3 to I− are both 1:3.

Following the addition of SPS, 1.484 μmol/L TPM-based levelers were injected into the electroplating solution. The cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.673 and 0.712 V for TPM-1 and TPM-2, respectively, which imply that at the same concentration, the inhibition effect of the quaternary ammonium TPM-2 was much stronger than the tertiary amine TPM-1. Comparing the molecular structures of TPM-1 and TPM-2, two differences were found: the quaternary ammonium structure and the I− ion. It has been reported that counter anion in a leveler influence its electrochemical behavior and I− can inhibite the $\mathsf { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction [29– 33]. To distinguish the stronger inhibition ability of TPM-2 was induced by the ammonium structure or I−, we designed and synthesized a new molecule TPM-5, which have the same cationic structure as TPM-2 but with Cl− instead of I− as the counter ion. When TPM-5 was injected in the copper electroplating solution, the potential drops from 0.559 to 0.654 V (fast adsorption) and then slowly moves back to 0.547 V(gradually deactivated by the SPS through the ion pairing interactions)[34–36]. The result indicates that though with the same cationic skeleton, TPM-5 has a much weaker inhibition effect against SPS than TPM-2. As shown in Fig. 2a, the steady potential after addition of TPM-5 is close to the initial value before the leveler injection, which means the adsorption of TPM-5 on the copper surface is weak and the adsorbed leveler was replaced by SPS gradually in the electroplating process. From the GMs of TPM-2 and TPM-5, it can be concluded that the extraordinarily strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 should be related to the anion I− instead of causing by the quaternized pyrrolidine group. In addition, from Fig. 2a, we can see that the inhibition effect of TPM-5 is also weaker than TPM-1. Therefore, by comparing the molecular structures and inhibition abilities of TPM-1, TPM-2 and TPM-5, it was found that the methylated quaternary ammonium structure actually weakens the leveler’s inhibition effect instead of strengthening it, and the exist of I− is the cause of dramatical improvement of the molecule’s inhibition ability.

TPM-3, in which three six-membered piperidine rings were introduced to replace the five-membered pyrrolidine rings in TPM-1, has also been added in the electroplating solution to investigate how the ring size of the nitrogen-containing groups affect their electrochemical properties. As shown in Fig. 2a, with the addition of TPM-3, the cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.646 V and then slowly moves back to 0.590 V. The results show that the antagonistic effect of TPM-3 against SPS is weaker than the TPM-1. Since the electronic structures of nitrogen atoms in pyrrolidine and piperidine are very close (the pKa value of pyrrolidine and piperidine are 11.27 and 11.22, respectievely [37]), the electrochemical property difference of TPM-1 and TPM-3 should mainly be caused by the steric hindrance, that is, a bigger head group of the nitrogen-containing group leads to a weaker antagonistic effect against SPS. While for the TPM-4, which also has I− as the counter ion, no surprise, the addition of the molecule leading to a strong polarization and the potential sharply drops to approximately 0.712 V just as TPM-2.

To further verify the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the I− alone or the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, equivalent amount of I− as in TPM-2 and TPM-4 was injected into the electroplating solution. As shown in Fig. 2a, the addition of I− alone in the presence of Cl−, PEG, and SPS leads a further polarization from 0.559 to 0.662 V, which means I− has a certain kind of antagonistic against SPS, however, the inhibiton ability is much weaker than that of TPM-2 and TPM-4 as shown in the GMs. The results clearly indicate that the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergistic effect of I− and its counterpart rather than I− itself alone. To further confirm whether the synergistic effect is related the quaternary ammoiunm structure, TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− with a molar ratio of 1:3 have aslo been injected together into the electroplating solution, respectively. Since TPM-1 and TPM-3 have no quaternary ammonium structure, the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 should be caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the whole structure of the TPM-based counterpart, rather than specifically interacted with the quaternary ammonium structures.

To charactrized the effect of the leveler concentrations on its electrochemical properties, cyclic voltammetry measurements with various concentrations of TPM-based levelers (or I−) in an electroplating solution containing 2 ppm SPS, 40 ppm Cl− and 200 ppm PEG have been carried out. As shown in Fig. 4, the increase of the TPM-based levelers (or I−) concentration all leads to a further polarization. For TPM-1, the addition of 0.05 ppm leveler not only decreases the absolute current density, but also changes the relative current density values in the forward (negative-going) and backward (positive-going) sweep. As reported, the current densities in the return sweep larger than the forward values indicate a positive feedback for the copper electroplating [38,39]. In addition, when the concentration of TPM-1 reaches as high as 8 ppm, an evident negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon was observed, which has been widely used to explain the mechanism of extremely bottom-up filling of Cu or other metals with one suppressor as the additive in electroplating [38,40–42]. Similarly, NDR has also been observed with other TPM-based levelers at relatively high concentrations (above 2 ppm for TPM-2 and TPM-4; above 8 for TPM-3; above 20 ppm for TPM-5). Though ternary additives (leveler, suppressor, and accelerator) were used in this research instead of one additive system reported in literature, extremely bottom-up microvia filling effect has also been otained with high concentrations of TPM-2 or TPM-4 (as shown in Figs. 7–2f, 7–2g, 7–4f, and 7–4g), which imply a gradual breakdown of the suppression starting from the microvia bottom. NDR is observed for all high concentration TPM-based levelers, however, only TPM-2 and TPM-4 result in the extremely bottom-up filling. One possible explanation is that due to the strong inhibition strength caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, the suppression layer formed by high concentration of TPM-2 (or TPM-4) plays a predominant effect on the cathod surface and overshadowed the effect of SPS (as shown in Fig. 3e and f). While for other TPM-based levelers (or I−), the antagonistic effect of SPS and the inhibitors contributes together to achieve the super-conformal electroplaitng, as described by the curvature enhanced adsorbate coverage (CEAC) [36] or convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) [43] mechanisms.

As suggested by the CDA mechanism [16,44], the electrolyte convection states inside and outside the microvia have a great influence on the microvia filling performance. Different rotating speeds of the working electrode has been widely used to simulate the convection states of the plating solution on the top (1000 rpm) or at the bottom (100 rpm) of a microvia. The potential difference $( \Delta \eta = \eta _ { 1 0 0 } - \eta _ { 1 0 0 0 } )$ measured from the two rotating speeds in GMs can be used to predict the microvia filling performance. Generally, a larger positive $\Delta \eta$ value implies a better microvia filling performance.

As reported, the electromigration resistance of copper film is affected largely by the (111) orientation [45,46]. The crystalline structure of the copper depositions electroplated with various TPMbased levelers were characterized by XRD. As shown in Fig. 9, without leveler in the electroplating solution, the preferred crystalline orientation of the copper layer is Cu (111). In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.

This work investigated the influence of Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) as a single additive on performance of copper foil. Electrochemical analysis indicates that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu<sup>2+</sup> to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> . Furthermore, a Turing oscillation growth model, supported by finite element simulations and AFM analysis, is proposed to describe the morphological evolution, wherein ZPS preferentially accumulates at valley regions, improving surface flatness through cyclic peak-valley transfer, though with inherently limited ultimate smoothing. Structurally, XRD shows ZPS promotes Cu (220) orientation, while HRTEM confirms the presence of twin boundaries, and lattice fringe measurements reveal a transition from (111)-dominated to (220)-dominated regions upon ZPS addition. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. In terms of performance, ZPS improves surface morphology and reduces roughness. Mechanical properties are optimized at 30 mg/L ZPS, with tensile strength reaching 331 MPa and elongation 3.78 %. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

With the progress of 5 G communication technology, there are new requirements for electronic devices, such as laptop, communication station, smart watch and phone and so on [1]. In these devices, printed Circuit Board (PCB), as the “mother board” for integrated circuit and all kinds of electronic components, has attracted researchers’ wide attention in recent years [2]. Copper clad laminate (CCL) is one of the key materials in PCB, consisting of copper foil and substrate, among which copper foil directly affects the electrical performance and mechanical performance of PCB [3]. There are two methods to prepare copper foil in industry, namely, electrolytic copper foil and rolled copper foil, among which rolled copper foil is fabricated by rolling and compressing pure copper [4]. However, the production cost of rolled copper foil is expensive and the thickness is limited [5]. In contrast, electrolyte copper foil is cost-friendly and suitable for scale-up production [6]. In widely-used acid sulfate copper electroplating process, free $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { 2 + } }$ obtain electrons and is reduced on Ti cathode surface to form copper foil [7,8]. However, it is hard to directly prepare satisfied electrolyte copper foil from acid sulfate copper solution without the aid of additives to satisfy the fabrication requirement of advanced electronic products [9].

As investigation method progresses, theoretical calculation [14], spectrum technology [15], microscopic technology [16] are widely used to gain deeper understanding of additives during copper electrodeposition, providing guidance for researchers. An et al. [17,18] coupled in situ Raman spectra and infrared spectra, DFT (density functional theory) calculation to study triphenylmethane-based levelers during copper electroplating and proposed difunctional mechanism of coordination and adsorption, providing insights into future leveler molecular design. Wheeler et al. [19] used ab initio MD simulation method and found that the adsorption strength order is $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } > N a ^ { + } > M P S > H _ { 2 } O . }$ . The addition of Cl⁻ results in the decline of copper substrate work function, indicating that electrons can transfer more readily from the metal to surface-active species. Meanwhile, sulfide bond of MPS adsorbs onto the copper substrate, whereas the sulfonate group tends to attract ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and reduce $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ with Cl<sup>−</sup> adsorption layer. Broekmann [20] investigated the accelerating mechanism of SPS by STM and found that SPS adsorbs on copper sub strate by disulfide. Laterally, SPS will break into two MPS molecules, among which one side (sulfide bond) adsorbs on copper substrate and the other side (sulfonate group) catches $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ , consistent with Ref [19]. The desorbed MPS will be oxidized to SPS or PDS. Overall, emerging advanced research technology provide support for the underlying mechanism of electroplating additives.

## 2.4. Electroplating

Electroplating was carried out in circulating cell with volume of 1 L and the circulating rate was 3 L/min. Phosphor copper plate was used as anode, while polished titanium plate was used as cathode. Before carrying out electroplating, titanium substrate was immersed in acetone at ultrasonic condition for 10 min to degrease oil and laterally was activated by 10 wt. % $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ . The current density used for electroplating was 30 $\mathrm { \sf A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ at 298 K for 40 s and the thickness of prepared copper foil was about 4.5 μm.

The growth process simulation of copper foil and current distribution simulation was calculated by COMSOL Multiphysics software. Electroplating module, coupled with surface reactions module and diluted species module, were used together to solve the growth process under the influence of ZPS. The parameters used in this work were obtained from experiments and theoretical calculations (details seen Supporting Information). Electrostatics module was used to calculate the current density distribution at high-frequency current.

The influencing effect of ZPS on copper electrodeposition was studied by applying cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS), while the nucleation and growth of copper foil was studied by chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM.

In this study, additive Sodium 3-(benzothiazole-2-ylthio)-1-pro panesulfonate (ZPS) has been systematically investigated for copper foil electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectra indicate that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM shows that the 3D diffusion controlled instantaneous nucleation and growth model is not changed but the active sites are increased by ZPS. Theoretical analysis suggests that ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and catch free $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ by -SO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> to accelerate the electro-reduction coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> through “bridging effect”. Adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed. Molecular dynamics simulation and in situ infrared spectroscopy verify the improved adsorption property of ZPS with increased cathodic polarization. A Turing oscillation growth model, validated by finite-element simulation and AFM, reveals that ZPS accumulates in valleys to locally accelerate growth, improving flatness via cyclic peakvalley transfer, but the smoothing effect is ultimately constrained by this oscillation. Structural characterization demonstrates that ZPS selectively promotes the Cu (220) crystal orientation and suppresses the (200) plane, while HRTEM directly visualizes twin boundaries, with lattice fringes showing a shift from (111) to (220) in twin-vicinity regions upon ZPS addition. EBSD confirms grain refinement (mean grain size reduced from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and a marked increase in twinboundary density, which together enhance mechanical performance through Hall-Petch strengthening and dislocation obstruction. Regarding copper foil performance, surface morphology is noticeably improved, while the optimal mechanical properties are achieved at 30 mg/L ZPS, yielding a tensile strength of 331 MPa and elongation of 3.78 %, attributed to grain refinement and twin-boundary strengthening. Finite-element simulation of skin effect demonstrates that the reduced roughness significantly lowers signal loss. Collectively, this work not only establishes ZPS as an effective single additive for industrial copper foil production but also advances the fundamental understanding of additive-induced structure-property relationships, offering a solid foundation for future additive design and process optimization.
# Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating
Keywords: Carbazole derivatives Nucleation process Through-hole electroplating Leveler Quantum chemical calculations

Electroplating additives, especially levelers of copper electroplating, are the most critical components of electroplating solutions in the manufacture of printed circuit boards and integrated circuits. A series of carbazole derivatives have been synthesized and used as levelers for through-hole electroplating. Electrochemical tests, theoretical calculations, and simulations were used to compare the various properties of the carbazole de rivatives. Among them, the carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB was preferably subjected to electroplating which was demonstrated by metallographic microscopy, SEM, and XRD. To further investigate the mechanism of leveler Cz-BPDB, the nucleation model theory was used to explain the phenomenon of flat and smooth electroplating surfaces. The electrostatic potential plot and the average local ionization energy plot were employed to analyze the active sites of the Cz-BPDB. Moreover, the galvanostatic measurements were applied to investigate the interaction of the Cz-BPDB with PEG and SPS. Therefore, a more reasonable through-hole electroplating mechanism was proposed in electroplating solution with Cz-BPDB used as leveler. This work introduced an excellent performance leveler and contributed to the continuing development of the copper electroplating mechanism.

With the wide application of 5G communication and related tech nologies, the miniaturization, lightweight, and high stability of various smart devices are increasingly valued and required. In this context, through-hole metallization in the manufacture of printed circuit boards (PCBs) [1,2] and the packaging of integrated circuits (ICs) [3–5] is one of the methods used to address the miniaturization of the devices. Copper, a low-resistance and high-conductivity metal, is also used as a through-hole metallization material for multilayer circuits to achieve faster transmission of electrical signals [6]. Therefore, to realize the metallization filling process of through holes, copper electroplating technology is proposed and developed continuously [7–9].

At present, the acidic copper sulfate solution is more commonly used for copper electroplating deposition [1], and the main components of the Virgin Make-up Solution (VMS) are copper sulfate (CuSO<sub>4</sub>), sulfuric acid (H SO ), and chloride ions (Cl<sup>−</sup> ) [10]. However, in through-hole electroplating, the orifice of through hole has higher current density and higher mass transfer [11]efficiency than the middle of through hole, resulting in very uneven metal deposition of through hole, which affects electrical signal transmission of the circuit and reduces the service life of electronic devices. Researchers have found that this problem can be solved by adding a variety of additives to the VMS, which has sparked increasing interest in the study of copper electroplating additives [12]. The additives of copper electroplating are generally divided into three categories: inhibitors (i.e. polyethylene glycol (PEG) [13–15], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [16] or their copolymers), accelerators (such as bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [17,18], or 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [19,20]), and levelers (i.e. Janus Green B (JGB) [11,21–23], Diazine Black [24], Alcian Blue, Safranin T [25], 2-mercaptopyridine [26,27], or 2,2-Dithiodipyridine [28]). With the synergistic effect of the three additives, a bright and uniform thickness of the electroplating inside and outside through hole is obtained. In previous work, our group reported aliphatic amine organics [29–31] and large conjugated molecules [32–39] as copper electroplating levelers, and all of these levelers performed excellently.

In this work, a family of water-soluble carbazole derivatives were synthesized in high yield. Electrochemical tests were employed to explore the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions. In theoretical calculations, molecular orbital calculations of carbazole derivatives demonstrated the ability of carbazole derivatives to adsorb onto copper surfaces. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations visualized the adsorption behavior of carbazole derivatives on copper. After through-hole electroplating experiments, the effect of compound Cz-BPDB as a leveler was demonstrated by various instruments. Metallographic microscopy was applied to test throwing power (TP) values. SEM and XRD were respectively employed to observe the flatness of electroplating surface and the dominant crystal orientation of electroplating layer. In addition, to investigate the mechanism of through-hole electroplating, nucleation model theory, molecular properties, and electrochemical properties were further analyzed. This work increased the options for copper electroplating levelers with carbazole materials as a new plating leveler and contributed to the continuing development of the copper electroplating mechanism.
## 2.4. Electroplating experiments

A double-sided copper-clad board with many through holes was used as an electroplating sample. The size of the electroplating board was 15 $\times ~ 5 ~ \mathrm { c m ^ { 2 } }$ . Moreover, the diameter and depth of through holes on the electroplating board were 300 μm and 3 mm, respectively. Before electroplating experiments, an electroplating board underwent a pretreatment process containing degreased by a degreasing agent, washed with deionized water, and acid washed with 10 % $\mathrm { H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } }$ solution. The middle of a 1500 mL Harring cell was placed into an electroplating board as the cathode, and two phosphorus-containing Cu plates were placed on both sides of the cell as the anode. During electroplating, a continuous flow of air bubbles was kept for enduring good mass transfer under 1.5 $\mathrm { \sf A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ current density and $^ { 7 5 }$ min electroplating time. The electroplating solution formula was based on the VMS with the addition of inhibitor (PEG, MW = 10,000), accelerator (SPS), and leveler (Cz-BPDB or JGB).

Metallographic microscopy was performed to show the thickness of copper electroplating deposition in the middle and outside of through holes to calculate the TP values of different formulas. The calculation method of the TP values is shown in Fig. 2. In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Sigma 300) was employed to observe the roughness of electroplating surfaces from various electroplating solutions. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D2 Phaser) was used to reveal the preferential orientation of electroplating surfaces for various electroplating solutions.

Potentiodynamic polarization curves were utilized to assess the ability of electroplating additives to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in electroplating solutions [32,44]. When the current density began to grow during the scanning potential test from positive to negative scanning, copper ions began to be reduced to copper and deposited on the cathode. The potential at which the current density began to increase was called the deposition potential. After adding organics as additives to the VMS, the higher deposition potential indicated that the organics were more capable of inhibiting the reduction and deposition of copper ions. In addition, a study [45] found that Br<sup>−</sup> had a positive effect on electroplating. In our studies, a series of comparative tests were done with VMS solutions containing the same concentration of bromine ions (Br<sup>−</sup> ) as a comparison sample.

The five carbazole derivatives and $\mathtt { B r } ^ { - }$ were characterized at different concentrations as shown in Fig. 3. The commercial JGB was characterized at different concentrations as shown in Fig. S1 in the Supporting Information. In the VMS without any additives, the current density increased as the scanning potential scanned from positive to negative from 0 V. And as can be seen in Fig. 3(a)-(e), the deposition potential increased as the concentration of carbazole derivatives increased. To exclude the effect of Br<sup>−</sup> on potentiodynamic polarization tests, a VMS solution containing $\mathrm { B r } ^ { - }$ was tested and the results were shown in Fig. 3(f). The deposition potential of the VMS solution con taining Br<sup>−</sup> was slightly larger than that of the VMS solution and much smaller than that of the carbazole derivatives (Cz-PD, Cz-BPD, Cz-BPDM, and Cz-BPDB), which implied that Br<sup>−</sup> had a weak effect on the depo sition potential. Fig. 4 shows the potentiodynamic polarization curves of adding 2 μmol/L of various compounds to VMS, which showed the order of the deposition potential (i.e. $\mathrm { V M S } < \mathrm { C z - T M A } < \mathrm { C z - P D < C z - B P D < C z - }$ BPDM < Cz-BPDB). As a result, it was obvious that Cz-BPDB was the strongest of the five carbazole derivatives in inhibiting the deposition of copper ions by reduction, and its inhibition ability was greater than that of commercial JGB, which had great potential as a better leveler for copper electroplating.

In electrochemical measurements, cyclic voltammetric curves were performed to test the ability of organics to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in the electroplating solution. The negative current density peak in the cyclic voltammetric curve was the copper deposition peak, which represented the ability of copper ions to be reduced to copper and deposited. While, the positive current density peak was the copper stripping peak, whose area represented the ability of the deposited copper to be oxidized to copper ions. The peak area of the copper stripping peak was positively correlated with the peak area of the copper deposition peak. Therefore, the smaller the peak of the copper deposition peak, the smaller the peak area of the copper stripping peak, which implied the stronger ability of the organics to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions [29,46].

The cyclic voltammetric curves of the five carbazole derivatives and Br<sup>−</sup> were shown in Fig. 5. The cyclic voltammetric curves of the commercial JGB were shown in Fig. S2. As seen in Fig. 5(a)-(e), the copper stripping peak of the VMS without any organic additives had the largest peak area, and the peak area of the copper stripping peak decreased as the concentration of the additives added to the electroplating solution increased. This indicated the carbazole derivatives had the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions.

To exclude the instability of electrochemical workstation instrumentation on electrochemical tests, the ratio of the peak area of the copper stripping peak (Q) of the electroplating solution containing different concentrations of additives to the peak area of the copper stripping peak (Q<sub>0</sub>) of the electroplating solution without any additives was proposed and adopted [47]. And smaller value of $\mathbf { Q } / \mathbf { Q } _ { 0 }$ represented greater ability of the organic additive to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in the electroplating solution. As shown in Fig. 6, five carbazole derivatives all inhibited the ability of copper ions to be reduced and deposited in this order of magnitude (i.e. Cz-TMA < $\mathrm { C z \mathrm { - } P D < C z \mathrm { - } B P D < C z \mathrm { - } B P D M < C z \mathrm { - } B P D B }$ ) and in agreement with the conclusion of the polarization curves. As shown in Figs. 5 (f) and 6, the $\mathbf { Q } / \mathbf { Q } _ { 0 }$ value of VMS containing $\mathtt { B r } ^ { - }$ was greater than those of the synthesized carbazole derivatives, which implied a weak effect of Br<sup>−</sup> on the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions. Meanwhile, all carbazole derivatives were stronger than the commercial JGB in inhibiting the reduction and deposition of copper ions. Among them, Cz-BPDB had the strongest inhibitory ability and had great potential to be a higher-quality leveler for copper electroplating.

Quantum chemical calculations were used to evaluate the potential of organics as electroplating levelers, and the results were shown in Fig. 7. According to the front-line orbital theory, $E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } }$ and $E _ { L U M O }$ were correlated with the electron-giving and electron-absorbing ability of the molecule, respectively. Higher $E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } }$ values represented greater tendency of the molecule to give electrons, while lower E<sub>LUMO</sub> values meant greater tendency of the molecule to give trapped electrons. Based on previous studies, a smaller value of ΔE represented stronger adsorption of organic molecules on copper [48,49].

## 3.5. Copper electroplating experiments and characterization

Based on the above results, Cz-BPDB exhibited optimal performance in the electrochemical tests, calculations, and simulations and was selected as the copper electroplating leveler to be added to the electroplating solution for copper electroplating experiments. Therefore, based on the VMS, various copper electroplating formulas were designed as shown in Table 2, and these formulas were used for copper electroplating experiments in order to characterize the through-hole filling properties (i.e. TP value), the surface morphology and the dominant crystal orientation of the electroplating surface.

After copper electroplating experiments, the cross-sectional images of through holes in Bath 1–5 were taken by metallographic microscope, as shown in Fig. 9 (a)-(e). The through-hole filling performance of JGB as a leveler was shown in Fig. 9 (f). The data from the through-hole copper electroplating experiments were shown in Table 3. According to previous studies, a TP value greater than 100 % implied that the through hole had the same thickness of copper deposited inside and outside the through hole, which was an important indicator of the electroplating filling of the through hole [39,44].

In Bath 1 electroplating solution without any additives, the TP value of through-hole electroplating filling was 52.87 %, which represented that the thickness of the electroplating in the middle of through hole was only half of which in the through-hole orifice, i.e., the filling effect was poor. In Bath 2 electroplating solution obtained by adding 200 ppm PEG and 2 ppm SPS to Bath 1 electroplating solution, the TP value increased to 66.57 %, but this still did not reach the desired requirement. In Bath 3, Bath 4, and Bath 5 electroplating solutions with 0.1 ppm, 0.3 ppm, and 0.5 ppm Cz-BPDB, respectively, the electroplating layers were dramatically improved. Among them, the TP value of Bath 5 was 104.77 %, which was in accordance with the requirement of through-hole electroplating. It can be concluded that the addition of Cz-BPDB to the copper electroplating solution increased the thickness of the electroplating layer in the middle of the through-hole. At the same time, the TP value of Bath 8 including 0.5 ppm JGB was only 64.11 %, which was far less effective than Cz-BPDB at the same concentration. Moreover, as shown in Fig. S4(a), the TP value of Bath 9 containing Br<sup>−</sup> was 58.94 %, which shows the ineffectiveness of $\mathtt { B r } ^ { - }$ in the improvement of through hole electroplating.

Subsequently, the effect of Cz-BPDB as a copper electroplating leveler on the surface morphology of the electroplating layer was further investigated by SEM [34,52]. As shown in Fig. 10, the surface of the electroplating layer obtained by electroplating deposition under Bath 1 electroplating solution without any additives was particularly rough and uneven with the presence of grooves. In Bath 2 electroplating solution with 200 ppm PEG and 2 ppm SPS, the electroplating surface was improved, but it was still obviously rough and uneven. In Bath 3, Bath 4, and Bath 5 electroplating solutions with 0.1 ppm, 0.3 ppm, and 0.5 ppm

Cz-BPDB, respectively, the electroplating surface was greatly improved and became smooth and flat. It can be seen that the addition of Cz-BPDB to the copper electroplating solution could make the electroplating layer smooth and flat. In addition, as shown in Fig. 10 (f)-(h), the improvement of the surface morphology of the electroplating layer by Cz-BPDB was close to that of JGB.

Meanwhile, in order to investigate the effect of Cz-BPDB as a levele on the dominant crystal orientation of the electroplating layer, XRD was employed to test the crystallographic orientation of the electroplating layer [39,53], and the test results were shown in Fig. 11. In Bath 1 electroplating solution, the dominant crystal orientation of the electroplating layer was (220) crystalline surface accounted for 100 %. In Bath 2 electroplating solution in the presence of PEG and SPS, the crystalline tendency of the electroplating layer was changed by adding (200) and (111) crystalline surface and the preferential orientation became (200). After adding Cz-BPDB to the electroplating solution, the crystalline tendency of the electroplating layer changed sharply, the preferential orientation became (111), and the percentage of (111) crystalline surface increased with the increase of Cz-BPDB concentration. However, the preferential orientation of JGB is (200) under the same concentration condition as shown in Fig. 11. It can be seen that the addition of Cz-BPDB changed the preferential orientation of the electroplating layer toward the lower energy and more stable Cu (111) crystalline surface.

In short, Cz-BPDB was superior to JGB in TP value and XRD preferential orientation, and Cz-BPDB was close to JGB in the flatness of the electroplating layer, which showed that Cz-BPDB was an excellent performing copper electroplating leveler.
## 3.6. Exploration of the mechanism of electroplating additives
Fig. 11. XRD patterns of copper electroplating layer in Bath 1–8.
To investigate the mechanism of action of the electroplating leveler, CA tests were employed to analyze the effect of Cz-BPDB on the reduction of copper ions to obtain copper nucleation. As shown in

Fig. 12, the red line was the instantaneous nucleation model and the blue line was the progressive nucleation model. In Fig. S6(a)-(d), the VPS electroplating system deviated from the nucleation model but converged to the instantaneous nucleation model in the VPS electroplating solution without the presence of Cz-BPDB. As in Fig. 12(a)-(d), the $\mathrm { V P S } \ + \ \mathrm { C z - B P D B }$ electroplating system further converged to the instantaneous nucleation model in the VPS + Cz-BPDB electroplating solution with the addition of 0.5 ppm Cz-BPDB. Among them, the instantaneous nucleation model was fitted well at the deposition potentials of −0.26 and −0.30 V. As shown in Table 5, D denoted the ion diffusion coefficient and N was the number of copper nuclei per square centimeter. After adding 0.5 ppm Cz-BPDB to the electroplating solution, D increased while N decreased, which indicated that Cz-BPDB inhibited the formation of copper nuclei $( \mathrm { i . e . } ,$ , inhibited the reductive deposition of copper ions). Meanwhile, this was consistent with the polarization curves and cyclic voltammetry tests. In conclusion, it can be drawn that Cz-BPDB could adsorb to the electroplating surface and prevent the reduction and deposition of copper ions.

The ALIE plot described the reactivity of the electrons in the molecule, where lower values of the average ionization energy indicated weaker binding and higher electron activity [39,50]. As shown in Fig. 13 (a), the low value of the average ionization energy (8.57 eV) was mainly distributed on the carbazole ring of Cz-BPDB, which indicated the high activity of the electrons on the carbazole ring of Cz-BPDB and the easy chemisorption to the electron-rich copper surface for electrophilic reaction. In addition, the ESP plot demonstrated the distribution of electron density, where high electrostatic potential values represent low current density [50,51]. As shown in Fig. 13(b), the high value (179.32 kcal/mol) in the ESP plot was mainly distributed on the positively charged bipyridine conjugate ring of Cz-BPDB, which indicated that the current density here was the lowest in the whole molecule. During electroplating, the positively charged bipyridine conjugate ring of Cz-BPDB tended to physically adsorb to the electron-rich copper surface to prevent the reduction and deposition of the copper ions.

To discuss in further detail the mechanism of additives on the filling of through-hole electroplating, GMs tests were used for solutions with different addition sequences or different rotational speeds [31,57], and the results of these tests were shown in Fig. 14. As shown in Fig. 14(a), at 1000 s, 200 ppm PEG was added to prevent copper ions from reductive deposition. This caused a sharp drop in potential $\left( - 0 . 0 4 \mathrm { t o } - 0 . 2 5 \mathrm { V } \right)$ and polarization. SPS promoted the reduction and deposition of copper ions after being added to the 1000 rmp-PSC bath at 2000 s; as a result, the potential significantly rose (from −0.25 to −0.15 V), and depolarization took place. When Cz-BPDB was added to the 1000 rmp-PCS solution, it also prevented copper ions from being reduced and deposited. A polarization and a modest drop in potential $( - 0 . 2 5 \mathrm { ~ t o ~ } - 0 . 2 6 \mathrm { ~ V } )$ were noticed. These showed, respectively, PEG’s antagonistic and synergistic effects with SPS and Cz-BPDB. The 1000 rmp-PSC bath’s potential significantly dropped (−0.15 to −0.23 V) after the addition of Cz-BPDB at 3000 s, and polarization occurred. Additionally, the potential slightly increased (from −0.25 to −0.23 V) after the addition of SPS to the 1000 rmp-PCS bath. It was clear from this that SPS and Cz-BPDB had an antagonistic effect.
Fig. 15. The additives mechanism diagram for through-hole electroplating.

As shown in Fig. 14(b), the PSC electroplating solutions were subjected to GMs tests under different rotational speeds of 1500rmp and 150rmp, respectively. The convection velocity was strong at high rmp. The smaller potential difference (Δη) between high and low rotational speeds indicated that the distribution of additives on through hole was less affected by convection velocity and more uniformly distributed inside and outside through hole. According to a previous study, the convection velocity inside through hole was lower than the convection velocity at the orifice [58]. Simultaneously, the current density at the through-hole orifice was high while the current density inside through hole was low [59].

Based on the above discussion and previous studies [39,60], a reasonable mechanism was introduced. As shown in Fig. 15, the red line represented the current density, and the higher density of the line represented the higher current density. And then, the blue represented the convective intensity, while the dark blue represented the high convective intensity. PEG was more uniformly distributed inside and outside the hole, while the main distribution of the leveler Cz-BPDB was positively correlated with the charge density (i.e., Cz-BPDB was mainly distributed at the orifice). Because PEG and more Cz-BPDB adsorbed to the orifice, the SPS lacked favorable conditions for adsorption at the orifice and adsorbed more to the interior of the holes under the guidance of high convective intensity to promote the reduction and deposition of copper ions inside the holes. It clearly explained the experimental phenomenon of increasing TP values in Fig. 9. Thus, a more reasonable through-hole filling mechanism was proposed for through-hole elec troplating with Cz-BPDB used for the leveler.

In conclusion, the synthesized carbazole derivatives were used as levelers for copper electroplating. Initially, Cz-BPDB was screened from five carbazole derivatives as the most effective leveler by electrochemical and computational studies. Hereafter, various formulations were designed to investigate the performance of Cz-BPDB. In Bath 5 with 0.5 ppm Cz-BPDB, the TP value of through-hole electroplating reached 104.77 %. Meanwhile, adding Cz-BPDB, the electroplating surface became smooth and flat from roughness as seen by SEM. And after, the dominant crystallographic orientation of the electroplating layer was (111). Further, a series of works were carried out to investigate the mechanism of action of Cz-BPDB. CA tests showed that the nucleation pattern of the VPS + Cz-BPDB solution conformed to the instantaneous nucleation model. The active sites of chemisorption and physisorption of Cz-BPDB were analyzed and localized to the carbazole and pyridine structures of Cz-BPDB in the ALIE plot and the ESP plot. Additionally, the GMs test results illustrated the preferential adsorption sites of the three additives in the electroplating through holes. Eventually, a reasonable mechanism for through-hole electroplating is proposed, which helps to promote the copper electroplating leveler to be further investigated and developed.
# Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection
• A novel safranine (SA)-based acidic sulfate copper plating behaves the excellent copper void-free filling of through hole.
Keywords: Acidic copper electronic plating Safranine Synergistic effect Through-hole void-free filling Molecule action mechanism

In this work, we develop a novel safranine (SA)-based acidic sulfate copper electronic plating process for through-hole copper void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection, and both the molecule actions and synergistic effects of safranine (SA) are carefully explored. Cyclic voltammetry experiments at rotating rates of 200 r/min and 1200 r/min demonstrate that SA itself can accelerate the electro-reduction of copper ion, heighten the inhibiting effect of polyethylene glycol (PEG) and acceleration effect of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS). The addition of SA to the virgin make-up solution (VMS) containing PEG and SPS makes the relative electric charge (ΔQ) between the low and high rotating rates be increased from 1.27 ± 0.04–22.53% ± 0.05, indicating the higher copper electronic plating amount at the center than that at the mouth of through-hole. In situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy together with theoretical calculations further illustrate that the molecule SA is adsorbed on the copper surface through the N atom in the aromatic ring, PEG and SPS can heighten the adsorption of SA on the Cu surface, and both PEG and SPS both synergistically influence with SA to achieve the void-free copper filling of through-hole.

With the rapid development of electronic products, advanced fabrication technologies for high-density interconnect (HDI) in the printed circuit board (PCB) are widely applied in 5 G communication, energy devices, wearable devices, and other booming fields [1–3]. Metallization of through-hole (TH) is one of the core technologies to realize the conduction of different layers in HDI-PCB [4,5]. Acidic sulfate copper electronic plating is the most universal process for the metallization of TH [6–9]. TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging and TH void-free copper filling are the two common metallization technologies. For the TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, only a homogeneous and conformal copper coating (about 20 µm) on its side wall is needed [10–14], then epoxy resin is used to fill the TH. For the TH void-free copper filling technology, copper coating is fully filled inside the TH without any void. It is worth noting that TH may crack under long-term heating due to the different thermal expansion coeffi cient between the resin and copper, resulting in the blocked signal transmission. Therefore, compared with TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, TH void-free copper filling technology behaves the advantages of higher reliability and better signal transmission quality. Nowadays, with the acceleration of communication speed, more heat is generated when the signal processing, the copper void-free filling of TH has therefore been widely employed for improving the heat dissipation efficiency.

The copper electronic plating is first performed to expound the excellent filling performance of the novel acidic copper sulfate electroplating process.
