# Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition
Keywords: Cu electrodeposition Accelerator SPS MPS Reduction potential

Organic additives play an important role in regulating <sup>fi</sup>lm growth and properties in Cu electrodeposition. 3‑Mercapto‑1‑propane sulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are representative accelerators that promote Cu electrodeposition rate. In this study, the formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS wa determined by measuring the equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reactions with the reference thiol/disul<sup>fi</sup>de pairs by <sup>1</sup>H nuclear magnetic resonance (<sup>1</sup>H NMR) spectroscopy. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS was 0.153 V (vs. standard hydrogen electrode). Based on this calculation, the cell potentials of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation reaction with either SPS or MPS, which is a key reaction in accelerating mechanism, were also estimated by ultraviolet–visible absorption and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectroscopies: they were found to be 0.202 V and 0.214 V for SPS and MPS, respectively. The positive cell potential indicates that the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes is thermodynamically favorable in the presence of additives.

Cu has been widely used as metallization material in the semi conductor industry owing to its low electrical resistivity and high electromigration resistance. Cu metallization is usually performed by electrodeposition, which e<sup>fi</sup>ciently yields high quality <sup>fi</sup>lms by a relatively simple and inexpensive process. Electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition typically contains small quantities of organic additives, which are essential to regulate <sup>fi</sup>lm growth and properties. Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate. Among them, 3‑mercap to‑1‑propanesulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are the most representative accelerators in Cu electrodeposition [1].

The accelerating e<sup>f</sup>ect of SPS or MPS has been explained by two mechanisms [2]. One describes competitive adsorption between accel erator and suppressor; the displacement of suppressor inhibition layer by SPS or MPS facilitates the approach of Cu ions to electrode surface, enhancing the deposition rate $[ 3 - 7 ]$ . The other mechanism focuses on direct catalytic reduction of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ion to $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ ion by forming Cu(I) (thiolate) complex [8–11]. The reduction of ${ \mathsf { C u } } ^ { 2 + } { \mathsf { t o } } { \mathsf { C u } } ^ { + }$ is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12]. Vereecken et al. reported that the amount of $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ near electrode surface is a key factor determining the deposition rate in Cu electrodeposition [13,14].

Herein, the formal reduction potential of SPS $( \operatorname { E q } .$ . (3)) was obtained, and the cell potentials of Eqs. (1) and (2) were estimated by spectroscopy. The formal reduction potential of SPS was obtained by measuring the chemical equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reaction between MPS/SPS pairs and reference thiol/disul<sup>fi</sup>de pairs, lipoic acid (Lip) and mercaptoethanol (ME). The calculation provides thermodynamic information of accelerating mechanism by either SPS or MPS in Cu electrodeposition.
Fig. 1. Linear sweep voltammograms of Cu electrodeposition with accelerators.

The accelerating e<sup>f</sup>ect of SPS or MPS in Cu electrodeposition was observed in LSV, as shown in Fig. 1. The addition of either SPS or MPS into deposition electrolyte increases Cu ion reduction current, indicating that the electrodeposition process is accelerated by direct catalytic reduction of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ via formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complex. It is notable that MPS exhibits slightly stronger acceleration e<sup>f</sup>ect than SPS at the same equivalent thiolate concentration, because MPS directly forms Cu(I)(thiolate) complex with major ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ , whereas SPS only combines with minor $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ , coming from the comproportio nation reaction between $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ and metallic Cu (Eq. (4)).

Cu(I)(thiolate) is formed by the reaction between $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ and SPS or $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ and MPS during Cu electrodeposition (Eqs. (1) and (2)) as proved by many studies based on the electrochemical analysis [14,18]. We veri<sup>fi</sup>ed the formation pathway in thermodynamic aspect by spectroscopic analysis.
Electrochemical half-cell reactions in Cu electrodeposition with either SPS or MPS.

In the conventional CuSO –based Cu electrodeposition solution, major Cu species in the electrolyte is $\mathsf { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ , not $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ . At this situation, there are two possible mechanisms for the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) in the presence of SPS. One is that SPS is reduced to MPS and then reacts with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ <sup>+</sup>. The other mechanism proposes that SPS forms Cu(I) (thiolate) complex with $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ formed via Eq. (4). However, many studies have shown that Cu(I)(thiolate) complex is formed via the latter mechanism, rather than the former [8,14]. Our UV–vis spectroscopy study also showed the same result (Fig. 4(e)). When $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } }$ solution was mixed with the equivalent concentration of SPS in the presence of Cu foil fragment (2 mm × 2 mm), a strong absorption was observed in the range between 300 nm and 450 nm, related to Cu(I)(thiolate). In contrast, the solution containing SPS and $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ without Cu foil did not show the complex formation, supporting that Cu(I)(thiolate) is dominantly formed via Eq. (2).

The thermodynamic information of half-cell reactions occurring in Cu electrodeposition electrolyte containing either SPS or MPS is listed in Table 2. We believe that the thermodynamic data obtained in this study will assist the mechanistic study of Cu electrodeposition.

The formal reduction potential of SPS was <sup>fi</sup>rst determined by using thiol–disulfide interchange reaction with ME and Lip. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS under the standard condition was 0.153 V (vs. SHE) in aqueous solution. The cell potential of the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes, which is the key reaction to explain the accelerating mechanism, was also estimated based on the formal reduction potential of SPS. The cell potential of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation between $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ and SPS was 0.202 V, and the reaction between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and MPS was 0.214 V. We believe that the thermodynamic values obtained in this study would be helpful in understanding or developing industrial Cu electrodeposition involving SPS.
# The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper <sup>fi</sup>lling
Keywords: Leveler Copper Electroplating Microvia Cracked Plating

A nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound N-(3-(5-Mercapto-1H-tetrazol-1-yl) phenyl) acetamide (named L) was investigated as a new leveler to develop the microvias Cu <sup>fi</sup>lling with or without cracked plating in blind via. The synergistic effects of L with other plating additives were investigated by galvanostatic measurements (GMs) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements. The GMs show that the Δη values (Potential difference at different speeds of Cu rotating disk electrode) are approximately 24 mV which usually suggests better Cu <sup>fi</sup>lling performance for the corresponding electrolyte additives. In addition, the optical microscope (OM) measurements indicated that microvias cracked plating was more likely to occur when there is no accelerator in the copper plating solution. The results of OM experiments also show that the microvia super-<sup>fi</sup>lling would not appear although the copper plating rate at the bottom of the blind hole is higher than that of the outer copper layer of the blind hole if there is no air agitation in the copper plating solution. The <sup>fi</sup>nest copper electroplating formula made up of the virgin acid solution (VAS) only added the PEP, L, SPS, Cl<sup>−</sup> was found and applied to carry out super<sup>fi</sup>lling of microvias.

Over recent years, the nano or micro-scale blind vias copper <sup>fi</sup>lling by electroplating has become one of the most practical methods for the fabrication of integrated circuit packaging substrates and circuit boards (PCBs) [1–6]. To achieve high-reliability interconnection by Cu <sup>fi</sup>lling blind holes between layers of electronic products is a long term and formidable task with high-density interconnection (HDI) technology. The super<sup>fi</sup>lling of blind holes is commonly regarded as an ef<sup>fi</sup>cient way and high performance with no void or seam during the microvia metallization process [7–8]. The super<sup>fi</sup>lling mode means the electrocrystallization rate speed of copper at the bottom of the blind via is much faster than that at the surface of the PCBs so called bottom-up deposition [9–10]. However, cracked plating that grows from the side and bottom of the blind hole penetrates the copper layer at the corners of the blind holes. It is often found as a serious fault in PCB industrial production, as shown in Fig. 1.

Cracked plating is an important reliability failure type of copper electroplating. It is manifested as copper cohesive cracks appearing at the corner locations of the microvias and will result in failures in electric and heat conductivity. The greater harm of the cracked plating phenomenon lies in its concealment. The conductivity of the copper layer for PCBs with cracked plating is usually the same as that of a normal printed circuit board at the early stages, so it is dif<sup>fi</sup>cult to be detected in electrical testing. However, some problems such as signal interruption and the sudden crash will occur and cause huge economic losses when the electronic devices and products smooth running for a period of time. Hence, there are urgent demands for developing processing guidelines for cracked plating that will lead to stable electroplating structures.

# Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating
Keywords: Printed circuit board Copper plating Levelling agent Small molecule five-membered heterocyclic compound Blind hole supperfilling

A defect free copper interconnect is crucial for ensuring the electrical connection and transmission of high density interconnect printed circuit boards. Leveling agent is a key regulatory factor for achieving dense cop per super filling from bottom to top in blind holes during the electroplating process of high-density interconnect boards. Here, two small molecule five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely 3- amino-5-mercapto-1,2,4-triazole (AMT) and 2–5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT), were selected to be as levelling agents to study their effect on the copper filling behavior on blind holes. Electrochemical tests including cyclic voltammetry solvation (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were firstly used to analyze the inhibitory effect of two leveling agents on copper deposition and it was indicated that the MMT has a more significant inhibitory effect on the copper deposition than the AMT. Subsequently, the influence of different concentrations of MMT on the inhibition of copper deposition and the blind hole filling performance were also further analyzed by LSV, CV, and constant current measurement (GM), where an optimal concentration of 7 ppm was obtained for the maximum inhibitory ability on the copper deposition accompanied by the best blind hole filling ability. The characterization analysis from the field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) also illuminates that the MMT leveling agent can effectively reduce the surface roughness of copper filled with micropores and promote the selective growth of copper coatings along the (11 1) crystallographic plane. The adsorption behavior of the levelling agent on the cathode surface during electrodeposition was further also studied by the quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics sim ulations combined with the in situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) experiments. It has been suggested that the thiol, sulfur, and alkyl groups in the leveling agent MMT molecule are nucleophilic groups, providing preferred active sites for adsorption reactions and thus generating effective inhibition ability on copper deposition formation. Thermal shock experiments based on tin immersion showed the copper layer obtained under the addition of the levelling agent MMT has excellent reliability. The comprehensive results indicated that 2-mercapto-5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT) was an effective levelling agent for the blind hole supperfilling.

Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores. In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid $\left( - S O _ { 3 ^ { - } } \right)$ groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. SPS and MPS are both common accelerator $[ 5 , 6 ]$ . During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth. Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. Traditiona levelling agents such as Janus Green B (JGB), Diazine Black (DB) Methylene Blue (MB), Alsin Blue (ABPV) [11–14]. However, these dye conventional levelling agents are prone to decomposition at high tem peratures, which makes the plating process not easy to control increasing the cost and also leading to copper plating quality problems. In response to the above problems, researchers have continued t develop new environmentally friendly high-performance small molecul copper plating levelling agents, such as benzyl quaternary ammonium containing compounds phenylacetyl chloride (BZC) [15], 2,2-dithiodi pyridine (DTDP) [16], 4,6-dimethyl-2-mercaptopyrimidine (DMP) [17], tricyclazole (TCA) [18], 1-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-tetrazole-5-thion (HPTT) [19]. # Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition
Keywords: Molecular structure Adsorption Butynediol DFT Electrodeposition

Cobalt electrodeposition is the core technology in chip manufacturing. Butynediol (BD) is the key component in cobalt electrodeposition. In this work, the molecule structure and adsorption ability of BD are successfully revealed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The number of transferred electrons (ΔN) value near 0, and the interaction between oxygen atom not alkynyl group in BD and cobalt, demonstrating that BD is physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface. The adsorption energy of BD on hexagonal closepacked (hcp)(101) is −0.67 eV, which is the highest adsorption energy among crystal faces, manifesting that (101) may be a potential preferred orientation. Then the effects of BD on the electroreduction behavior of cobalt is revealed by electro chemical experimental techniques. BD can inhibit the electroreduction of cobalt ions based on kinetics and decreases the diffusion coefficient from 3.43 × 10<sup>−</sup> <sup>6</sup> to 1.33 × 10<sup>−</sup> <sup>6</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/s, but the reaction is irreversible with diffusion control whether it contains BD or not. BD can make the charge transfer resistance increase from 241 Ω/cm<sup>2</sup> to 496 Ω/cm<sup>2</sup>. BD has some effects on the cobalt electroreduction kinetics, it does not change the instantaneous nucleation mechanism. Finally, the morphology, composition and structure of the cobalt coating are characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). BD can refine the grains and improving the uniformity of the cobalt coating. Although the properties of the mixed crystals have not changed, the preferred orientation has changed due to the addition of BD. A new peak of hcp(101) arises resulted from the adsorption of BD to form a retained surface, which are consistent with the calculation results. And the relatively positive values of stress change indicates that BD causes the internal stress of cobalt coating to be tensile stress.

Electrodeposition plays a vital role in advanced chip manufacturing as it is a key technology for electrical interconnects. With the rapid development of technology, the length of metal wiring inside the chip has been significantly extended, at the same time, the number of layers inside the chip has also continued to increase. To improve energy efficiency and performance, the size of transistors and metals must continue to shrink [1–4]. However, this process inevitably exacerbates the size effect (grain boundary and interface diffusion of electrons in metals), significantly increases the current load and resistance, and causes serious RC delay and thermal damage to chip performance. Metal cobalt has a small mean free path and low size effect, making it an ideal metal

Metal cobalt interconnect layer is mainly prepared by electrodeposition technology. In the process of metal cobalt electrodeposition, additives are key components that can adjust the cobalt deposition rate in via and trench, improve the uniformity of the deposited cobalt film, and thus improve chip performance [6–9]. However, due to the confidentiality of the technology, there are relatively few related studies and reports, but this does not affect its importance and application prospects. Li et al. [10] introduced that dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride could refine cobalt grains and achieve microvia superconformal filling. Huang et al. [11,12] showed that dimethylglyoxime had a strong suppression effect and made cobalt a three-dimensional nucleation. Wu et al. [13] discovered that Akyne-PEG4-amine could be used as an inhibitor to achieve nanometer scale superfilling of cobalt electrode position. Kiruba et al. [14] presented that butynediol (BD) would change the interfacial pH to regulate and control the formation of cobalt. It is worth noting that BD as a typical type-II brightener has attracted much attention among the many cobalt additives. Jeyabharathi et al. [15] deemed that BD would cause electrochemical oscillation due to the hydrogenation of BD during cobalt electrodeposition. Pan et al. [16] showed that BD and saccharin together could decrease the microhard ness of cobalt deposits as a result of increased grain size. Although it is well known that BD can be used as an additive, the effect of its molecular structure on the interface of cobalt electrodeposition has not been elucidated at a molecular level. Therefore, it is necessary to carry out relevant research. This study demonstrates the adsorption state of BD on cobalt surface and the effects of adsorption on crystal growth and orientation. This enriches the understanding of the role of additives in the cobalt electrodeposition process, revealing that BD achieves uniformity and compact film morphology through interactions with the cobalt surface, which is conducive to promote the development of high-performance chip interconnection technology.

With the rapid development of the electronics industry, an increasing number of consumer products, such as computers, electronic watches, wearable devices, smartphones, and communication equipment, are becoming more intelligent, lightweight, and miniaturized[1–3]. Currently, the most widely used technology in the through-hole plating process of circuit boards is acid copper plating, which typically involves a conventional acid copper plating solution containing copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, and trace amounts of plating additives[10]. Traditional electroplating additives can be categorized into suppressors, accelerators, and levelers[11–13]. In the context of through-hole electroplating, the key substance capable of enhancing the TP value is the leveler, which, as a crucial component in the acid copper plating solution, requires only a small addition to effectively increase the TP value [14,15]. As a critical metric for assessing the performance of throughhole copper plating, the TP value is calculated as the ratio of the copper thickness on the surface to the copper layer thickness inside the hole [16]. Copper plating process is widely applied in PCB and TSV industries due to its excellent conductivity properties and low cost. On the other hand, the miniaturization requirements of 3D packagings force manufacturers to adopt multiple layers wiring interconnection structure to reducing the interconnect line length and corresponding signal loss. However, these levelers are associated with a slower copper filling rate and can result in excessively thick copper layers on the surface. For example, the depth of the diameter of micro blind is about 100um and the surface copper is generally 20 \~ 25 μm, which is not easy to prepare fine circuit. In contrast, compounds such as imidazole and polyepoxides, when utilized as levelers, have demon strated advantages including a rapid filling rate for blind vias and a thinner copper layer on the surface [5–10]. The CMHT has a relatively small molecular weight and it contains thiol groups (−SH) and nitrogencontaining heterocycles. Considering the structure of CMHT tetrazoles is similar to imidazole as shown in Fig. 1, therefore, it is necessary to study the conditions for obtaining excellent blind hole filling effect by controlling the plating temperature, selecting appropriate current density and time, and making the additives in the plating solution have a high synergistic effect.

This phenomenon may be attributed to excessively high current densities can lead to a loose crystalline structure in the copper plating layer base on electroplating charring, weakening the adsorption capacity of additives and decreasing the performance of top-down hole filling [31]. Chrome plating has been highly favored for its advantages (e.g., high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance), whereas the environmental pollution and health hazards arising from hexavalent chromium in the plating solution have aroused rising attention.<sup>1,2</sup> Electroplated Ni− Co−P alloy coatings have been considered a promising alternative to chrome plating for their prominent thermal stability, corrosion resistance, and wear resistance, as reported in existing research.<sup>3−6</sup> However, several problems (e.g., severe hydrogen evolution at the cathode and unstable plating solution) during the electroplating process of Ni−W−B alloy coatings can trigger cracked coatings, lack of metallic luster, and inadequate decorative properties.<sup>7,8</sup> Accordingly, the electroplating process of the Ni−W−B alloy should be investigated in depth.

Additives take on critical significance in electroplating, even though they are employed in small quantities. They exert notable efects on the performance exhibited by the plating solutions and coatings. Surfactants are capable of reducing the surface tension of the plating solution such that the plating solution can spread more smoothly on the substrate surface. Moreover, surfactants facilitate the release of hydrogen gas adsorbed on the cathode surface such that the occurrence of pinholes and pitting on the coating surface can be reduced and a smoother surface can be generated. Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), i.e., a commonly used surfactant, can efectively hinder the formation of pinholes and pitting in coatings.<sup>9</sup> However, excessive addition can lead to rough coatings. Song et al.<sup>10</sup> investigated the efects exerted by three diferent surfactants on the performance of electroplated ${ \mathrm { N i - P } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { A l } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ composite coatings. As indicated by the results, the addition of SDS leads to optimal stability in the plating solution, resulting in uniform coatings with improved hardness and corrosion resistance compared with coatings with cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS), or triethanolamine (TEOA). The addition of brighteners notably enhances the glossiness of the coatings, resulting in a mirrorlike surface. Moreover, it can enhance hardness, corrosion resistance, and other properties. Zhu et al.<sup>11</sup> investigated the efects of thiourea, 1,4-butyne diol, and sodium saccharin on the electroplated tin−nickel−copper alloy coatings. To be specific, they determined the optimal additive formulation using response surface methodology (RSM), such that gun black tin−nickel−copper alloy coatings with excellent corrosion resistance, high hardness, and brightness were prepared. The use of appropriate additives can refine the grain structure of ${ \mathrm { N i } } { - } \mathrm { C o }$ alloy coatings, resulting in higher hardness. Furthermore, the addition of an appropriate amount of 1,4-butyne diol can produce uniform and bright Ni−W alloy coatings.<sup>13,14</sup> However, the addition of 1,4-butyne diol can decrease the current eficiency. Adding a suitable amount of auxiliary brighteners to the plating solution has been considered to be a common method to facilitate the distribution of the plating solution and achieve diverse coating properties. Matsui et al.<sup>13</sup> introduced sodium allyl sulfonate (ALS), sodium saccharin, and other additives to Ni−W alloy and identified improvements in properties $\left( \mathrm { e . g . } \right.$ , tensile elongation). The performance of the plating solution and coatings can be significantly enhanced by the addition of appropriate additives. 15−18

The efects of additives on $_ { \mathrm { N i - C o - P } }$ coatings in electroplating have rarely been investigated. In this study, the preliminary screening of surfactants and brighteners was conducted through single-factor experiments based on the basic formulation of the electroplated Ni−Co−P alloy. RSM was employed to design experiments and investigate the efects of additives $( \mathrm { e . g . , } \mathrm { S D S } ,$ thiourea, and ALS) on the hardness and glossiness of the coatings. Stable plating solutions and coatings with excellent performance were obtained through compre hensive analysis and optimization. This study aimed at providing more insights into the efects of process conditions and plating solution composition on the coating performance. It can lay a solid basis for in-depth research on $\mathrm { \bar { N i } { - } C o { - } P }$ and its composite coatings while providing a useful reference for the industrial production of electroplated Ni−Co−P compo site coatings.

# Influence of PUB2 on the Leveling Efect of Chip Copper Connection Electroplating: Mechanism and Applications

ABSTRACT: The copper connectivity technique is essential for achieving electrical interconnection in wafer level packaging (WLP), system in packaging (SiP), and 3D packaging. The essential processing material for copper connectivity is a copper sulfate electroplating solution in which organic additives play a crucial role in the regularity of copper electrodeposition. In this study, electrochemical tests, X-ray difraction, 3D profiling, and scanning electron microscopy were used to investigate the leveling efect and mechanism of polyquaternary ammonium urea-containing polymer (PUB2) in the process of copper electrodeposition on-chip copper connections. PUB2 has excellent polarization ability on the target surface, remains unafected by the sulfur additive SPS and poly(ethylene glycol), and displays a strong ability to regulate the copper deposition rate of through-holes and surface wiring. The waviness of the wafer surface wiring was reduced from 130 to approximately 70 nm after optimizing the PUB2 concentration, and the surface roughness was reduced from 10 to approximately 7 nm. The coating was dispersed evenly, and the rate of through-hole filling was improved by 57%. This study not only examined PUB2 leveling performance and mechanisms but also devised a research method and system for electroplating additives to facilitate the development and application of new electroplating additives.

Microchip technology has entered the post-Moore era, and chip packaging technology has continually evolved. Transitioning from two-dimensional packaging, such as the double-line inline and square flat packaging of the last century, we have now entered an era ofultrahigh-density three-dimensional packaging. Compared to two-dimensional packaging, three-dimensional packaging enables higher chip density, shorter transmission distances, and lower chip power consumption.<sup>1,2</sup> Copper is used as an interconnecting material based on its low resistivity and strong electromigration resistance. In comparison to traditional aluminum interconnects, the electromigration resistance of copper interconnects is improved by 2 orders of magnitude, significantly enhancing the reliability of integrated circuits (ICs).<sup>3</sup> Copper electroplating stands as a fundamental technology for interconnecting devices, including ICs, IC packaging substrates, and printed circuit boards (Table 1).

However, copper sulfate plating solutions often cause problems such as uneven coating, defects, and faults during microhole plating. Therefore, plating solutions often contain various additives for auxiliary plating, including Cl<sup>−</sup>, accelerators, inhibitors, and leveling agents to improve the plating performance of copper sulfate plating solutions and meet the plating requirements of diferent scales and diferent conditions to obtain an ideal copper plating layer.<sup>4−7</sup> Research at home and abroad mainly focuses on organic additives, such as accelerators and inhibitors. Additionally, dye leveling agents such as Jenner green B (JGB) have been studied extensively and organic amine leveling agents are novel leveling agents that have started attracting significant attention.<sup>8−11</sup> Dow et al. considered that the convection-dependent adsorption behavior of a plating solution can be used as an indicator to determine whether the plating solution is suitable for micropore filling<sup>12</sup> and Chang et al.<sup>13</sup> studied the leveling efect of 2-mercaptopyridine. It was determined that 2-mercaptopyridine has a stronger inhibitory efect on Cu deposition than JGB. Considering the complexity and broad variety of chip processes, there are diferences between the plating solutions used for diferent plating processes, plating machines, and semiconductor manufacturers. As a result, plating solutions are typically customized develop ment products. However, there are three main issues associated with the research on leveling agents both domestically and internationally. First, current research mostly uses theoretical calculations, electrochemical methods, and electroplating experiments to investigate the mechanisms and efects of electroplating additives. Unlike traditional electrodeposition, chip copper interconnection involves precise deposition in a narrow space or surface at the micronano level. The morphology and uniformity of the copper deposition layer have a direct impact on the electrical performance of the copper interconnection line, thereby influencing the overall chip performance.<sup>14,15</sup> Its characteristics mainly include small electroplating dimensions, dificulty in filling microholes with uneven current density, and high coating quality requirements. However, there is a distinct lack of comprehensive research on electroplating with structured wafers, which renders most research results unable to be applied in practice. Second, copper sulfate electroplating leveling agents are primarily composed of dye organic polymers such as JGB, which tend to generate significant pollution. With the development of wafer-level, system-level, and 3D packaging, the performance ofelectroplating additives is facing increased scrutiny and evaluation. As a result, the industry is urgently requiring the development of novel electroplating leveling agents. Third, the majority of the existing research is focused on developing independent research models for wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling. However, in practical IC manufacturing, through-hole filling and wiring are performed concurrently, which causes a gap between study findings and application.<sup>16−18</sup> Therefore, it is crucial to develop an application-based screening and evaluation strategy for electroplating additives.

To address these concerns, the efects of PUB2 on the electrochemical behavior of copper electrodeposition in a copper sulfate environment were investigated through cyclic voltammetry (CV) and chronopotentiometry (CP) experiments in this study. X-ray difraction (XRD) analysis was utilized to determine the crystal orientations of electrodeposited copper layers and assess the leveling process facilitated by PUB2. Additionally, Hull and Haring cell electroplating tests were performed to validate the mechanisms and efects of PUB2 leveling.

2.3. Hull Cell Plating Tests. Hull cell experiments were conducted to examine the efect of various PUB2 additive concentrations on the morphology of electroplated copper. A copper plate served as the cathode, and phosphorus copper served as the anode. The primary solution had a current density of 1 ASD and contained the following ingredients: 220 g/L $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } } , \mathrm { 5 5 ~ g / L ~ H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } } ,$ additive inhibitor polyethylene glycol (PEG)-2000 at 100 ppm, accelerator SPS at 4 ppm, and Cl<sup>−</sup> at 50 ppm. Electroplating tests were conducted with PUB2 additives at concentrations of 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, and 100 ppm.

2.4. Haring Cell Plating Tests. The leveling efects of the PUB2 additive on wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling were verified through the use of a Haring cell. The anode comprised phosphorus copper, while the cathode consisted of a wafer with a through-hole structure. Preplating was conducted for 1 min at a current density of 1 ASD, followed by 8 min of electroplating at the same current density.

2.6. Analysis and Testing Procedure. The crystal structure of the copper layer was studied by using an XRD device (Shimadzu XRD) after Hull cell plating. Following the completion of Haring cell wafer plating, the surface coatings of wafers plated with varying concentrations ofPUB2 were studied microscopically, and the surface conditions, thickness, rough ness, and through-hole filling height were observed and assessed. A metallographic microscope was used to examine the wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling. Additionally, a 3D profiler (SNEOFAR Sneox) was used to analyze the wafer local wiring and through-hole filling efect and characterize coating performance parameters such as wiring height, roughness, waviness, and through-hole filling height. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss SIGMA 500) was used to investigate the microstructures ofthe coated surfaces and grain structures of the coatings.

As shown in Figures 2 and 3, 0 to 100 ppm of $\mathrm { P U B } 2 ^ { 2 0 }$ was injected into VMS-Cl systems rotating at speeds of 100 and 1000 rpm, respectively, to examine the through-hole filling capacity of the PUB2 additive. Without PUB2, the results indicate that the copper deposition rate on the wafer surface is higher than the through-hole filling rate without additives and that the amount of copper deposition at 1000 rpm (i.e., integral area of the stripping peak) is higher than that at 100 rpm.

The results are reversed when PUB2 is added, and the copper deposition rate on the wafer surface is lower than the through hole filling rate, demonstrating that PUB2 has a stronger inhibitory efect on the copper deposition rate on the wafer surface than that in the through-holes. This inhibitory efect increases as the PUB2 content increases, and the growth rate gradually slows after the PUB2 content reaches 50 ppm. The PUB2 concentration in the through-holes is significantly lower than that on the surface of the coating as a result of PUB2’s strong adsorption on the surface of Cu and slow difusion into the microchannels of through-holes. 19,21−23

The CP curves measured at various rotation speeds are presented in Figure 4. The potential is significantly reduced, and strong polarization occurs when PUB2 is added at $3 0 0 \ s , \mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ is added at $8 0 0 s , S \mathrm { P S }$ is added at 1300 s, and PEG is added at 1800 s at both high and low speeds. Overall, rotational speed appears to have minimal to negligible impact on system potential, indicating that PUB2 acts solely on the electrodeposition process.<sup>24</sup> Following the addition of $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - } ,$ , SPS, and PEG successively, the curve potential stabilizes at approximately −0.71 V. The cathode potential negative shift rate and amplitude are essentially the same after adding PUB2 at high and low speeds, further indicating that PUB2 primarily controls the kinetics of the electrodeposition process.<sup>25</sup> Furthermore, in the presence of PUB2, the deposition potential at 100 rpm is lower than that at 1000 rpm, indicating a reduced cathode overpotential at the center of the through-holes compared to that on the surface after times > 1800 s. This condition is more favorable for achieving uniform through-hole electrodeposition.

The copper coating crystal orientation has a significant impac on how well the coating resists corrosion. Low energy, strong corrosion resistance, and high density are properties of the copper (111) crystal plane. As a result, the performance and dependability of electroplated copper coating are optimal when the most prominent crystal plane is the (111) crystal plane.<sup>26−28</sup> The copper plating layer XRD patterns for the $\mathrm { V M S } + \mathrm { C l } + \mathrm { S P S }$ + PEG +JGB, VMS + Cl + SPS + PEG + PUB2, VMS + Cl + SPS + PUB2, and VMS + Cl systems are presented in Figure 5. These results indicate that following the addition ofthe PUB2 solution, the peak of the Cu(111) crystal plane grows steadily stronger than that observed for the JGB solution. The most prominent crystal plane for the copper plating layer using the VMS + Cl + SPS + PEG + PUB2 system is the crystal plane (111), which suggests that PUB2 has a positive impact on crystal regulation.

3.2. PUB2 Additive Efects in a Hull Cell Electroplating Test. In general, a metal surface’s reflecting capacity increases with its flatness and smoothness. By examining the brightness of a metal plating surface layer, we can infer the flatness of the surface. As shown in Figure 6, regardless ofthe amount ofPUB2 additive, the coating gradually becomes brighter as the distance between the hull groove and phosphorus copper increases (polar distance), which corresponds to an increasing current density.

3.3. Efects of Diferent Concentrations of PUB2 Additives on Wafer Filling and Wiring. As illustrated in Figure 7, the flaws and roughness of the wafer slice coating are significantly reduced with the addition ofPUB2; however, as the PUB2 continuously increases, stripes begin to develop in the wiring of the through-hole attachment, particularly when the concentration reaches 100 ppm.

Figure 8 indicates that the PUB2 additive enhances the plating impact on the wafer surface and significantly increases the regularity ofthrough-hole filling. When PUB2 is not applied, the wiring edge has burrs, protrusions, and unevenness and the through-holes and closed holes have uneven filling. Wiring roughness and homogeneity significantly improve as the PUB2 additive concentration increases. The optimal efect is achieved when the PUB2 additive concentration is between 30 and 50 ppm. When the PUB2 additive concentration increases further, the coating becomes uneven and develops pinholes. Addition ally, the rate of through-hole filling slows considerably, leading to unsatisfactory outcomes.

The filling height of a single hole grew from approximately 3800 to 6000 nm with the addition of PUB2, representing an increase of 57%. One can observe that adding PUB2 efectively reduces the electroplating electrodeposition speed on the coating surface, which benefits through-hole electrodeposition and enhances through-hole filling uniformity.

The electrochemical behavior and leveling mechanisms of PUB2 during the copper electrodeposition process were comprehensively investigated in this study. The leveling performance and efects of PUB2 were validated and adjusted through practical applications combined with Hull cell and Haring cell wafer electroplating tests, providing theoretical support for the use of PUB2 as a leveling agent. Building on this foundation, a research method and screening and evaluation system for electroplating additives were established, providing support for the develop ment and application of new electroplating additives. The main findings of our study can be summarized as follows:

(1) The rate of copper electrodeposition can be controlled by PUB2 through its adsorption onto the surface of Cu(111), a process found to be independent of PUB2 mass transfer, as indicated by the results of electro chemical tests and XRD analysis. Conversely, PUB2 selectively influences the crystal shape of Cu electro deposition.

(2) The incorporation of PUB2 significantly enhances through-hole filling and wafer wiring efects. This is primarily due to PUB2 inhibiting the deposition rate of Cu atoms, refining the grain size, and promoting a more uniform grain distribution. The wafer surface waviness decreases from approximately 130 to 70 nm, the surface roughness decreases from approximately 10 to 7 nm, and the through-hole filling rate increases by 57% when the concentration of PUB2 ranges from 10 to 30 ppm.

# Efect of 3-mercapto-1-propane sulfonate sulfonic acid and polyvinylpyrrolidone on the growth of cobalt pillar by electrodeposition

Abstract: Cobalt is a promising material for electronic interconnections in the post-Moore law period. However, the vertical cobalt pillar is not fully compatible with the current electroplating-involved manufacturing process due to hydrogen evolution at the cathode and poor throwing power of the products. In this article, electrodeposition with multiple organic additives was employed to realize the fabrication of cobalt pillars. Electrochemical measurements were used to investigate the depolarization of 3- mercapto-1-propane sulfonate sulfonic acid (MPS) and the polarization of the polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) during cobalt electrodeposition. Notably, the competitive adsorption between MPS and PVP was verified and discussed in cobalt electrodeposition. In order to understand the adsorption and functional groups of the additives, quantum chemical calculations were performed to simulate the distribution of electrostatic potential and molecular orbital energy of the additives. Accordingly, the thiol group of MPS and the amide group of PVP were speculated to be the molecular adsorption sites in cobalt electrodeposition. The mechanism including three stages was proposed for cobalt pillar electrodeposition in solution with MPS and PVP. The electrodeposition of practical cobalt pillars with a depth of 50 µm and diameters of 60, 80, and 100 µm was successfully achieved by electroplating experiments, thereby promoting the application of metal cobalt for electronic packaging.
Keywords: cobalt electrodeposition, additive, cobalt pillar, adsorption

With the booming development in the miniaturization of electronic products in the 5G era, the system-in-package technology and chip interconnection have reached the scale of a single micron in recent years [1,2]. However, copper as one of the major conductors can hardly fulfill all the needs of functions including low resistance and capacitance (RC) delay and low bulk resistivity for signal transmission embedded in chips because of the inherent long electron mean free path, high thermal expansion coeficient and low efective resistance at the contact interface of copper [3–9]. Cobalt as an alternative conductor is an excellent substitute for copper in particular electronic applications [10–13]. It has been widely attempted to use cobalt as a magnetic alloy material for miniaturized magnetic electronic components, memory devices, and other special apparatus [14]. As a good candidate of alternative metal in the post-Moore law period, cobalt exhibits several advantages such as the low electron mean free path and low thermal expansion coeficient [15,16]. In this way, it is reasonable to assume that the cobalt structures from the compatible electroplating process will promote the productivity and reliability of cobalt formation. Electronic interconnection in the vertical section can be realized by metal pillars in three-dimensional (3D) packaging.

However, conventional pillar electrodeposition has not been widely implemented for cobalt yet because of the hydrogen evolution and poor electrodeposited throwing power [17,18]. In the cobalt pillar electrodeposition, the growth of cobalt along the wall of the hole is faster than that in the middle, leading to the overgrowth outside of the hole without enough cobalt deposition in the middle.

It is well-known that organic additives can efectively improve the quality of electroplating, especially in coating uniformity and filling completeness. Additive mixtures facilitate the super-filling of holes by adjusting the overpotential and the kinetics of plating in damascene copper electrodeposition [19]. The accelerator and various levelers were investigated in copper micro-via filling, and the convection-dependent adsorption of additives was proposed [20,21]. In cobalt electrodeposition, the cobalt nucleation and the morphology of nanograin were also afected by organic additives and electrolytes [22,23]. The group of additives for metal electrodeposition mainly contains accelerators and inhibitors. The selective adsorption (such as convection adsorption) of accelerators and inhibitors causes a higher deposition rate at the bottom of the hole than the rate outside the hole. leading to a complete hole filling [24]. The accelerator for metal electrodeposition, such as 3-mercapto-1-propane sulfonate sulfonic acid (MPS), is a crucial additive in the copper hole filling [25]. Previous studies indicated that MPS molecules adsorbed on the surface of the co er la er through the sulfhydryl group, while the sulfonic acid group captured copper ions in solution to accelerate the deposition of copper [26]. Cobalt performs close electron-donating and -accepting ability similar to copper so similar additives could be chosen during electrodeposition. However, current studies on the mechanism of MPS are still insuficient to explain cobalt pillar electrodeposition and the cobalt hole filling. On the other hand, inhibitors are usually necessary for metal electrodeposition. The inhibitor molecules can selectively adsorb on the surface of the metal laver or generate complex with metal jons to improve the quality of the metal coating and electrodeposition eficiency [27]. For instance, polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) undergoes a convection-dependent adsorption inhibition efect on cobalt electrodeposition [28]. The PVP molecule has great absorption at sites with strong convection (such as the upper part of the hole). In contrast, the sites with weak convection (such as the bottom of the hole) has relatively low PVP absorption, thereby making PVP a suitable additive in the hole filling for cobalt electrodeposition [28]. However, PVP brings an inherent suppressing efect on the overall deposition rate and the quality of the deposited cobalt layer, so the practical application of

PVP is hindered in the manufacture of cobalt devices. In this article, competitive adsorption of MPS and PVP in cobalt electrodeposition was proposed first and cobalt pillar was successfully realized. Notably, the morphology of cobalt particles was modified and the uniformity of the cobalt layer was improved.

In this work, the polarization of PVP and depolarization of MPS in cobalt electrodeposition were investigated by the electrochemical method. The corresponding competitive adsorption of MPS and PVP was discussed during cobalt pillar electrodeposition. Quantum chemical calculations for simulation on the distribution of electrostatic potential and molecular orbital energy helps to explain the adsorption behavior of the additives. The mechanism of three stages was proposed for the electrodeposition of the cobalt pillar. Furthermore, cobalt pillar electrodeposition was successfully carried out in solution with MPS and PVP by galvanostatic electrodeposition.
## 2.3 Electrodeposition

The cobalt electrodeposition was conducted in a 500 mL bath with a direct current from the DC power supply (INT-ERLOCK IPD-3305SLU). Cobalt electrodeposition was performed in the solution containing 0.3 mol/L $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } 0$ 0.57 $\mathrm { m o l / L H _ { 3 } B O _ { 3 } } ,$ and 0.84 mmol/L $\mathrm { C o C l } _ { 2 } { \cdot } 6 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } 0$ . PVP (100 g/L) and 1 g/L MPS were prepared in advance for the injection in the electroplating solution before electrodeposition. $\mathtt { R u O } _ { 2 ^ { - } }$ coated titanium was connected to the cathode of the power and 2 L/min airflow was used to improve the convection in the electroplating solution. Cobalt was electrodeposited on the copper layer on a printed circuit board (PCB) with photopolymer film after imaging transfer at a current density of $1 0 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } .$ . The depth of the hole in the photopolymer film was 50 µm and three diferent diameters of the holes were 100, 80, and $6 0 \mu \mathrm { m } .$ , respectively. A scanning electron microscope (SEM, HITACHI S3400) was used to analyze the morphology, while a metallographic microscope (ASIDA-JX23RT, China) was used to observe the top view and cross-section of the cobalt pillar. The crystal phases of the coating were measured by an X-ray difractometer (Rigaku MINIFLEX 600). The roughness tests of the coating were observed by a 3D measuring laser microscope (Olympus S4100) and the contact angle was measured by a contact angle tester (JY-PHa, China).

The efect of MPS on cobalt electrodeposition was investigated to observe the electrochemical behavior with electrochemical measurements. As shown in Figure 1a, the oxidation peak current density (from 1.72 to $2 . 0 8 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } )$ and the cobalt oxidation area increases when 7 mg/L MPS is added to solution I. The change of the peak current density and oxidation area indicates the promotion of the cobalt electroplating process. In addition, the potential during cobalt deposition is shifted positively, revealing that MPS with a depolarization efect accelerates the electrodeposition of cobalt. With the addition of MPS, the stripping peak current density further increases to enhance the depolarization behavior during cobalt electrodeposition. The GM tests were also employed to verify the depolarization efect of MPS in cobalt electrodeposition (Figure 1b). As shown in Figure 1b, the potential shifted positively from −1.476 V to −1.362 V after the addition of $7 { \mathrm { m g / L } } { \mathrm { M P S } }$ . This potential pattern indicates that MPS has a significant acceleration efect on cobalt electroplating.

The electrochemical performance of the solution with MPS and PVP is further investigated to analyze the com petitive adsorption behavior of MPS and PVP. The inhibitive efect and adsorption behavior of PVP in cobalt electrodeposition has been reported in the previous work and the oxidation peak current density reduces obviously with the addition of PVP in the solution without MPS [28]. In this work, as shown in Figure $^ { \mathrm { 1 b , } }$ the inhibition behavior of PVP is also observed in the solution with MPS because the potential sharply dropped by 33 mV after the addition of 5 mg/L PVP. In addition, as presented in Figure 2a, the oxidation peak current density decreases when 5 mg/L PVP is injected into the plating solution with 7 mg/L MPS. In contrast. the decrease of the peak current density in the previous work is higher in the plating solution without MPS [28]. Overall, solution II containing both 7 mg/L MPS and 5 mg/L PVP still exhibits an inhibition behavior on cobalt electrode osition although the inhibi tion of PVP is attenuated by MPS. Meantime, in Figure 2b, a current density of −1.6 V for the solution with the addi tion of both MPS and PVP is generall lower than the one with only MPS or without additives. The above changes of the oxidation peak current density, deposition potential, and electrodeposition current density are attributed to the dynamic adsorption status of MPS and PVP molecules in the plating solution. In the first stage, the adsorption spon taneously occurred after MPS was added to the solution. In the presence of MPS in the solution, the sulfhydryl groups for the transfer of electrons and sulfonate groups for cap turing the metal cations synergistically contribute to accel erating the de osition of metal cations [42,43]. However, the adsorption sites of MPS are partially replaced with PVP when PVP is added in the solution with MPS because PVP is attracted to the cathode surface and weakens the accel eration level of MPS. Therefore, the cobalt deposition rate on the outside of the hole could be relatively inhibited by PVP. Meanwhile, MPS, as a relatively small molecule, is able to difuse into the hole easily and accumulate in the bottom of the hole. As a result, the deposition rate of cobalt increases at the bottom of the hole.

Based on the above electrochemical characterization and quantum chemical calculation, the mechanism including three stages is proposed for the cobalt pillar electrodeposition in Figure 5. In the first stage, cobalt atoms are electrodeposited on the bottom of the hole and then grow along the wall of the hole with the formation of the cobalt nanoparticles layer. In a solution with MPS and PVP, cobalt deposition is suppressed on the upper part of the hole but the rate of cobalt atom deposition is promoted on the bottom of the hole. In the second stage, MPS and PVP molecules both adsorb to the cobalt surface in the presence of chloride ions. In this way, PVP suppresses the growth of cobalt, especially in the area with stronger convection when MPS and PVP are added to the plating solution. In the third stage, the deposition of cobalt on the upper side of the hole is inhibited more than that in the hole. In fact, MPS with a small molecule structure easily difuses into the hole so that it accelerates the deposition process of cobalt. As a result, on the upper side of the hole, cobalt deposition is suppressed but on the bottom cobalt growth is accelerated, thereby leading to the balanced deposition rate and successful filling for regular manufacture.

Besides, the amide groups of PVP mainly contribute to the HOMO orbital as a probable main electrophilic attack region. The cobalt pillars with diferent diameters are successfully fabricated with the use of competitive adsorption between MPS and PVP. # Synthesis and application of isoindigo quaternary ammonium salts in copper plating

Achieving uniform through-hole filling by copper electrodeposition is important for the fabrication of printed circuit boards (PCBs), and the development of suitable additives is a key process to realize eficient electrodeposition. Five isoindigo (IID) quaternary ammonium salts were synthesized using isoindigo molecules as the core skeleton. Electrochemical tests, theoretical calculations, and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated that the isoindigo derivatives have the ability to act as leveler and exhibit electrode absorption capacity, among which IID-C4-QL showed the best inhibition of copper deposition as well as the best cathodic adsorption ability The high through-hole filling and excellent leveling performance of IID-C4-QL were confirmed by actual electroplating tests.

With the continuous development of the information age, electronic devices are being more widely used, and high-density interconnection (HDI) printed circuit boards (PCBs) are one of the key components in the preparation of electronic products,<sup>1,2</sup> in which through-hole (TH) metallization is a pivotal technology for PCB electrical interconnection. Considering the economic cost and the performance advantages of copper metal such as good electrical conductivity and high electromigration resistance, copper electrodeposition is mostly used to realize uniform through-hole filling.<sup>3–5</sup> With the increasing technological demands in the field of electronics manufacturing, PCBs also need to develop in the direction of high density and high integration,<sup>6</sup> and achieving a higher level of through-hole filling presents a great challenge for the development of copper electrodeposition.<sup>7,8</sup>

In order to achieve the bottom-up filling efect without defects in the through-hole, the main option is to add functional additives during copper deposition,<sup>9</sup> which are usually classified into three categories according to the functions they perform in copper plating: inhibitors, levelers and accelerators.<sup>10–13</sup> Inhibitors are mainly polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), polypropylene glycol (PPG), and most of the large organic molecules with their molecular weights in the range of 6000–10 000, which mainly inhibit the deposition of copper.<sup>14,15</sup> The most common accelerator is sodium polydithiodipropane sulphonate (SPS), which is able to synergize with chloride ions to increase the rate of copper deposition and refine the copper crystalline particles, resulting in a bright copper coating.<sup>16,17</sup> Levelers are the most complex of the additives and a special kind of inhibitor, which can further enhance the dispersing ability of the plating solution and the flatness of the copper layer.<sup>18,19</sup> A series of dye-based levelers with large conjugation planes, such as diketopyrrolopyrrole derivatives, anthraquinone derivatives, 3,3<sup>0</sup>-bicarbazole derivatives, etc., have been reported in previous works of our group,<sup>2,20,21</sup> and it is hypothesized that molecules possessing good planarity as well as large conjugation are better at leveling.

The synthesized isoindigo quaternary ammonium salts (IID-QAS) were electrochemically tested to evaluate their inhibitory performance and convective adsorption, and the energy band gap and adsorption energy of five quaternary ammonium salts were calculated by combining quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations to analyze their adsorp tion behaviors on the surface of copper, and the better quaternary ammonium salts were screened out from them for the next step of the actual copper plating test. The TP values were measured by making metallographic gel of copper plated through holes, and the morphology of the copper-plated surface was analyzed by SEM and XRD, which was corroborated via the electrochemical test. The results showed that IID-C4-QL had outstanding inhibition performance in the electrochemical test, and had a leveling efect in the actual copper-plating, which visually improved the TP value, refined copper grain size on the copper surface, and made the surface bright and flat, and the optimum amount of the quaternary ammonium salt was 1.5 ppm. The use of isoindigo derivatives as novel levelers broadens the application scope of isoindigo dyes and lays the foundation for exploring other conjugate structures that can be used as electroplating levelers.

In this paper, five synthesized isoindigo quaternary ammonium salts were electrochemically characterized via cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements, potentiodynamic polarization, and galvanostatic measurements (GMs). A three-electrode system (rotating disc electrode for the working electrode, Ag/AgCl electrode for the reference electrode, and Pt electrode for the auxiliary electrode) was used for the electrochemical tests, and the virgin make-up solution (VMS) used in the tests was composed of 200 $\begin{array} { r } { \textrm { g L } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } , \ 6 0 \ \textrm { g L } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { C u } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } , } \end{array}$ and 50 ppm Cl<sup>-</sup>. In the cyclic voltammetry test, the scanning potential was in the range of $1 . 5 7 \mathrm { ~ t o ~ } { - 0 . 2 5 } \mathrm { ~ V } ,$ , and the constant scanning rate was 50 mV $\mathbf { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The polarization curve test was performed with 120 s of electrode pretreatment before the test, and the copper electrodeposition was carried out for a short period of time in a blank plating solution, with the scanning point set from 0 to -0.8 V and the scanning rate at $2 0 \ \mathrm { m V } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } .$ Galvanostatic measurements set the high speed to 1500 rpm $\mathbf { S } ^ { - 1 }$ and the low speed to 150 rpm $\mathbf { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , and testing was performed for 4000 s at a constant current of 3 mA.

Cyclic voltammetry is one of the commonly used methods for analyzing the inhibitory efect of additives on metal electrodeposition.<sup>24</sup> The negative peak in the curve represents the cathodic reduction peak of copper ions, while the positive peak represents the anodic stripping peak of copper. The peak areas in the copper deposition zone and the copper stripping zone correspond to the deposition amount of copper ions and the stripping amount of metallic copper, respectively, and these two quantities are directly proportional.<sup>25</sup> Therefore, the deposition of copper ions is represented by the positive peak area, and the smaller the positive peak area, the stronger the inhibitory efect of the additive on copper ion deposition.<sup>26</sup> The results in Fig. 3 show that at a concentration of 2 mmol $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ the peak areas of all six additives (including JGB) decreased compared to VMS, indicating that all additives have inhibitory efects. Table 1 calculates the peak areas of all positive peaks using integration, where the peak areas of IID-C4-QL, IID-C4- DMAP, and IID-C4-Bpy are all smaller than that of JGB.

The polarization curve can analyze the corresponding change of copper electrodeposition on the cathode surface, and the potential of the transverse coordinate of the folding point in the curve where the current density rises rapidly is the reduction potential of copper ions.<sup>27,28</sup> A larger absolute value of the reduction potential represents a decrease in the rate of deposition, indicating that the compounds are more inhibitory, which can be combined with cyclic voltammetry curves to mutually confirm the inhibitory ability of the diferent IID-QAS. Their reduction potentials shifted to -0.166 V and -0.171 V, respectively, consistent with the cyclic voltammetry data. In summary, five isoindigo quaternary ammonium salt derivatives were synthesized in this paper using isoindigo as the parent body to explore their application as levelers in PCB through-hole plating. The results of electrochemical experiments show that five IID-QAS exhibit diferent degrees of copper deposition inhibition, among which IID-C4-QL has the best inhibition performance and strong convective adsorption ability. Theoretical calculations and molecular simulations show that IID-C4-QL has the strongest adsorption capacity among the five compounds. In the actual copper plating test, the highest TP value of 120.77% can be obtained with the addition of IID-C4-QL at 1.5 ppm, and the SEM results show that IID-C4-QL can obtain the flattest layer at the same concentration, while the addition of more than 1.5 ppm will compete with SPS for adsorption, resulting in the ‘‘cavity phenomenon’’ and decrease of the TP value of the layer. XRD results show that the addition of IID-C4-QL transforms the crystallographic orientation of the copper layer from (220) to the most stable (111) crystallographic plane. The present work enriches the study of isoindigo on this field and exploits the great potential and scope of isoindigo derivatives for acid plating applications.
Synthesis of Quinacridone Derivatives and Their Application as High Performance Levelers in Electroplating

A series of quaternary ammonium salts base on quinacridone aromatic ring were synthesized using 2,9-quinacridone as the parent material, and their leveling performance were evaluated using constant-current chronoamperometry addition curves. Additionally, the adsorption abilities of the leveler molecules on copper surfaces were investigated through quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, and their specific adsorption sites on the copper surface were investigated by XPS, then the efect of concentration on the leveling performance was probed by through-hole plating, and the copper surface was characterized by XRD and SEM. Among four quinacridone aryl quaternary ammonium salts, DCQA-C -MI exhibits optimal leveling efects, serving as an excellent leveler with outstanding performance. This study expands the application scope of quinacridone aromatic heterocyclic quaternary ammonium salts and ofers insights for exploring eficient organic additives for copper electrodeposition.

With the rapid advancement of the semiconductor industry and electronic information technology, there is a growing demand for miniaturization, lightweight, and high stability in various intelligent devices and communication equipment.<sup>1</sup> Consequently, the manufacturing of printed circuit boards (PCBs) and integrated circuits (ICs), as well as the large-scale integration of chips, assumes paramount importance.<sup>2,3</sup> Copper metal, owing to its high electrical conductivity, robust thermal conductivity, excellent ductility, and stable chemical properties, finds extensive application in electronic chemical manufacturing.<sup>4,5</sup> Copper plating technology holds a crucial position in the production of PCBs, integrated circuits, and other electronic chemicals.<sup>6</sup>

To meet the high-performance requirements of electronic products, the filling of microvias with copper plating is imperative to achieve seamlessness or gap-free structures, referred to as “superfilling” or “bottom-up filling,” thereby posing a challenge to the copper plating process.<sup>7,8</sup> Presently, the copper plating process encounters dificulties in actual production due to the edge efect, wherein the local current density at the aperture opening surpasses that of other hole regions, leading to the formation of defective cavities.<sup>9,10</sup> Moreover, there exists a certain lack of copper layer flatness, diminishing the quality and reliability of copper interconnections and impacting the service life of electronic chemicals. Consequently, further investigation into plating additives is warranted.<sup>11</sup>

Plating additives utilized in acid copper sulfate plating predominantly encompass inhibitors, accelerators, and levelers, each playing pivotal roles in the copper plating process through distinct mechanisms.<sup>12,13</sup> Inhibitors form a polymer film on the plating surface, curtailing copper deposition, commonly comprising poly ether chain compounds like polyethylene glycol (PEG).<sup>14,15</sup> Accelerators expedite copper deposition in conjunction with chloride ions, typically represented by sulfonate compounds such as sodium polydithiodipropane sulphonate (SPS).<sup>16</sup> Among these additives, levelers assume paramount importance and are extensively researched for their ability to selectively impede copper deposition during plating, thus optimizing copper filling in vias and achieving a flat copper layer.<sup>17</sup>–<sup>19</sup> Presently, common levelers predominantly consist of organic dye molecules like Janus Green B (JGB) and DPP.<sup>20,21</sup> However, limitations such as planarity issues afecting adsorption performance and incomplete understanding of underlying mechanisms highlight the need for further research in this area.<sup>22,23</sup>

The unique structure of the quinacridone molecule, characterized by a conjugated five-membered ring and strong electronegative groups like the carbonyl and $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ hybridized N atoms, makes it highly suitable for electrode surface adsorption and efective charge dispersion.<sup>24</sup>–<sup>26</sup> This inherent potential motivated the present study to synthesize a series of quinacridone aromatic heterocyclic quaternary ammonium salts from 2,9 dichloroquinacridone, and these compounds were analyzed and tested to explore their properties in terms of electroplating.
## 2.4 Electroplating experiment

Copper-clad plates featuring double-sided and multiple vias were utilized as plating samples, with dimensions of $1 5 \times 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . The through-holes had a diameter of 300 µm and a depth of 3 mm. Prior to plating experiments, the plates underwent degreasing with a degreasing agent, followed by washing with deionized water and acid-washing using $1 0 \% \quad \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } .$ Plating experiments were conducted in a 1500 mL Harring cell, positioning the plating plate at the center as the cathode and two phosphorus-containing copper plates on both sides of the cell as the anode. Throughout the plating process, a constant current density of $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ was maintained for 75 minutes. An air pump was employed to ensure continuous flow of bubbles, facilitating efective mass transfer within the system. ABSTRACT: Electrodeposition technology is the key core technology for achieving micro/nanoscale interconnection in high-end chip manufacturing. Recently, cobalt interconnect structures have been the ideal choice for constructing electronic pathways in process nodes below 14 nm due to the fact that cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path compared to copper; thus, studying the electroplating filling behavior of cobalt in micronano scale space has become a hot topic in the field of chip manufacturing. In this article, an electroplating solution containing a new 5-alkynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor is designed for electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry. The results indicate that the 5-EP significantly inhibits cobalt electrodeposition. The change in the nucleation mode of cobalt in an electroplating solution with the inhibitor (5-EP) was revealed by chronoamperometry, where cobalt atoms nucleate in a three-dimensional continuous manner instead of three-dimensional instantaneous nucleation. In situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy is used to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. The energy gap value of the additive molecule obtained through quantum chemical calculations is $\begin{array} { r } { \triangle E = E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } - \bar { E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } } = 3 . 3 0 2 ~ \mathrm { e V } , } \end{array}$ indicating that the additive molecule has high reactivity and higher adsorption strength at the metal interface. The calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values imply higher electron density. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the adsorption energy of the additive molecule (5-EP) on Co(100) to be −133.96 kcal/mol, indicating that the 5-EP molecule has good adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments reveal that the addition of 6 ppm 5-EP to the plating solution enables defect-free filling of blind holes. Finally, it is also revealed by characterization tests (scanning electron microscopy/atomic force microscopy/X-ray difraction) that the inhibitor (5-EP) efectively reduces the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and, meantime, promotes the preferential growth of cobalt along the 100 and 110 crystal planes.

Damascene copper plating technology has remained the best choice for metal interconnects in logic chips and memory chips.<sup>1</sup> As semiconductor processes advance toward 10 nm and below, the use of copper as a conductor material begins to encounter issues with RC delay, which severely impacts the interconnect performance of chips. This has led to bottlenecks in process technology at the 10- and 7-nanometer nodes,<sup>2,3</sup> necessitating the search for new alternative interconnect materials. Researchers have found that metals such as Co, Ni, Mo, and Nb show greater potential than Cu.<sup>4</sup> However, when considering other parameters such as process and material costs, only Co is highlighted as a promising material. It has been reported that Co has already been used in the contact interconnect layers at the 10 nm node and is also considered suitable for use as a conductor in higher metal layers.<sup>5</sup> Compared to copper, cobalt has a shorter mean free path for electrons and a higher melting point. At the nanoscale, cobalt interconnects exhibit minimal size efects and superior resistance to electromigration.<sup>6</sup> The deposition quality of chip interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of the chip, directly afecting the chip’s yield, reliability, and stability. This places higher demands on the chip interconnect process. Electroplating technology is the primary technique for forming micro and nano interconnect structures.<sup>7</sup> In this complex process, additives play a critical role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metals.<sup>8</sup> Similar to the traditional Damascene copper interconnect process, the cobalt interconnect plating system also requires additives that can increase the metal deposition overpotential to achieve void-free superfilling in micro and nano structures.<sup>9</sup> The cobalt superfilling additives reported to date often contain unsaturated carbon bonds, nitrogencontaining functional groups, or a combination of both. The nitrogen-containing functional groups exist in the forms of amines $( - \mathrm { N H } _ { 2 } , \mathsf { \Gamma } - \mathrm { N H } )$ , oxime groups $( - \mathrm { C = N - O H } )$ and nitrogen-containing heterocycles. Utilizing the S-shaped negative diferential resistance (S-NDR) mechanism for ultraconformal deposition, Mofat et al.<sup>10</sup> observed bottom up filling of cobalt in 8 μm × 56 μm silicon through-holes. They achieved this by utilizing polyethylenimine (PEI) as an inhibitor. Jungkyu Kang et al.<sup>11,12</sup> found that void-free filling could be achieved even in low aspect ratio trenches in the presence of benzimidazole (BZI) and 2-mercaptobenzimida zole (MBI). An et al. demonstrated the potential application of nitrogen-containing organic heterocyclic molecules, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT)<sup>13</sup> and malachite green (MG),<sup>14</sup> as inhibitors. Their research found that the heterocyclic structures of the additive molecules preferentially adsorb on the cathode surface, serving as a mechanism to inhibit cobalt deposition. Huang et al.<sup>15−17</sup> utilized electrochemical methods such as EQCM and cyclic voltammetry to investigate the inhibitory properties of oxime-containing compounds, including cyclo hexanedione dioxime (CHD), furandione dioxime (FD), and dimethylglyoxime (DMG), on cobalt electrodeposition. However, the actual pore-filling performance and the micro scopic mechanisms involved still require further exploration He et al.<sup>18,19</sup> studied the inhibitory efects of polyvinylpyrro lidone (PVP) using cyclic voltammetry and other electro chemical methods, finding that PVP efectively inhibited cobalt electrodeposition, and that Cl<sup>−</sup> enhanced this inhibitory efect. To investigate the adsorption behavior of the inhibitor molecule (5-EP) on the cobalt surface, a combination of conventional Raman spectroscopy and in situ surfaceenhanced Raman spectroscopy was employed at diferent potentials. As shown in Figure 4a, the conventional Raman spectrum of the 5-EP molecule exhibits prominent Raman peaks at 1092, 1414, 1573, 2125, and $3 0 4 8 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ . As the potentia changes and reaches a specific value, the additive molecules begin to significantly adsorb on the cobalt metal surface, allowing the detection of characteristic peaks.
