As illustrated in Figure 4b, by observing the in situ surface enhanced Raman spectra at diferent potentials, it is evident that with potential steps, the peak intensities at $1 0 9 2 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ (ring vibration, C−H in-plane deformation shear vibration), $\mathrm { i } 4 1 \overline { { 4 } } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (pyrimidine ring skeleton ${ \mathrm { N } } { = } { \mathrm { C } } { = } { \mathrm { N } }$ plane bending vibration), ${ \hat { 1 } } { \dot { 5 } } 7 3 \ \mathrm { ~ c m } ^ { - 1 }$ (overall bending vibration of the pyrimidine ring skeleton), and $2 1 2 5 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ (carbon−carbon triple bond $( { \mathrm { C } } { \bar { = } } { \mathrm { C } } )$ stretching vibration) are enhanced. The ESP results also elucidate the impact of the functional groups of the 5-EP molecule on cobalt electrodeposition, providing insights into the adsorption and polarization mechanisms of the additive. As shown in Figure 5c, the ESP calculation results can represent the electron density contributions of the groups, identifying potential chemical reaction sites. The ESP values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values indicate higher electron density. In summary, the 5-EP molecule, with its acetylene group $\left( - \mathrm { C } \equiv \right.$ C−), can efectively adsorb onto cobalt, thereby inhibiting the process of cobalt electrodeposition.

In summary, this study employs 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and LSV reveal that 5-EP efectively suppresses the reduction of ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ . Additionally, electrochemical tests indicate the significant role of the ethynyl functional group $( - \mathrm { C } \mathrm { \equiv } \mathrm { C } - )$ in the cobalt electrodeposition process. Further studies on the impact of 5-EP on cobalt nucleation showed that in th absence of 5-EP, cobalt nucleation occurred through a three dimensional instantaneous process, whereas the addition of 5- EP shifted the nucleation to a three-dimensional progressive process. 5-EP efectively reduced the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and promoted the growth of cobalt grains in the directions of Co(100) and Co(110). The resistivity of the cobalt coating remained essentially at 10 μΩ·cm. According to quantum chemical calculations and MD simulations, it was discovered that 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP), which contains an ethynyl group $( - \mathrm { C } \mathrm { \equiv } \mathrm { C } - )$ , can efectively adsorb onto cobalt The adsorption energy of 5-EP was calculated to be −133.96 kcal/mol on the Co(100) surface, indicating its strong adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments showed that adding 6 ppm of 5-EP to the plating solution and electroplating for 5 h resulted in defect-free filling of blind holes. Finally, in situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy was employed to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. By observing in situ enhanced Raman spectra at different potentials. it was found that as the potential stepped, the peak intensities at $1 0 9 2 c m ^ { - 1 }$ (ring vibration, C−H in-plane deformation shear vibration), 1414 $\mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } }$ (pyrimidine ring skeleton ${ \mathrm { N } } { = } { \mathrm { C } } { = } { \mathrm { N } }$ plane bending vibration), 1573 cm<sup>−1</sup> (overall bending vibration of the pyrimidine ring skeleton), and $2 1 2 5 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ (carbon−carbon triple bond $( { \mathrm { C } } { \equiv } { \mathrm { C } } )$ stretching vibration) increased. This indicates that during the electroplating process, the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules primarily adsorb onto the cobalt layer surface through these functional groups, thereby inhibiting the deposition of cobalt. The contact angle test showed that the contact angle of the plated surface decreased from 99.7 to $5 . 6 ^ { \circ }$ with the increase in deposition time, and the inhibitor (5-EP) significantly improved the wettability of the plating solution which helped to improve the quality of the plated layer. This can indicate the efectiveness of using 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5- EP) as a single inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition.

# Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating

Literature reports indicate that existing synthesis methods for leveling agents often sufer from complex procedures, high environmental burden, challenging purification processes, and insuficient via filling eficiency. To address these limitations, a novel leveling agent (CDT) was synthesized using environmentally friendly materials through a simplified, cost-efective process that eliminates the need for post-synthesis purification. This study systematically investigates the influence of CDT on blind via filling performance in an acidic copper sulfate plating bath containing polyethylene glycol (PEG), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), and chloride ions. The chemical structure of CDT was characterized by Fouriertransform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and gel permeation chromatography (GPC). Quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that CDT exhibits stronger adsorption on copper surfaces compared to conventional leveling agents. Electrochemical measurements confirmed its ability to suppress copper deposition and helped determine the optimal working concentration of CDT. Electroplating experiments further demonstrated CDT’s capability to achieve superfilling, indicating its suitability for printed circuit board (PCB) manufacturing. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results corroborated the validity of the optimal concentration established by electrochemical tests. Finally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed strong interfacial interactions between CDT and the copper surface. These findings collectively suggest that CDT is a highly promising candidate for advanced leveling agent applications.

Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) are indispensable components in modern daily life. As current electronic devices trend toward lighter, thinner, and smaller designs, PCB technology is correspondingly evolving toward multi-layer and high-density configurations. In the PCB manufacturing industry, blind via technology plays a crucial role as it facilitates conductive connections between the layers of multi-layer circuit boards. Therefore, the metallization technology for blind vias is particularly critical in this rapidly advancing field [1–4].

To meet the high-performance demands of current electronic devices, copper electroplating in blind vias must achieve flawless filling without cracks and gaps. This typically involves superfilling or botom-up filling techniques, where superfilling refers to a deposition process during electroplating in which the copper deposition rate at the botom of the blind vias is significantly higher than at the opening and surface, thereby achieving perfect filling of the vias [5]. To accomplish superfilling, an acidic copper sulfate system is com monly used in industrial applications. In this system, the choice of additives is crucial, primarily including accelerators, suppressors, and leveling agents. Accelerators, usually sulfur-containing organic compounds, adsorb on the electrode surface, refine the copper crystal structure, and promote copper nucleation. Their primary function is to combine with chloride ions to achieve depolarization, thus increasing the cathodic current density [6–9]. The most widely studied and used accelerators include SPS and MPS [10, 11]. Sup pressors, such as polyether polymers (e.g., PEG and PPG) [12–14], mainly inhibit the deposition of copper during electroplating by adsorbing on the surface of the plated parts and preventing the difusion of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ [15–17]. In systems containing both accelerators and suppressors, the role of leveling agents is indispensable. Leveling agents typically include certain nitrogencontaining organic compounds [18, 19], such as the dye-type leveling agents JGB [20], DB [18], ABPV [21, 22], and heterocyclic non-dye leveling agents such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole [23] (AMBT) and 2-mercaptopyridine [24, 25] (2-MP). Their main func tion is to work synergistically with suppressors to inhibit copper deposition on the surface of the plated parts, optimize current density distribution, enhance filling eficiency, and thereby prevent premature hole sealing that leads to voids [25–30]. Although the most efective leveling agents are often commercial secrets, high costs and poor environmental friendliness in the market make the development of new leveling agents both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Consequently, to date, only a few superfilling leveling agents have been specifically reported [31–33].

The importance of leveling agents in superfilling copper electroplating has been corroborated by numerous researchers. Literatures [34, 35] frequently mention Janus Green B (JGB) as an efective leveling agent that not only enhances the fill rate of blind vias but also reduces the issue of protrusions during filling. Myung Hyun Lee and other researchers [36] synthesized a leveling agent containing two quaternary ammonium groups and hexaglycerol, which successfully achieved seamless and void-free filling of blind vias. Xu and colleagues [29] designed and synthesized quaternary ammonium salts of diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) with various aryl substituents. Additionally, Kim and others [37] developed a choline-based leveling agent, 1,5-bis(2-N,N,Ntrimethylaminoethyl) pentanedioate diiodide, used as a modulator in copper electroplating solutions. Meanwhile, TCA [23] and DMP [38] have also been reported as potential leveling agents. Their synthesis processes are complex, the purification is challenging, and the raw material costs are high, all factors that are unfavorable for industrial production.

This study, based on a comprehensive analysis of existing literature, aims to develop a novel superfilling leveling agent. During the synthesis process, dimethylimidazole, imidazole, and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether were selected as raw materials, and a detailed characterization of the organic structure of the resulting leveling agent was performed. By integrating quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, this research thoroughly analyzed active sites and adsorption behaviors to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between the organic molecules and the copper surface. Furthermore, the filling mechanism of the leveling agent was investigated using theoretical calculations, electrochemical measurements, and techniques such as Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS). Additionally, electroplating experiments were conducted to validate the filling eficacy of the leveling agent and confirm its suitability for specific requirements in Printed Circuit Board (PCB) applications.
## 2.4 Copper electroplating experiments

In this study, the blind hole test boards used were FR-4 copper-clad laminates, with dimensions of 5 × 12 cm, blind hole diameters of 140–160 μm, and hole depths of $7 0 { - } 8 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The thickness of the copper layer inside the holes was achieved to be 4–6 μm through chemical copper deposition and flash plating processes. The composition of the base plating solution used included $\mathrm { C u S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ at 220 g/L, ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 }$ at 60 g/L, and chloride ions at 60 mg/L. Polyethylene glycol (PEG 10000) was used as a suppressor, bis-(3-sulphopropyl) disulfide (SPS) as an accelerator, and the synthesized leveling agent CDT. The pre-treatment process for the test boards included (1) degreasing with an acidic solution for one minute to remove surface oils, followed by a one-minute water rinse; (2) micro-etching in a sulfuric acid-sodium persulfate system for 30 s, then rinsed with water; (3) soaking in a 3–5% sulfuric acid solution for one minute before transferring to a 1.5 L Hull cell for electroplating. A phosphor copper anode plate measuring $5 \times 1 2$ cm was used during electroplating, with the water bath temperature controlled at $2 5 ^ { \circ } C ,$ current density set at $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ,$ plating time of 45 min, and an aeration device activated to agitate the plating solution. A schematic diagram of the electroplating principle is shown in Fig. 3. After electroplating, a metallographic microscope (MD 50-B) was used to observe the cross section of the blind holes, and the filling rate of the blind holes $\mathrm { F } = \left( \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { B } \right) \times 1 0 0 \%$ was calculated to evaluate the plating efect, as shown in Fig. 4.

In this study, field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, model S-3400N) was utilized to conduct detailed scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of the copper surface morphologies under different electroplating solution conditions. To ensure accurate observation of surface morphologies, a dilute sulfuric acid solution was used to remove the oxide layer from the copper surface prior to the experiments.

To further understand the role of additives in the electroplating process, molecular dynamics simulations were utilized to provide valuable insights. Using Materials Studio software, molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to explore the adsorption of leveling agent molecules on the Cu(111) crystal surface. The Cu(111) surface was selected for molecular dynamics simulation because it is the most stable, low Miller index copper surface and the most prevalent surface. Additionally, the symmetric Cu(111) surface offers advantages for systematically exploring the potential energy surface of the adsorption system [46–48].

Galvanostatic measurement (GM) was employed to elucidate the interactions among the inhibitor (PEG), accelerator (SPS), and leveling agent [52]. Under a fixed current density of $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ,$ , various additives were sequentially injected, and the time–potential curves at diferent rotation speeds are shown in Fig. 10 for the base electrolyte. The potential diference $\Delta \eta$ (η100–η1000 rpm) at diferent rotation speeds can be used to evaluate the filling efect of the electroplating solution on micro-vias and is also an important parameter for assessing convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior during electroplating [53, 54]. If $\Delta \eta > 0 ,$ , it indicates that under strong convection conditions, the plating solution efectively inhibits copper reduction, allowing for perfect filling of micro-vias; conversely, when $\begin{array} { r } { \Delta \eta \le 0 , } \end{array}$ the rate of copper deposition at the mouth of the via exceeds that at the botom, likely leading to voids in the micro-vias and inefective filling. As observed in Fig. 10, after the addition of 200 mg/L ${ \mathrm { P E G } } ,$ compared to SMSE, the cathode potential drops sharply. This is because in the presence of Cl<sup>−</sup>, PEG forms a complex with $\mathsf { C u } ^ { + } \left( \mathsf { P E G - C u - C l } ^ { - } \right)$ [33, 51, 55] that can rapidly adsorb onto the cathode through intermolecular forces, inhibiting the reduction of copper ions [26, 56]. Before the addition of SPS, $\Delta \eta$ values are zero, indicating non-CDA behavior at this stage. At 1000 s, with the injection of 1 mg/L SPS, the potential of Cu deposition gradually increases, enhancing the kinetics of Cu deposition during this phase. At this time, PEG adsorbed on the WE surface is gradually replaced by SPS, and the potential at 100 rpm is slightly higher than at 1000 rpm, indicating CDA behavior during this stage. After injecting 5 mg/L CDT at 2000s, cathodic polarization is enhanced, and the deposition potential rapidly decreases. The cathodic potential difference $\Delta \eta$ between 100 and 1000 rpm for CDT (20 mV) is significantly greater than that reported in the literature for JGB (4.8 mV) [57], suggesting that CDT exhibits beter CDA behavior than JGB. When PEG and Cl<sup>−</sup> coexist, CDT efectively inhibits the accelerating activity of SPS in copper deposition. High-speed electrodes exhibit stronger cathodic polarization than slow-speed electrodes. That ${ \mathrm { i } } s ,$ the higher the rotation speed, the greater the inhibitory efect of CDT on copper deposition, with the copper reduction rate at the botom of the micro-via exceeding that at the mouth. These phenomena are consistent with previous results discussed in cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry, further proving the efectiveness of CDT in filling micro-vias without gaps. CDT can be selected as the leveling agent for micro-via electroplating fill applications.
## 3.4 Electroplating experimental analysis

Based on the research and analysis presented, it can be inferred that CDT can serve as a leveling agent for micro-via filling in PCBs. To evaluate the filling efficacy of CDT as a leveling agent, electroplating experiments were conducted at various concentrations of CDT and compared with a commercial JGB formulation. Figure 11 shows the cross-sectional optical microscopy images of the micro-vias after electroplating. As depicted in Fig. 11a, without the addition of a leveling agent, a significant void is observed at the botom of the via, resulting from uneven current density due to varying convection intensities. With the injection of 1 mg/L CDT, the filling performance of the micro-vias notably improves. As illustrated in Figs. 11b–f, the optimal micro-via filling performance occurs at a CDT concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with the previous electrochemical testing results. When the CDT concentration is increased to 6 mg/L, the filling rate decreases, and the performance deteriorates, indicating that there is a specific operational concentration range for the leveling agent. If the concentration is too low, the inhibitory efect is insuficient, leading to void formation. Conversely, if the concen tration is too high, it disrupts the balance among the additives, resulting in poor filling performance. The JGB electroplating formula, commonly used in the industry, serves as a benchmark for comparing the filling performance of newly discovered leveling agents. Figure 11h shows the filling efect using the commercial JGB electroplating solution, which is inferior to the efect achieved with 5 mg/L CDT. The JGB formula results in some concavity and does not completely fill the blind vias, whereas CDT achieves superfilling of micro-vias, demonstrating its potential as an efective leveling agent.

The influence of different concentrations of CDT on the surface morphology of copper is depicted in Fig. 12. In the absence of CDT in the plating solution, the copper plating surface exhibits a rough, blocky, and distinctly porous appearance. Conversely, compared to the CDT-free condition, the addition of varying concentrations of CDT to the plating solution significantly improves the surface morphology of the copper plating (Figs. 12b–h). The formation of smooth planes is due to the modification of the plating layer after adding CDT, which initiates crystal refinement. However, when the CDT concentration is increased to 5 mg/L, a proliferation of small blocky crystals appears on the copper surface, becoming denser with increasing concentrations of CDT. These results indicate that CDT demonstrates its leveling capability efectively within a certain concentration range, but as the concentration of the leveling agent increases, the synergistic interactions among the additives are disrupted. Similar results have been reported in copper electrodepositing studies [18, 21].

While molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and XPS ofer diferent perspectives—thermodynamic interaction versus chemical bonding—they provide complementary evidence supporting the strong adsorption of CDT on the copper surface. Figure 13a displays the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) full spectrum of a copper sample after soaking for 40 min in an electroplating solution containing CDT. This full spectrum, obtained through detailed scanning, reveals the presence of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and copper on the copper surface, confirming the adsorption of CDT. Detailed spectra for Cu2p3/2, C1s, and N1s can be found in Figs. 13b–d. In Fig. 13b, the chemi cal states on the copper surface are shown by the peaks of Cu2p3/2 and Cu2p1/2, located at binding energies of 931.8 and 951.6 eV, respectively. The Cu2p3/2 peak in Fig. 13b can be further divided into subpeaks for Cu<sub>2</sub>O (931.8 eV) and CuO (933.7 eV) [58], indicating the formation of a copper oxide layer on the copper surface due to oxidation in air and reaction with water molecules in the solution, predominantly in the form of Cu O [59]. Figure 13c focuses on the N1s spectrum, displaying two peaks at 397.8 eV (C–N or C=N) and 399.2 eV (Cu–N), which deviate slightly from the nitrogen binding energies reported in previous literature, suggesting the possible formation of structures such as Cu–N–C or Cu–N=C on the CDT-modified copper surface [60–62]. The C1s spectrum (seen in Fig. 13d) reveals six diferent peaks corresponding to 283.66 eV (C=C), 284.03 eV (C–C), 284.42 eV (C–H), 284.92 eV (C–N), 285.9 eV (C–O), and 287.63 eV (C=O) [63–65]. The presence of these peaks indicates a rich variety of carbon environments within the CDT molecule, such as double bonds between carbons, single bonds, combinations of carbon with hydrogen, and carbon with nitrogen, providing crucial clues for understanding how CDT achieves adsorption on the copper surface.

In summary, we have selected the nitrogen-heterocyclic compound CDT as an electroplating leveling agent for copper micro-via filling. The synthesis of CDT was successfully confirmed by infrared, hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography results. Quantum chemical simulations suggest that CDT possesses the potential to occupy metal vacant orbitals for adsorption. Moreover, molecular dynamics simulations indicate that CDT exhibits strong affinity for copper surfaces. Electrochemical tests revealed that the optimal working concentration of CDT is 5 mg/L. Chronopotentiometric measurements further demonstrated that CDT can synergistically suppress copper deposition when combined with other additives, exhibiting a potential diference as high as 20 mV, which indicates its strong inhibitory efect on copper electrodeposition. Electroplating tests show that the best plating results occur at a concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with electrochemical findings. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) results showed that CDT can refine copper grain structures within an appropriate concentration range; however, when the concentration exceeds the optimal level, crystal agglomeration reoccurs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed the efective adsorption of CDT on the copper surface, and the strong interaction between them provides a foundation for the suppression of copper deposition. Collectively, our research conclusively proves that CDT is a promising leveling agent for copper micro-via filling, providing theoretical guidance for the discovery and improvement of electroplating technologies for micro-via filling.
# Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler
Keywords: Coumarin Structural modification Electroplating leveler Electrochemical analysis Electroplating additive interaction

In this paper, five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts, including a new highly efficient through-hole (TH) electroplating leveler, were synthesized from environmentally harmless coumarin compounds. The inhib itory properties of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were tested by electrochemical method, leading to the selection of the optimal leveler (C2). The adsorption capacity, adsorption state and adsorption sites of different coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts on copper surface were systematically analyzed, and the reasons for the different inhibition capacity of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts with different molecular structures were explained. The effect of C2 content on throwing power (TP) was studied, when C2 content was only 0.6 ppm, TP value was greater than 100 %. The adsorption behavior of C2 on copper cathode and the interaction between C2 and other additives were studied by the galvanostatic measurements (GMs). SEM and XRD tests were conducted to analyze the effects of different amounts of C2 on the copper plating surface.

With the continuous improvement of the modern electronic indus try’s requirements for electronic components, the demand for electronic components such as electronic chips that achieve miniaturization and high efficiency has also increased. The realization of high-density interconnection between printed circuit boards (PCBs) through micropore connection is an important means to realize the miniaturization of electronic products, so as to obtain more excellent electrical conductivity and space performance [1–3]. Acid copper electroplating is a key technology for copper interconnects in through-holes (THs), and it is also an indispensable technology in the manufacturing process of PCB. In order to obtain a flat and smooth plating layer and efficient TH filling, electroplating additives need to be added to the electroplating solution [4,5].

Electroplating additives are generally divided into inhibitors (generally polyethylene glycol and other polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol, polypropylene glycol [6,7]), accelerators (generally containing S–H bonds or S–S sulfonate compounds, such as sodium 3,3′-dithiodipropane sulfonate, bis-(sodium sulfoethyl)-disulfide [8,9]) and levelers (generally N-containing compounds, such as Janus Green B, diketopyrrolopyrrole [10–16]).

In the process of copper plating, through the interaction of different plating additives, the microhole can be overfilled. In the current research on electroplating additives, electroplating levelers have attracted much attention due to their irreplaceable properties. The leveler is mainly adsorbed on the surface of TH and inhibits the deposition of copper ions on the surface of TH, but has less inhibition on the deposition of copper ions inside TH, so as to achieve the effect of conductive copper interconnection or bottom-up copper electroplating [17–19]. The current research on levelers mainly includes the research of new leveler molecules (small molecule compounds [20–22], quaternary ammonium compounds [23–26] and macromolecular polymers [27,28]), interaction of different electroplating additives [29] and the effect of leveler concentration on filling efficiency and copper electroplating surface morphology [30]. Among them, quaternary ammonium salts have received more attention as leveler due to their superior leveling performance. For example, Myung JunKim [31] synthesized choline-based quaternary ammonium salt levelers and used them in TSV (Through Silicon Via) electrodeposition copper, Jinge Lv [32] designed and synthesized three water-soluble naphthalimide derivatives (NPI) and used them as levelers for microporous electrodeposition. Van Quy Dinh [33] used sulfonated diallyl dimethyl ammonium bromide copol ymer to fill the TSV bottom-up electrodeposition for 5 min to achieve no gaps. These studies have shown that quaternary ammonium compounds have good application prospects in the field of electroplating levelers, but it is still a difficult task to develop electroplating levelers with small additive amount, good leveling effect and environmental friendliness.

In our previous work, we found that the large plane quaternary ammonium salt leveler has more efficient leveling performance than the general quaternary ammonium salts, when the concentration is 0.2 ppm (0.278 μmol/L), a very efficient leveling effect can be achieved [34]. Combining the previous work, and the working principle of the leveler −- the leveler molecules are adsorbed on the copper surface during the electrodeposition process to inhibit the electrodeposition of copper ions [14,34,35], we speculate that $^ { 4 , }$ 4-bipyridine can be used to connect rigid planar molecules to synthesize larger coplanar quaternary ammonium salts. If such large flat molecules can be adsorbed on copper surfaces, they have the potential to be effective levelers [15,34]. As a common natural product, coumarins (Fig. 1) are planar compounds with two conjugated six-membered rings, and its $^ { 7 }$ position is relatively electron-rich, indicating that its $^ { 7 }$ position is prone to electrophilic substitution reaction. When a hydroxyl group is present, it is easy to undergo substitution reaction with dibromoalkane, thereby further reacting with $^ { 4 , }$ 4-bipyridine to obtain a coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salt.

Herein, five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were synthesized by connecting coumarin-based compounds with pyridine-like compounds, including the first synthesis of large plane dicoumarinbased pyridinium quaternary ammonium salt C2 through a four-step reaction. The results of cyclic voltammetry (CV) test and polarization curve test show that C2 can be used as the preferred leveler. The band gap and electron cloud density distribution of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were obtained by quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics simulation, in order to study the relationship between the molecular structure and inhibitory ability of these levelers. The experimental results of TH copper plating show that in a certain range, the content of C2 has a positive correlation with the TP value of TH electroplating, and can make the surface morphology of copper plating layer more smooth, and optimize the orientation of the crystal surface of copper particles. GMs results show that C2 can exert inhibition alone and has strong convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior. C2 has competitive adsorption with SPS, no interaction with Cl<sup>-</sup>, and synergistic inhibition with PEG to form stable PEG-C2 complexes. This study expanded the application of coumarin derivatives and the design range of electroplating leveler molecules, hoping to provide some reference ideas for the development of more efficient levele molecules in the future.

Sections of the PCB board after electro deposition were made into a metallographic section, and the throwing power (TP) of the copper boards was observed using a metallographic microscope (zeiss, Axio Observer A1m). The five compounds were paired with 200 ppm PEG and 2 ppm SPS, respectively, and the results of TH electroplating are shown in Fig. 10.

Based on the above results, leveler C2 has the strongest copper plating inhibition ability, so C2 was selected as the preferred leveler for application in actual through-hole copper plating, and the effect of different additions of C2 on the filling ability was investigated.

GMs can simulate the convection inside and on the surface of the though-hole during the actual through hole electroplating by rotating the disc electrode at different speeds, and test the potential difference after adding different additives to VMS, so as to analyze the effect of different additives and the interaction between additives. ## 3.6. Effect of leveler C2 on the surface of copper electroplating layer

The surface morphology of the copper plating layer is also the focus of the PCB manufacturing process. SEM test and XRD test can well observe the microscopic surface morphology of the copper plating layer, and analyze the size of copper grains by testing the crystallographic plane orientation of the copper plating layer.

# Integrated Electrochemical and Computational Elucidation of Nitro Blue Tetrazolium Chloride as an Efficient Leveler for Copper Microvia Superfilling

Abstract: Levelers are indispensable additives for achieving void-free, bottom-up superconformal copper filling of microvias. Establishing the molecular-level correlation between leveler structure and performance is therefore essential to the continued advancement of microelectronic copper-plating technology. Herein, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT) is identified as an efficient leveler for copper microvia superfilling. A multiscale strategy—combining electrochemical measurements, X-ray photoelectron spec troscopy (XPS), density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—is employed to elucidate the action mechanism of NBT and pinpoint its electroactive sites. Electrochemical tests show that NBT markedly suppresses copper deposition and, together with polyethylene glycol (PEG), effectively resists competitive ad sorption by bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), thereby enhancing the microvia superfilling performance of the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system. DFT results reveal that the nitro groups and tetrazolium rings constitute the primary adsorption centers on the copper surface; the nitro groups additionally strengthen intermolecular interactions between NBT and PEG. MD simulations further confirm that NBT anchors onto the Cu(111) surface predominantly through these $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and the tetrazolium ring, while co-adsorbed PEG enhances the overall adsorption strength of NBT. The electroplating experiment demonstrates that NBT can act as an effective leveler for microvia superfilling. Moreover, XPS analyses further confirm the synergistic co-adsorption of NBT and PEG and verify that the $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and tetrazolium rings are the dominant adsorption sites of NBT. Collectively, the electroplating, XPS, electrochemical, DFT, and MD findings clarify the structure–activity relationship of NBT and provide rational guidelines for designing next-generation copper-plating levelers.
Keywords: microvias filling; electroplating leveler; copper electroplating; quantum chemical calculation; molecular dynamics simulations

Electrochemical copper deposition offers distinct advantages for constructing microand nano-scale features and is therefore indispensable in manufacturing advanced interconnects such as integrated circuits (ICs) [1,2]. For high-aspect-ratio structures—including Damascene trenches in ICs and microvias in substrates and printed-circuit boards (PCBs)— voids generated during plating remain a persistent threat to electrical performance and reliability [3,4]. Eliminating these defects has therefore become a primary objective in microvia electroplating [5,6].

Industrial practice predominantly relies on organic additive systems to locally regulate the deposition rate for achieving superfilling of microvias. In two-component systems the competitive adsorption of a suppressor and an accelerator is often sufficient for sub-100 nm Damascene features [7–9]; larger microvias, however, require a third component—a leveler— to suppress copper deposition at high-current-density sites (feature mouths and protrusions), thereby ensuring void-free bottom-up growth and surface planarization [10–12]. Among the numerous levelers reported, Janus Green B (JGB) is the most classic, as it can achieve not only superfilling in microvias [13] but also high throwing power (TP) electroplated in through-holes [14]. Additionally, previous studies have demonstrated that the azo group and the positively charged quaternary-ammonium group are the primary active functional groups in JGB [13,15].

Building on this insight, numerous researchers have designed levelers that incorporate either the azo or quaternary-ammonium group. Wang et al. employed gentian violet, which contains a positively charged quaternary-ammonium group, as a leveler for through-hole electrodeposition and demonstrated that this leveler exhibited plating performance as excellent as that of JGB [16]. However, other researchers introduced quaternary-ammonium groups with varying chain lengths onto the quinacridone skeleton to develop a novel leveler [17], and the novel leveler exhibited superior plating performance compared to JGB. Additionally, they also grafted quaternary-ammonium chains onto the Sudan I scaffold, reinforcing electrostatic adsorption while preserving the azo-naphthalene π–π interactions, thereby further enhancing plating performance [18]. Another group employed quaternary-ammonium salts of varying alkyl-chain lengths as plating levelers and further observed that these levelers delivered suppression performance superior to that of polyethylene glycol (PEG) [19]. Taken together, these studies further confirm that the positively charged quaternary-ammonium group constitutes the key active functional moiety of leveler molecules.

However, growing evidence indicates that, beyond the classic active groups— positively charged quaternary-ammonium and azo groups—auxiliary modification groups such as electronegative substituents or heteroaromatic rings can markedly reinforce leveler adsorption [20], alter the diffusion ability of molecules [21,22], and enhance synergism with other additives [23]. Dow et al. compared JGB with its derivative Diamond Black (DB), revealing significant electrochemical differences despite the two molecules differing by only a single peripheral functional substituent [24]. Similarly, Wang et al. observed that Safranine T (ST), which lacks several peripheral functional substituents present in JGB, exhibited significantly reduced through-hole throwing power compared to JGB [25], whereas Zhu et al. restored microvia superfilling by introducing hydroxyl (-OH) groups into ST [20]. Therefore, using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to unravel how individual functional groups dictate adsorption energetics and electron distribution is very necessary. For example, many research groups have used DFT and MD simulations to examine how different modifying functional groups affect the leveling performance of tetrazolium derivatives, because the tetrazolium scaffold is an excellent leveler backbone: the tetrazolium ring carries an intrinsic positive charge comparable to that of quaternary-ammonium groups, while offering high structural stability and low cost. Lei et al. used DFT calculations to show that introducing N/O heteroatom substituents alters the electronic structure of tetrazolium derivatives, increases their electron activity, and thereby markedly improves microvia superfilling [26]. Similarly, combined DFT and MD studies by Wei et al. revealed that electronegative groups such as $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ and I redistribute the electrostatic potential of the tetrazolium backbone, create additional chemically active sites, and strengthen intermolecular interactions, ultimately enhancing microvia filling [23]. In the same vein, Teng et al. [27] combined DFT with experiments to elucidate how various tetrazolium derivatives interact synergistically with a propylene-oxide–ethylene-oxide–propylene-oxide (PEP) triblock copolymer; highly electronegative substituents were found to promote stronger cooperation with the suppressor PEP and thus further boost superfilling performance.

As is well known, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT), a commercially available tetrazolium dye, has demonstrated excellent performance as a leveler in through-hole copper filling [28–30]. In contrast, blind microvias present a far more challenging environment: with only one opening, electrolyte circulation is severely restricted, the diffusion layer thickens, and a pronounced ohmic and activation overpotential gradient develops. These factors make void-free filling in blind microvias significantly more difficult than in through-holes. To date, however, the suitability of NBT for blind-microvia superfilling has not been reported, nor has its structure–performance relationship been elucidated—an omission that limits the molecular-level insight into tetrazolium-based levelers and the rational design of cost-effective additives. Accordingly, NBT was chosen as the leveler in this study to assess its effectiveness in copper superfilling of microvias, of which the molecular structure is shown in Figure 1. By combining electrochemical analyses, electroplating experiments, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), MD simulations, and DFT calculations, we elucidate how NBT’s NO<sub>2</sub> groups and tetrazolium ring govern the adsorption on Cu(111) and synergism with PEG and other species. The insights provide rational guidelines for engineering the next-generation, robust, and economical levelers.

## 2.1. Microvia Electrodeplating and Electrochemical Measurements

Rectangular PCB fragments containing microvias with a diameter of 120 µm and a depth of 100 µm were employed as substrates for copper electrodeposition experiments. The electrodeposition experiments were performed in the basic plating solutions containing 0.88 M $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 H _ { 2 } O , 0 . 5 4 M H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } }$ (98%, analytical reagent), and 50 ppm HCl along with three-component system additives where NBT functioned as the leveler, PEG acted as the suppressor, and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) served as the accelerator. The PCB substrates were electroplated at a constant current density of $- 1 0 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$

The CV profiles further validate the strong synergistic suppression by PEG and NBT (Figure 3b). Compared with the PEG-only baseline, the onset of copper deposition shifts progressively negative as NBT concentration increases, confirming enhanced inhibition. Unlike NBT alone (Figure 2b), the PEG–NBT curves display a large $\Delta \mathrm { E _ { h y s } }$ value that largens with rising NBT concentration, while the $\mathrm { E _ { r e c o v e r } }$ remains essentially constant across all NBT concentrations—indicating the formation of a potential-sensitive PEG–NBT complex film. Higher NBT concentrations produce a denser suppressor layer that is more resistant to breakdown by electrode potential. Taken together, the PEG–NBT suppressor exhibits pronounced sensitivity to both convection and potential—properties that favor PEG–NBT-selective coverage at the microvia mouth rather than microvia bottom and promote void-free superfilling. This is due to the fact that the PEG–NBT concentration is relatively low at microvia bottom (weak convection) compared to the microvia mouth (strong convection), making the suppressor film at microvia bottom more susceptible to potential-induced collapse and thereby facilitating ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. Conversely, at the microvia mouth the higher local PEG–NBT coverage resists breakdown and, once collapsed, rapidly re-forms, ensuring sustained suppression [38,39].

Although NBT and PEG exhibit electrochemical behaviors that facilitate the superfilling of microvias, the achievement of efficient microvia superfilling electroplating often necessitates the synergistic effect of SPS. Specifically, SPS focuses on accelerating copper deposition at the bottom of the microvias, while PEG–NBT is responsible for suppressing copper deposition in the microvias’ entrance region. GM for the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system (Figure 4a) further confirmed the distinct yet synergistic functions of each component. After the electrode-potential drop caused by 200 ppm PEG, injection of 1 ppm SPS partially breaks through the PEG– $- \mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ film, producing a marked depolarization [40]. Subsequent addition of 10 ppm NBT immediately reverses this trend: the potential shifts to values even more negative than those recorded with PEG alone, indicating that the PEG– NBT co-adsorbate effectively resists displacement by SPS and restores a robust suppressor layer. The differences between the depolarization curves at 100 rpm and 1000 rpm indicate that the system still exhibits a certain sensitivity to convection $( \Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 4 } , \Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 5 } , \Delta \mathfrak { n } _ { 6 } > 0 )$ , which is consistent with the characteristics of PEG–NBT adsorption being diffusion-limited.

The CV curves validated the observations obtained from the GM curves, as shown in Figure 4b. Relative to the PEG–SPS baseline, increasing NBT concentration again shifts the copper deposition onset to more negative potentials and produces a larger $\Delta \mathrm { E _ { h y s } }$ value, while the $\mathrm { E _ { r e c o v e r } }$ remains unchanged across all NBT concentrations. This behavior indicates that higher NBT concentrations generate a denser PEG–NBT suppressor film that not only resists breakdown by applied potential but also effectively withstands SPS attack. Collectively, these electrochemical features indicate that the PEG–NBT layer remains strongly adsorbed at the microvia mouth (as discussed above in Figure 3b)—blocking SPS there—and confines accelerator action to the convection-limited via the bottom, thereby achieving void-free, bottom-up superfilling.

The average local ionization energy (ALIE) quantifies the local propensity for electron removal within a molecule. The lowest ALIE values (≈219 kcal $\mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$ occur on themethoxy-substituted phenyl rings (Ph3-Meo, Ph3<sup>′</sup>-Meo<sup>′</sup>) and the adjacent phenyl rings (Ph2, Ph2<sup>′</sup>) (Figure 6c), indicating that these sites are most susceptible to electrophilic attack and can donate electron density to positive species at the cathode, strengthening chemisorp tion [44,45]. In contrast, the local electron-attachment energy (LEAE) quantifies the ability to accept electrons; smaller values mean stronger nucleophilicity [46]. The minimum LEAE (−46.32 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup>) is found on the tetrazolium rings and the neighboring nitro-substituted phenyl rings (Figure 6d). This confirms that the nitro groups greatly enhance the nu cleophilic reactivity of NBT, enabling efficient electron uptake from Cu 3d orbitals and the formation of robust back-donation π bonds. Such strong adsorption—especially at high-field sites such as microvia mouths—rationalizes the superior leveling performance of NBT. Moreover, this conclusion is fundamentally consistent with the findings derived from FMO.

To fully predict a leveler’s performance, one must assess not only its electronic active sites but also its interactions with other species and their corresponding adsorption sites. Accordingly, DFT calculations were carried out to investigate NBT’s interactions with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ions and with the suppressor PEG. Atom in Molecules (AIM) and interaction region indicator (IRI) calculations were carried out for the ${ \mathrm { N B T } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ complex, while the NBT–PEG interaction was analyzed with the independent-gradient model based on Hirshfeld parti tion (IGMH), as shown in Figure 7. As shown in Figure $^ { 7 } \mathbf { a } ,$ the shortest contact between $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ and NBT is the Cu–N bond to the tetrazolium nitrogen (1.994 Å). The Cu–O distance to the methoxy group is longer (2.177 $\mathring \mathrm { A } )$ , indicating that the Cu–N interaction is stronger than the Cu–O one. To evaluate the bond nature, we calculated the bond-critical-point (BCP) parameters (Table 1). For both Cu–N and Cu–O bonds, the electron density at the BCP (ρ ) is below 0.10 a.u. and the Laplacian of electron density $( \nabla ^ { 2 } \rho _ { \mathrm { B C P } } )$ value is positive, showing that the two bonds for Cu–N and Cu–O are ionic bonds [47,48]. However, only the Cu–N bond has negative energy density $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { B C P } } \right)$ and negative potential energy density (Vr ), which confirms that the Cu–N bond is the stronger bond [49]. IRI analysis (Figure 7b) reveals blue isosurfaces between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the tetrazolium nitrogen, as well as between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the methoxy oxygen, indicating strong Cu–N and Cu–O interactions. The two-dimensional IRI map (Figure 7c) further supports these observations, confirming robust coordination between NBT and $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ions. These findings indicate that NBT coordi nates predominantly with ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ via the nitrogen atom of the tetrazolium ring, forming a strong ionic bond that retards ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. This selective coordination promotes NBT adsorption at Cu-rich sites—such as microvia mouths or cathode protrusions—thereby efficiently inhibiting local deposition.
## 3.3. Electrodeposition and Characterization Analysis

The study above indicates that NBT possesses the key attributes required of an electroplating leveler. To assess its practical performance, the microvia electrodeposition was carried out with 10–40 ppm NBT, and the cross-sectional results are given in Figure 10. At a low concentration of 10–20 ppm, NBT fails to support bottom-up filling: only little copper grows at the microvia’s bottom, while accelerated deposition at the mouth causes premature closure and large voids. This behavior is attributed to an insufficiently dense PEG–NBT suppressor film; its inhibition strength and potential sensitivity are too low, consistent with the narrow CV hysteresis observed in electrochemical analysis above.

However, when the NBT concentration is raised to 30–40 ppm, the filling mode switches to void-free bottom-up superfilling. The higher NBT level forms a denser, higherpotential-sensitivity PEG–NBT film that adsorbs preferentially at the relatively positive microvia’s mouth, strongly suppressing copper there. Meanwhile, SPS adsorbed at the microvia bottom—where convection is weak—accelerates copper deposition in that region, enabling void-free microvia superfilling. These plating results confirm the findings derived from electrochemical analysis, DFT calculations, and MD simulations: NBT synergizes with PEG to form a robust suppressor film that localizes at high-potential, high-convection regions, thereby enabling reliable void-free bottom-up copper filling of microvias.

In this work, the tetrazolium derivative NBT was assessed as a leveler for copper superfilling of microvias. A combination of GM tests, CV, AFM, and XPS was applied, together with DFT calculations and MD simulations. The major findings are as follows:

(4) Electroplating experiments confirm that 30–40 ppm NBT yields void-free bottom-up filling in microvias. XPS verifies co-adsorption of PEG and NBT; the NBT anchors to the copper surface through its nitro, tetrazolium, methoxy, and aromatic sites. These mutually consistent results clarify the structure–function relationship that underlies the effectiveness of NBT as a leveler for microvia superfilling.
# Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia

Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling. The synergistic efects between TW and other additives were verified by means of chronopotentiometry, cyclic voltammetry, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The outcomes of the electrochemical tests revealed that the competitive adsorption behavior between bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and TW is contingent upon the current density and the intensity of convection. Metallographic section analysis demonstrated that TW exhibits outstanding microvia filling capabilities for micro blind vias with a diameter of 150 µm and a depth of 80 µm. Notably, TW-80 was able to attain a filling rate of 96.15% following electrodeposition for 60 min at a current density of 2 A/dm<sup>2</sup>. Quantum chemical calculations suggested that the relatively smaller band gap and the clustered molecular structure of TW-80 are more conducive to its adsorption onto the electrode surface, leading to the formation of a barrier layer, which in turn restrains the deposition of copper.
Keywords Tween · Suppressor · Copper electroplating · Microvia filling

In the realm of microelectronics manufacturing, acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has emerged as a pivotal process, ensuring reliable electrical interconnections within printed circuit boards (PCBs) and advanced packaging substrates [1–4]. The quality of via filling, characterized by void—free and uniform deposition, directly impacts the performance, reliability, and miniaturization potential of electronic devices [5–7]. To achieve this, a complex mixture of additives, including suppressors, accelerators, and levelers, is incorporated into the electroplating bath [8–11]. Among these, suppressors play a crucial role in controlling the deposition rate at diferent surface sites, preventing over—plating at the via openings and promoting bottom—up filling.

The additives utilized in the acidic sulfate copper plating process primarily consist of chloride ions (Cl-) [12], accelerators, suppressors and levelers. These additives interact with one another to enhance the performance of resulting formed copper plating layer [13, 14, 5, 15–17]. Previous research on suppressors for acid copper electroplating has predominantly focused on polymers and surfactants with diverse molecular structures. For instance, polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based polymers have been widely studied and utilized as suppressors due to their ability to adsorb on the copper surface and inhibit the deposition reaction [18, 19]. However, their high molecular weight and complex synthesis processes often lead to issues such as poor bath stability and dificulty in waste treatment, raising environmental concerns. Polyetheramine (PEP) has also been investigated as a potential suppressor, leveraging its unique amine-containing structure that allows for specific interactions with the copper surface [17, 20]. While PEP shows promise in adjusting the deposition rate, its relatively high cost and limited biodegradability pose challenges for large—scale industrial application. Additionally, ethylene—propylene copolymer (EPE) has been explored, as its alternating structure can provide a balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties, influencing the deposition behavior [21, 22]. Nevertheless, EPE may sufer from inconsistent performance under varying electroplating conditions, and its efect on the quality of microvia filling in high—aspect—ratio scenarios remains suboptimal. Moreover, some non—ionic surfactants like Triton X—series have been investigated, but they may exhibit limited eficiency in microvia filling under high— aspect—ratio conditions and can also pose potential toxicity risks.

Against this backdrop, considering their excellent emulsifying, dispersing, and wetting properties, as well as their relatively low toxicity and good biodegradability, Tween compounds present a compelling option for electroplating applications. However, their application as suppressors in acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has remained largely unexplored. This study aims to investigate the inhibitory efects of TW-20 and TW-80 (as shown in Fig. 1) and their synergistic efects with other additives through electrochemical methods, optical microscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. By doing so, it systematically evaluates Tween compounds as eco-friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, filling this research gap. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the development of more environmentally friendly and eficient electroplating processes, meeting the growing demands of the microelectronics industry for sustainable manufacturing.

Based on the research on Tween compounds as eco— friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, several key guidelines are proposed. Firstly, when selecting Tween compounds, factors like their hydrophilic—lipophilic balance, molecular weight, and branching structure should be carefully considered to ensure proper adsorption and inhibitory efects. Secondly, concentration optimization is crucial, as both too low and too high concentrations can negatively impact microvia filling quality, thus requiring systematic studies to find the optimal balance. Thirdly, using Tween compounds in combination with other electroplating additives and understanding their synergistic efects can enhance the overall plating performance, although their compatibility and interaction mechanisms need thorough investigation. Finally, environmental considerations are essential, including minimizing compound loss during bath operation and adopting appropriate biodegradation processes for waste treatment. # Structure Performance Correlation of N-Heterocyclic Oligomer Leveler for Acid Copper Plating of Advanced Interconnects

Abstract: Levelers, as an essential part of organic additives in copper electroplating, play a crucial role in the fabrication of sophisticated interconnects in integrated circuits, packaging substrates, and printed circuit boards. In this work, four N-heterocyclic oligomers were synthesized and characterized, along with investigations of their electrochemical behaviors and their synergism with other bath components. The corresponding effects of the oligomers on the deposited copper films were analyzed by morphological and compositional characterizations. The leveling mechanism of the oligomers was further discussed with the aid of quantum chemical calculations. The results exhibit that each of these N-heterocyclic oligomers holds a particular degree of leveling ability. The oligomer of 1,3-bis(1-imidazolyl)propane and 1,3-dichloro-2-propanol (IPIEP) is the best leveler for THs plating compared with the other three oligomers. It was found that the hydroxyl group in IPIEP enhances the hydrophilicity of the modified molecule and triggers a more stable complexation between IPIEP and H O−Cu(I)−MPS. Moreover, imidazole demonstrates a better practicality than piperazine. This work recommends the combination of N-heterocycles in planar conformation with modification by the hydroxyl group to synthesize high-performance straight-chain levelers
Keywords: copper electroplating; oligomer; throwing power; leveler

Fifth-generation communication promotes the development of electronic interconnects with a high integration, high bandwidth, and high frequency transmission. Copper electroplating technology is the primary method for forming electronic interconnection in integrated circuits (ICs), packaging substrates, and printed circuit boards (PCBs), which plays a crucial role in the booming electronics industry [1–3].

Under the synergistic effects of organic additives (brighteners, suppressors, and levelers), electroplated copper is uniformly deposited on the inner wall of through holes (THs) as the conformal layer or micro-through-hole filler [3]. The performance of electroplating copper film in THs is decided by the shape of holes, electrolyte formula, plating current, solution convection, etc. [4,5]. The conformal deposition in THs has been explained by the theory of secondary current distribution, but the via filling was considered abnormal and termed as super filling due to its behavior [6,7]. Moffat proposed and then revised the curvature-enhanced adsorbate coverage (CEAC) model based on the growth process, revealing the accelerating effect of the brightener in the bottom-up growth of vias [6,7]. Later, Dow discovered the convection-dependent property of levelers [8], and Broekmann found the N-type negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon in the bath solution [9]. These findings have established a systematic via-filling theory and emphasized the importance of levelers in copper electroplating.

Typically, the suppressor is chosen from PEG or its derivatives [10–12], and the brightener is sodium bis-(3-Sulfopropyl)disulfide (SPS) or sodium 3-mercapto propane sulphonate (MPS) [8,13]. In contrast, there are a few levelers with quite different leveling performances [14–17] that are applied to various plating formulas to meet the multifarious demands of interconnecting man ufacture. High-performance levelers, therefore, play an essential role in the commercial plating formula. Levelers were generally selected from dyes in the early days of copper electroplating, such as Janus Green B [18,19], a classic one in the literature [19–21]. Early work suggested that the leveling ability of JGB originated from the electrochemical reduction and cleavage of its −N=N− group at the tip or protrusion of the cathode surface [22]. However, this hypothesis implies a large amount of JGB consumption and low current efficiency of copper deposition, which is not consistent with the actual situation.

Besides dye-based levelers, in recent years, organic oligomer levelers (nitrogencontaining heterocycles chained by linker groups) have attracted increasing attention in research and application [15,23,24]. Due to the unclear structure–property relationships of these oligomers, the need to develop new oligomer leveler machines with a high through-hole filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. Several research groups have started to purposefully design various oligomer levelers to investigate their structure–property relationships in THs filling. Quaternary ammonium salts have been systematically studied because of their excellent via filling properties [25,26]. Broekmann used polymerizates of imidazole and epichlorohydrin (IMEP) as a model leveler to study the oscillatory behavior during electrodeposition and concluded that the leveling effect originates from the coordination between Cu(I) and the leveler, in which the hydroxyl functional group coordinates Cu(I) to form the IMEP−Cu(I)−MPS complex, inhibiting the activity of MPS [27]. In contrast, Bandas claimed that the activity of MPS is inhibited by electrostatic pairing with the N-heterocyclic leveler and the deposition of copper ions is occluded by the steric chemical structure of the oligomers [28].

To develop a high-performance leveler, it is significant to reveal the relationship between the chemical composition of levelers and the leveling properties. The interfacial electrochemical mechanism also needs elucidation. In this work, a series of oligomers involving N-heterocyclic groups and O-functional groups via methylene links were prepared and characterized to study the structure–performance correlation of levelers. The electrochemical behavior of these oligomers in the plating bath and their interactions with other additive components were also investigated. The effects on the microstructure and surface morphology of the electrodeposited copper were characterized. Quantum chemical calculations and the THs plating results were combined to propose the probable mechanism of these leveling candidates. This work further promotes the theoretical study of levelers based on Broekmann and Schmidt’s theory, providing a possible path to advanced levelers.

## 3.5. Electroplating

The test samples for electroplating were $1 5 \times 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ PCBs with multiple THs (Section 2.2). The diameter and depth of the THs were 0.15 mm and 1.5 mm, respectively. Two phosphorated copper plates were used as the anodes and directly placed in a Haring cell with 1500 mL electrolyte. The PCBs were electroplated at a current density of $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { \breve { 2 } }$ for 70 min at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ To ensure adequate mass transportation, a continuous air bubble flow was adopted during the electroplating process. The leveling performance of the leveler was evaluated by the TP [47], whose definition and calculation are shown in supporting information (Figure S1).

In this work, we successfully synthesized and characterized a series of oligomers involving N-heterocyclic groups and O-functional groups via methylene links. The conformational relationship between the molecular structure design and its electroplating leveling ability was investigated. The electroplating of THs with the oligomers demonstrates (Section 2.2) that all four oligomers possess a leveling ability. The DFT calculation results suggest that the types of N-heterocyclic functionality affect the performance and electroplating behaviors (Sections 2.1–2.3) of the oligomers and that imidazole exhibits a better performance than piperazine for the synthesis of high-performance straight-chain levelers.

Most importantly, a chemical model (Figure 10) for the four oligomers is proposed (Sections 2.4 and 2.5). The inhibition of MPS activity is the key factor of this model, and is caused by the electrostatic pairing between the cationic amine functionalities of oligomers and the negatively charged sulfonate of MPS. The additional inter- or intra-chain anion–cation pairing between H O−Cu(I)−MPS complexes and the functional groups of oligomers also contributes to the mechanism of leveling. Among these oligomers, IPIEP is the best leveler for THs plating because the modification of the hydroxyl en hances the hydrophilicity of IPIEP and triggers a more stable coupling between IPIEP and $_ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } }$ −Cu(I)−MPS (Section 2.5). Notably, the hydroxyl or carbonyl group is the key to initiating the coordination process between levelers and $H _ { 2 } O \mathrm { - } \mathrm { C u ( I ) } - \bar { \mathrm { M P S } } ,$ which implies that the other O-functional groups, such as the carboxyl group and aldehyde group, will also bring the extra coupling process. Research focusing on the detailed mechanism of related additives in electroplating baths will be carried out in the follow-up work.

# Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime

Co has recently gained more and more attention as a material to replace the traditional Ta liner.<sup>10,11</sup> Compared with Ta, Co provides a better wettability of PVD Cu seed, enables a more conformal Cu seed coverage and therefore improves the extendibility of Cu electroplating in smaller dimensions.<sup>12</sup> In addition, the enhanced grain growth of Cu electroplated on Co seed<sup>13</sup> and the self-formation of a barrier layer enabled by the Mn diffusion through Co layer<sup>14</sup> potentially provide additional performance gain on the reliability of the interconnect structures.

Electrodeposition of cobalt and its alloys has been studied extensively in the past for their magnetic properties. Among them, CoNiFe<sup>22–25</sup> and CoFe<sup>26–28</sup> alloys were used in commercial hard disk drive writing heads for their low coercivities and high moments. The two additives commonly used in magnetic thin film plating, saccharin and thiourea, were studied with scanning tunneling microscope and were found to adsorb on Au(111) surface through physisorption and chemisorption respectively.<sup>29</sup> The different sulfur incorporation behaviors resulted in different coercivities of the deposited films.

In an effort to search for a suppressing additive for a onecomponent Co deposition chemistry, this paper presents a study of the effect of dimethylglyoxime (DMG) on the electrodeposition of cobalt. Metallisation processes, represented by copper pillar bumps (CPBs), are taking the spotlight in the field of semiconductor advanced packaging. Eficient filling of a uniform, levelling copper layer within a defined pattern by electroplating is the final goal pursued. In addition to its levelling capabilities, the leveller Janus Green B (JGB) has an undesired convection-dependence for CPBs, resulting in a convex front upstream or downstream of the copper filling layer. In this paper, the JGB is identified as the source of convection-dependence based on an in-situ observation platform. Electrochemical and spectroscopic evidence supports the conclusion that the reduction reaction (including protonation of the phenazine ring, hydrogenation reduction or even further cleavage of the azo group) of JGB also occurs along with the copper electrodeposition process. The introduction of convection produces a stronger suppression efect and thus a non-uniform distribution of the filled layer within the microcavity.

The deposit leveller takes an important role in plating-related processes such as copper damascene interconnection,<sup>1–3</sup> copper pillar bumps,<sup>4,5</sup> and microvias.<sup>6,7</sup> Janus Green B (JGB) is the commonly used leveller which has been studied extensively. Kelly et $a I . ^ { 1 }$ and Cao et $a / . ^ { 8 }$ firstly proposed a four-component additive containing JGB to achieve the levelling efect and suggested a competitive adsorption relationship between these additives. Dow et al.<sup>9–11</sup> found that the inhibiting efect of JGB was enhanced in the presence of convection and proposed the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) theory, suggesting that the CDA behaviour of the additive was a crucial factor to achieve bottom-up filling. Li et $a I . ^ { 1 2 }$ determined the structure of the reduction product of JGB by mass spectrometry (MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and proposed that the reduction product of JGB is the true leveller in the copper filling process. Mao et al.<sup>13</sup> provided molecular spectroscopic evidence on the reductive decomposition of the JGB azo group by in-situ attenuated total reflection-surface enhanced infrared spectroscopy. Hai et al.<sup>14</sup> further stated that the consumption of JGB should also include the reduction of heterocycles. In the present authors’ previous work, JGB-induced convection-dependence has been observed,<sup>15</sup> but molecular-level understanding of its genesis is still absent.

In this study, the JGB-induced convection-dependent filling process is visualised as benefitting from the CPBs in-situ observation platform. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), ultra violet-visible spectroscopy (UV-vis), and in-situ electrochemi cal surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) were performed to identify the decomposition of JGB. The weakening of the inhibitory capacity of JGB reduction product relative to JGB was confirmed by cyclic voltammetry stripping (CVS). Electrochemical and spectroscopic evidence supports the idea that inhomogeneous flow field inside the microvia leads to enhanced renewal of JGB and its reduction product on the higher flow rate side, and suppressed the deposition of copper on that side.

A microcavity electrode (MCE) (aspect ratio, AR ∼1) was etched and assembled in an in-situ observation platform according to the authors’ previous work.<sup>15</sup> In brief, epoxysealed nickel wire was etched in 1 M NaCl + 5 mM ${ \sf H } _ { 2 } { \sf S } { \sf O } _ { 4 }$ to form the MCE, which was then placed in the trench (5 × 20 × 5 mm) of the Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) cell. A 1 mm platinum wire and a 0.7 mm copper wire embedded in the cell were used as counter and reference electrode, respectively. The cell was sealed by an epoxy-coated 0.5 mm thickness glass cover plate, and the plating bath was circulated through the fluidic chamber $( 3 0 \times 5 \times 7$ mm) at a rate of 1.26 cm s<sup>−1</sup> by means of a peristaltic pump (Kamoer, DI Pump 550, China).

Figure 2 shows the surface morphology of MCEs obtained under diferent additive combinations. While the addition of PEG and SPS results in refined grains with respect to the basic plating bath, the lower roughness surface clearly requires the injection of JGB. Therefore, taking into account the roles played by the flow field and the leveller JGB in the convection-dependent morphology generation, it is necessary to reconsider the properties of JGB.

Taking into account that the deposition of copper has more negative reduction potential than the reduction of JGB, it is suggested that the reduction of JGB during the plating process generates a new product (JGB\_Red), which plays a real role in surface inhibition.<sup>12,14,18</sup> The flow rate diference within the microvias leads to an accelerated exchange rate of JGB-JGB\_Red on the surface, thus exhibiting diferent deposition rates on the left and right sides of microvias.

As a final component of this study, the diference in inhibition of copper deposition by JGB and JGB\_Red needs to be evaluated. The cyclic voltammetry stripping (CVS) method<sup>27</sup> was used to compare the changes in the inhibition ability of the plating solution when JGB or JGB\_Red was added to the basic plating bath (Figure 6).

So far, based on the above spectroscopic evidence and electrochemical studies, the convective dependence exhibited by JGB can be explained: JGB initially protonates in acidic solutions and subsequently becomes further decom posed during copper deposition, and the inhibition of the redox is much weaker. For regions with strong convection (e.g. mouth of the microvia,<sup>9,10</sup> and downstream of microcavity<sup>15,28</sup>), where suficient raw material supply can maintain the inhibition ability, the growth of copper can be slowed down, while, for the weaker convective regions (e.g. bottom of the microvia, and upstream of microcavity), the inhibition is rela tively weak, which will be preferred for copper growth.

In this paper, the mechanism of convection-dependent morphology induced by the leveller JGB has been investigated based on an in-situ observation platform simulating the work conditions of CPBs electrodeposition. The results of CV. UV-vis. and FC-SERS experiments indicate that the decomposition of JGB involves the protonation of the phenazine ring and the reduction of the azo group. The CVS studies further indicate that the reduction of JGB will result in a weak ening of its inhibitory capacity. Enhanced convection can ensure suficient supply of JGB to maintain its inhibitory capacity, while the decomposition of JGB in the weak convection region will deteriorate the capacity. This is believed to be the reason why the plating layer height distribution is afected by convection during the filling process. The revelation of this decomposition mechanism will contribute to the understanding of the role played by phenazine-type leveller, and facilitate the molecular design of leveller and the quality control of plating bath in the CPBs and microvia filling process.
# Simultaneously filling process and mechanism of through-hole and blind hole by copper electroplating
# Simultaneously filling process and mechanism of through-hole and blind hole by copper electroplating

In this study, a traditional copper electroplating formula was used to fill microvias, which indicated that when the concentrations of Janus Green B (JGB) and bis-(sodium sulphopropyl) disulphide (SPS) were both controlled at 6 mg L<sup>−1</sup>, through-holes and blind holes can be simultaneously and perfect filled with deposited copper by regulating the convection intensity. As a result, the dimple at the mouth of through-hole was only 5 μm, and the filling performance of blind hole was 88%. Galvanostatic measurements (GMs) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) were employed to study the microvia filling mechanism. It demonstrated that the plating solution in the centre of the through-hole was nearly stagnant under the weak convection, which resulted in the accelerator SPS being preferentially adsorbed and further enhanced the copper deposition here. It led to the formation of butterfly-like deposited copper layer in the through-hole and finally filled the through-holes and blind holes simultaneously.
