To meet the demands of modern electronic products for multifunctionality and miniaturisation, high-density interconnect (HDI) technology has been widely adopted in the advanced manufacturing of printed circuit boards (PCBs), particularly in fields such as 5G communications and wearable devices<sup>1–3</sup>. Currently, the integration of blind holes and through-holes plays a critical role in HDI for multilayer PCBs; the filling process of blind holes and through-holes is one of the key technologies for HDI<sup>4,5</sup>. Typically, there are two main methods for filling through-holes and blind holes. The first method involves filling the holes with insulating resin or conductive paste after the metallisation. However, due to diferences in the coeficients of thermal expansion (CTE) between the resin and copper, prolonged usage may compromise the reliability of the PCB<sup>6,7</sup>. The second method involves the complete filling of through-holes and blind holes with copper electroplating. This approach not only achieves electrical interconnection but also significantly shortens the PCB production cycle through a one-step holefilling process. Additionally, it markedly enhances the reliability, conductivity, thermal performance and mechanical properties of HDI<sup>8–10</sup>. Therefore, the copper electroplating for through-holes and blind holes has become the mainstream process to meet the requirements of HDI<sup>11</sup>.

For through-hole plating, the relatively complex pulse electroplating technique has been commonly employed<sup>12–14</sup>. Zhang et al.<sup>15</sup> optimised the periodic reverse pulse plating process using numerical simulation methods, achieving conformal filling of through-holes with an aspect ratio of 10:1. Ning et al.<sup>16</sup> utilised horizontal pulse copper electroplating technology to successfully achieve conformal thickening of high-aspect-ratio through-holes and super-filling of blind holes, ultimately obtaining a smooth copper layer. Compared to the complex pulse electroplating process, direct current (DC) copper electroplating ofers advantages such as lower equipment costs, simpler operational parameters and higher process stability. Liu et al.<sup>9</sup> developed an electroplating solution formulation suitable for the simultaneous filling of through-holes and blind holes, which can be implemented using only a direct current (DC) power supply. Additionally, they optimised the process by improving the pattern plating method, thereby minimising the thickness of the surface copper. Zhao et al.<sup>17</sup> employed 1-dodecyl-2-methyl-3-benzylimidazolium chloride (DMBI) as a leveller, successfully achieving conformal thickening in through-holes and void-free filling in blind holes. In situ ATR-SEIRAS spectroscopy and electrochemical experiments revealed that DMBI inhibits the electroreduction of copper ions by competing with SPS. Currently, the simultaneous electroplating process for through-holes and blind holes primarily focuses on achieving conformal thickening of through-holes. However, this conformal thickening approach may lead to reduced signal transmission reliability and insuficient thermal performance during the long-term use of HDI<sup>18–20</sup>. To address these issues, it is necessary to achieve complete filling of through-holes. Therefore, this study aims to develop an acidic sulphate copper plating process based on a low-voltage DC power supply to achieve simultaneous and complete filling of through-holes and blind holes.

In this study, the commonly used SPS and JGB were employed as the accelerator and leveller, respectively. Based on a clear understanding of the efects of convection intensity and additive concentration on the copper plating filling performance, a novel method of optimising the filling efect through gradient regulation of convection intensity was proposed. This approach successfully achieved simultaneous and flawless filling of through-holes and blind holes, significantly enhancing the metallisation eficiency of HDI.

## 3.3. Microvia filling mechanism

The GMs were carried out in the optimal electroplating solution under diferent rotation speeds and the results are shown in Figure 7. It could be noted that the copper deposition potential increased gradually with the increase of rotation speed, which could lead to decrease of the copper deposition rate. Under both weak and strong convection, the copper deposition rate at the centre of the throughhole and the bottom of the blind hole is faster than that on the PCB surface. This indicates that SPS showed stronger adsorption strength than that of JGB in these regions. Actually, according to CDA theory, SPS preferentially adsorbed onto the surface where the convection was relatively weaker, such as in the centre of the through-hole and on the bottom of the blind hole, thereby accelerating the copper deposition rate in these regions. It finally resulted in the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling in through-holes and the ‘bottom-up’ filling in blind holes.

Therefore, to clarify the velocity diferences between the inside and outside of the through-hole under weak convective during the initial stage of electroplating, and to reveal the formation mechanism of the ‘butterfly’ filling behaviour within the through-hole, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) were conducted on the through-hole structure. The simulation results are shown in Figure 8.

Under the influence of the electric field, the solution flowed from the bulk towards the PCB surface, with the velocity concentrated outside the PCB surface. When the solution flowed into the through-hole, the velocity significantly increased at the hole entrance due to the diameter restriction and flow convergence. After entering the through-hole, the flow converged at the centre of the hole. Due to the spatial constraints inside the throughhole, the velocity vectors within the hole were nearly symmetrical, and their resultant vector approached zero. This indicates that the plating solution at the centre of the through-hole was almost stationary. This velocity distri bution pattern resulted in the flow rate outside the through-hole being significantly higher than that inside the through-hole. Combined with the electrochemical testing results, the copper deposition potential under stationary conditions is lower than that under weak convection. As a result, copper preferentially deposited at the centre of the through-hole, which led to the ‘butterflyshaped’ filling in the through-hole.

Figure 9d illustrated the copper deposition process after achieving a ‘bridge’ inside the through-hole and switching to strong convection. At this stage, the ‘bridge’ had been achieved inside the through-hole and changed it into two symmetrical blind holes. Upon switching to strong convection, the concentration diferences of the components in the plating solution were eliminated, and chloride ions as well as additives on the copper surface were replenished and re-adsorbed. The accelerator preferentially adsorbed at the bottom of the blind holes, where the convection was weak. Meanwhile, the leveller and suppressor preferentially adsorbed on the surface and at the hole openings, where the convection was strong. This ultimately resulted in overfilling of the two symmetrical blind holes.

The distribution of additives during the blind hole filling process was similar to that of through-holes. The convection intensity being switched from weak to strong could efectively eliminate the concentration diferences in the plating solution. It promoted the additive molecules to re-adsorb uniformly onto the copper surface, finally producing a deposited copper layer which was smooth and bright.

This study demonstrated that simultaneous filling of throughholes and blind holes could not be achieved through continuous strong convection alone. While continuous weak convection enabled filling, it resulted in uneven copper deposition surfaces. These challenges were efectively resolved by implementing time-dependent convection control. Using the plating solution containing 6 mg L<sup>−1</sup> bis(3-sulphopropyl)

disulphide (SPS) and 6 mg ${ \mathsf { L } } ^ { - 1 }$ Janus Green B (JGB), the optimised process involved initial electroplating under weak convection for 60 min to establish a characteristic ‘butterflyshaped’ filling pattern and central ‘bridge’ formation within through-holes. Subsequent switching to strong convection for 30 min yielded complete void-free filling with superior surface morphology. Specifically, the depth of the dimple at the mouth of the through-hole was maintained at 5 μm, while the blind hole filling eficiency reached 88%.

Electrochemical analysis coupled with CFD simulations enabled the development of a novel TH filling mechanism model. The model elucidated two critical phenomena: (1) a substantial convection gradient existed between the external and internal through-hole regions and (2) weak convection conditions promoted lower copper deposition potentials. These factors synergistically facilitated preferential copper deposition at the through-hole centre, initiating the charac teristic butterfly-shaped filling pattern. Following bridge for mation, the through-hole efectively transformed into two symmetrical blind holes, allowing subsequent strong convection to enhance both filling uniformity and surface quality.
# Prediction and Efect Verification of Thiamine as a Leveling Agent in Chip Wafer Electroplating

ABSTRACT: Thiamine, a nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound, is explored for the first time as a novel leveling agent in this study. Based on the density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the adsorption process of thiamine and the commonly used leveling agent JGB, the average values of the binding energies after equilibrium of thiamine and JGB are similar, which indicates that the thiamine molecules have strong bonding ability with the surface of copper and can be adsorbed tightly on the surface of copper. By cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve, thiamine was found to inhibit copper deposition and the inhibition efect was stronger than JGB. The chrono potential curve (CP) test found that the potential diference $\triangle \eta = 8 7 > 5 0$ mV at high and low speeds of thiamine, which indicates that thiamine has the potential to be used as a leveling agent. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) testing found that thiamine inhibited copper precipitation by inhibiting the reactions of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + } \to \mathrm { C u } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { C u } ^ { + } $ Cu. According to electroplating experiments, thiamine has a leveling efect on wafer electroplating and can be used as a leveling agent because the copper layer on the wafer obtained by adding it has a smoother surface compared to the copper layer obtained without adding it. It was found that wafer electroplating does not require PEG, and only adding 55 mg/L Cl<sup>−</sup>, 6 mg/L SPS, and 4 mg/L thiamine as additives can achieve a good filling efect.

Silicon through hole (TSV) technology, as one of the core technologies of 3D packaging, has been studied by a large number of scholars at present.<sup>1−3</sup> TSV is the interconnection of diferent chips and wafers by filling them with conductive metal through microvia. Compared with most metals, copper has lower resistivity and better resistance to electromigration, so the conductive metal used in TSV technology is mainly copper.<sup>4</sup> Direct use of the copper sulfate electroplating solution for microporous electroplating frequently results in issues, including uneven coating, flaws, and defects. Therefore, the electroplating solution often contains some additives for auxiliary electroplating, such as Cl<sup>−</sup>, accelerator, inhibitor, and leveling agent. The synergistic efect between appropriate additives can achieve better filling efect in microporous electroplating.<sup>5−7</sup>

Leveling agents, like inhibitors, have the same efect on inhibiting copper deposition.<sup>8</sup> Currently, there is no complete consensus on the mechanism of action of leveling agents. According to reports, leveling agents can be roughly divided into two categories: quaternary ammonium cation or positively charged nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound.<sup>9</sup> JGB is one of the most studied leveling agents. As shown in Figure 1, JGB is a nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound with a positive charge. Since JGB contains N<sup>+</sup> during the electroplating process, it tends to adsorb in high charge density areas like plating raised points and microporous orifices and other locations to inhibit the copper from rising, while the depression adsorbs less leveling agent, by the inhibitory efect being less, and can therefore play the role of leveling. At present, many academics hold this belief.<sup>10</sup> Thiamine is a positively charged quaternary ammonium cation macromolecule, and its molecular weight (300.5) is smaller than that ofJGB (510. 5), and its mass charge ratio is lower. Under the same volume, thiamine absorbs more in the high charge density area. If thiamine has the efect of inhibiting copper deposition, it may be easier to inhibit and level the efect relative to JGB.

Currently, there are few studies on the leveling efect of thiamine applied to electroplated copper deposition, and this study is the first study of the leveling efect of thiamine. Through electrochemical tests, quantum chemical theory calculations, molecular dynamics simulation, and other methods, we compared the properties of thiamine with those of the published leveling agent JGB and found that it has a better inhibition of copper electroplating deposition and a stronger adsorption capacity on the copper surface. In the wafer plating test, it was discovered that as compared to the plating solution without thiamine molecules, the plating solution including thiamine molecules plated the copper layer and greatly reduced the surface roughness of the wafer.

In this experiment, through theoretical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, the diference between thiamine and the leveling agent JGB was compared, and it was determined that the adsorption capacity and adsorption behavior of thiamine on the copper surface would inhibit the deposition of copper better. By conducting CV and CP tests on leveling agent JGB and new leveling agent thiamine, the study shows that the CV oxidation peak area obtained after adding thiamine is smaller than that of adding JGB, and the potential diference of thiamine at high and low rotational speeds $\triangle \eta = 8 7 ~ \mathrm { m V } > 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m V } ,$ suggesting its potential as a leveling agent. Through EIS testing, it was found that the addition of thiamine not only inhibited the $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + } \to \mathrm { C u } ^ { + }$ reaction but also suppressed the $\mathrm { C u } ^ { + } \to \mathrm { C u }$ reaction. ABSTRACT: Acid copper electroplating stands as a core technology in advanced packaging processes, facilitating the realization of metal interconnects, bumps, vias, and substrate wiring between transistors. The deposition quality of copper interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of chips, directly influencing their yield, reliability, and stability. In this intricate process, additives play a pivotal role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metal copper. This mini-review comprehensively summarizes the recent research progress in the field of electroplating copper additives for advanced packaging, both domestically and internationally, delving into the types and mechanisms of various additive molecules, including accelerators, inhibitors, and leveling agents. Through in-depth research on these additives, we gain a profound understanding of their specific roles in the electroplating process and the intricate

interaction mechanisms among them, providing theoretical support for optimizing the electroplating process. Furthermore, this minireview also delves into a thorough analysis of the current issues and challenges facing acid copper electroplating, exploring the key factors that constrain the further development of electroplating copper technology. Based on this analysis, we propose several potential solutions and research directions, ofering crucial references for the development and application of electroplating copper additives in advanced packaging. In conclusion, this mini-review aims to provide a comprehensive perspective and profound understanding of the development and application of electroplating copper additives through a review and analysis of recent research progress, ultimately aiming to promote the further advancement of advanced packaging technology.

As modern electronic information products continue to evolve toward miniaturization, integration, functionality, and high reliability, there is a growing need for Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) to transition toward High-Density Interconnect (HDI) technology. This shift aims to facilitate the interconnection of electronic components, functional units, and chips on the PCB, ensuring optimal electrical connectivity. Integrated circuit packaging technology is progressing beyond two-dimensional spatial connections and moving toward three-dimensional spatial stacking techniques. HDI boards incorporate micro vias and fine-line technology into printed circuit boards. Electroplating stands out as a newcomer in the electronic packaging industry, bridging two significant national strategic emerging industries-information electronics and new materials.

Electroplating is the method of supplying electrons to the electroplating solution, facilitating the conversion of metal ions into elemental metal. Based on the source of electrons, electroplating can be categorized into three forms: electrolytic plating (electrons supplied by a power source), chemical plating (electrons provided by reducing agents in the electroplating solution), and displacement plating (electrons furnished by the substrate metal to be plated). Due to the dificulties in controlling chemical plating and displacement plating, their low eficiency, expensive chemical additives, and the frequent need for plating solution renewal, production generally opts for electrolytic plating for metal deposition. Compared to the other two processes, electrolytic plating is more eficient and does not require complex processing equipment. Additionally, electrolytic plating operates at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, featuring relatively simple process conditions. It stands out as one of the more extensively utilized methods at present.
## 2. DEVELOPMENT PROCESS OF THE ELECTROPLATING COPPER PROCESS

The utilization ofelectroplated copper for gap filling has become an essential technology. It is widely applied for metallization in high-density interconnects in integrated circuits, as well as for filling microvias in printed circuit boards and silicon vias in chip packaging. The copper electrodeposition method involves bottom-up filling within the hole to ensure gap-free coverage. This signifies that, during the electroplating process, the bottom of the hole exhibits the highest rate of copper deposition. As shown in Figure 1, the uneven distribution of primary and secondary currents results in lower current density at the bottom of the hole and higher current density at the mouth of the hole. The uneven distribution of local current density leads to less copper deposition at the bottom of the hole during the electroplating process, with more copper deposited at the mouth of the hole. This causes the gradual closure of the hole mouth, leading to the formation of voids or gaps in the middle of the hole.

## 3. MODELS FOR FILLING THROUGH-HOLES AND MICROVIA

Printed circuit boards play a crucial role in the electronics industry, bridging various components. In multilayer PCBs, achieving interlayer connectivity stands out as the most critical challenge. Interlayer connectivity encompasses three primary forms: through holes (TH), microvia, and buried holes. The following section focuses on through-holes and microvia. Additives are essential components in copper electroplating to meet the demand for void-free filling.

The methods of electroplating copper to fill microvia mainly include superequivalent-angle deposition, equivalent-angle deposition, and subequivalent-angle deposition. Among these methods, superequivalent-angle deposition is considered the ideal filling approach (i.e., filling from the bottom up). The fundamental principle of superequivalent-angle filling lies in the alteration ofcurrent distribution inside and outside the hole due to the action of additives. This leads to a higher copper deposition rate at the hole’s bottom than outside, facilitating a bottom-up filling process. Hence, the occurrence of voids and cracks is minimized. In contrast, equivalent-angle deposition and subequivalent-angle deposition may lead to issues such as cracks and voids inside the holes, compromising the reliability of hole interconnection.

Concerning the mechanism of superequivalent-angle electroplating filling, both the Curvature-Enhanced Accelerator Coverage (CEAC) model and the Convection-Dependent Adsorption (CDA) model can provide reasonable explanations for the flawless bottom-up filling process ofmicrovias. However, each model has its limitations (Figure 4).

CDA model:<sup>16</sup> It utilizes the convective intensity to influence the distribution of Cl<sup>−</sup> on the electrode surface in the plating solution, thereby determining the adsorption of additives. Specifically, strong convection increases the adsorption of Cl<sup>−</sup> on the electrode surface, thereby enhancing the adsorption of inhibitors and improving their inhibitory efect on the deposition of copper ions. In an environment with weak convection and low Cl<sup>−</sup> concentration, it is more conducive for the accelerator to enhance its depolarization efect, thereby expediting the deposition of copper. Consequently, there is a disparity in the copper deposition rates at the mouth and bottom of the hole, realizing the bottom-up filling of microvias.

CEAC model:<sup>17</sup> This model emphasizes changes in the geometric shape of microvias rather than the interaction of various additives. With the progression of the electroplating process, the hole surface undergoes internal contraction, leading to a reduction in the hole bottom surface area and a corresponding increase in curvature. At this stage, a significant amount of accelerator is adsorbed at the bottom of the microvia with a large curvature, further expediting the deposition of copper inside the hole and achieving bottom-up filling of microvias.

Ho et al.<sup>18,19</sup> conducted research on the filling process of microvias with diferent air flow rates and discovered that microvias filled in a butterfly pattern at an air flow rate of 70/ min. The filling process can be categorized into three stages: a. prefilling shape, b. shape-preserving equiangular deposition, c. burst filling period (formation of crosspoints). The common ality between filling through-holes and filling microvias is that, for filling through-holes, it is essential to first deposit a butterfly shaped “X-shaped” copper layer in the middle of the through hole. When the middle wings are closed, it is akin to electroplating two microvias simultaneously on opposite sides of the board in opposite directions, transitioning the electroplating from “X-shaped” to “V-shaped” filling. In practice, a comparable microvia filling process can be achieved by precovering the bottom of the through-hole with copper foil, filling it, and subsequently etching away the covered copper foil layer.

4.3. Inhibitors. In electroplating additives, inhibitors achieve the suppression of surface copper deposition by adsorbing onto the copper surface, enhancing cathodic polarization, and inhibiting the deposition of copper on the surface. Inhibitors are generally polyether substances with a certain molecular weight. Common inhibitors include polyethylene glycol (PEG), polypropylene glycol (PPG), and a copolymer of ethylene glycol and 1, 2-Propanediol (EPE). The molecular weight of PEG is around 6000 to 10000. Inhibitors have a larger molecular weight and are easily consumed during the electrodeposition process. Therefore, during electroplating, inhibitors primarily exhibit a gradient distribution on the surface ofthe plated piece. For PCB electroplated copper pillars, the bottom of microblind holes is relatively distant from the bulk solution, leading to a reduced distribution of inhibitors in this area. The concentration of inhibitors at the opening of the hole is closer to the concentration of inhibitors in the bulk solution. Additionally, as these polyol substances are excellent surfactants, they also function as wetting agents in copper electroplating. When the amount of inhibitor added is too small, resulting in insuficient wetting of the board surface, it causes the surface to appear red and dull.

It is important to note that inhibitors can only exhibit efective inhibitory efects when Cl<sup>−</sup> is present in the electroplating solution. 4.4.3. Methods for Screening Leveling Agents. Electroplating copper technology is the foundation for achieving electrical interconnection in printed circuit boards, packaging substrates, and integrated circuits. In the present era of rapid development in the electronics and information industry, unprecedented challenges have emerged. Electroplating is presently the most direct and accurate experimental method for studying copper electroplating technology, albeit with a lengthy experimental cycle and high costs. The use of electrochemical analysis and numerical simulation methods allows for the prediction ofadditive performance, thereby saving experimental time. 4.5. Interactions among Electroplating Additives. There is currently no fully unified understanding regarding the specific mechanism of accelerators. Currently, the more widely accepted view is the MPS-accelerated copper deposition mechanism proposed by Dow<sup>30</sup> and others (Figure 10). In this mechanism, MPS initially adsorbs on the electrode surface through the thiol group, and subsequently, its tail sulfonic acid group captures $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ in the solution and interacts with Cl<sup>−</sup> ions. The entire process involves an inner-sphere electron transfer mechanism. In the absence of Cl<sup>−</sup> ions in the plating solution, MPS or SPS will only exert inhibitory efects. The accelerating efect of SPS mainly results from the breaking of the disulfide bonds in its molecules into two MPS molecules under the influence of an electric field, and MPS is the substance that truly accelerates the process.

Dow et al.<sup>38</sup> proposed that when JGB serves as a leveling agent, there is a synergistic efect between JGB, PEG, and chloride ions, enhancing their inhibitory efects. This enhanced efect is realized through the formation of PEG-JGB-Cl<sup>−</sup> complexes generated during the electroplating process. The synergistic efect is related to the convection intensity, causing the inhibition of PEG-JGB-Cl<sup>−</sup> complexes in high convection areas and the accumulation of SPS at the bottom of blind holes, thereby achieving overfilling of the blind holes. Bandas et al.<sup>39</sup> studied the catalytic efect of amine leveling agents on SPS at the interface between copper and the electroplating solution, revealing that the influence of leveling agents on accelerators is related to the molecular weight of the leveling agent.
## 5. CHALLENGES AND ISSUES IN ACIDIC COPPERELECTROPLATING

The primary challenge in acidic copper electroplating lies in the incomplete understanding of the mechanisms of additives in the copper plating system, especially those of accelerators and leveling agents. Among them, the mechanism of leveling agents is of paramount importance. As leveling agents are vital for achieving uniform copper coatings, the challenge lies in correctly selecting and using appropriate additives when altering electroplating conditions, particularly in high current density electroplating.<sup>38</sup> Currently, in industrial electroplating practices, the current density for through-hole electroplating is generally strictly controlled below 3 A/dm,<sup>2</sup> and for plating blind holes, it is even lower, typically strictly controlled below 2 A/dm.<sup>2</sup> There are two main impacts of increasing current density.

First, it seriously diminishes the uniformity of the coating, resulting in greater diferences in thickness between the copper surface and the copper coating inside the hole. Excessively thin hole copper can lead to severe damage to the electrical performance and reliability of PCBs, which is strictly prohibited in electroplating production. Second, increasing current density will impact existing additive systems, necessitating the develop ment of new additive systems. However, developing an entirely new electroplating solution system has become increasingly challenging, requiring higher costs and more funding. Furthermore, higher current density will accelerate the consumption of accelerators, increase the dificulty of additive control, and significantly impact coating quality.

As chip integration continues to soar, the standards for copper filling capabilities and quality in silicon vias with exceptional aspect ratios, including through-silicon vias (TSVs) and blind vias, have escalated significantly. Presently, domestic inquiries into electroplating additives remain insuficiently exhaustive, with a scarcity of inquiries into the intricate interaction mechanisms among these additives. Consequently, electro plating solutions utilized in domestic chip manufacturing still heavily rely on imports, necessitating the urgent development of high-performance domestic electroplating copper additives. Therefore, the quest for additives that possess low toxicity, environmental friendliness, stability, and electroplating eficacy is paramount for attaining independent chip localization.

The subsequent electroplating solution development emphasizes the investigation of the electrochemical behavior’s influence on the grain growth and microstructure of electroplated copper during acidic deposition. This encompasses elucidating the copper crystal form transformation, meticulously controlling the microstructure, and comprehension of the copper coating’s mechanical property variations. Furthermore, revealing the regulatory mechanisms of additives on the mechanical properties of the copper coating material is paramount. Establishing a screening and design framework for organic additives with targeted functional groups is imperative, facilitating the creation of electroplating solutions tailored to meet the requirements of diverse semiconductor manufacturing processes.

# Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias†

The void-free blind microvia copper electroplating process is a key technology in HDI PCB manufacturing. This work systematically studied the influence of the Acid Blue 1 (AB1) leveler on blind microvia filling. AB1 exhibits excellent suppression during electroplating, with its efect strengthening as the AB1 concentration increases. Chronopotentiometry was used to study the interaction among AB1, SPS, and PEG. There is a synergistic suppressing interaction between the new leveler AB1 and suppressor PEG, while there is competition between AB1 and accelerator SPS. During electrodeposition, AB1 can adsorb on the copper substrate to reduce active sites and suppress copper electrodeposition, based on theoretical studies and in situ infrared spectroscopy. At the optimized electroplating process, void-free microvia filling is achieved with 20 mg L<sup>-1</sup> AB1 and successive electroplating confirms the stability of AB1. Based on difusion diferences among additives and the competition between AB1 and SPS, a gradient competitive adsorption superfilling mechanism was proposed to illustrate the filling process of the AB1–SPS–PEG system. AB1 is beneficial to improving flatness and lowering surface roughness of the copper layer, which is conducive to reducing signal losses during high-frequency transmission. Additionally, AB1 can modulate the preferential formation of Cu(111) and Cu(200) and facilitate grain refinement.

High-density interconnect (HDI) printed circuit boards (PCBs) serve as a foundational platform for connecting all kinds of electronic components in electronic products, thus attracting significant research attention.<sup>1</sup> With the trend toward smallersized electronic devices with higher performance, stricter requirements are imposed on PCB design and manufacturing technology.<sup>2,3</sup> Especially in the fields of high-performance computing, high-speed communication, and precision instruments, the reliability and performance of PCBs are directly related to the performance and stability of the final products. Blind microvia filling is a key interconnect technology in the manufacturing process of PCBs, allowing for electrical connections between diferent layers in the circuit board.<sup>4,5</sup> The application of this technology enhances PCB design flexibility, enabling more complex circuit layouts and greater space utilization.

Copper is widely used as an interconnect line in blind microvias for PCB manufacturing due to its good electronic (thermal and electrical conductivity) and mechanical (wear resistance and elongation, etc.) properties.<sup>6,7</sup> The filling of blind microvias with copper is achieved through electroplating technology.<sup>8–10</sup> In PCBs, copper not only provides a stable electrical connection but also enhances the structural strength of HDI PCBs, improving heat and wear resistance.<sup>11</sup> Moreover, copper interconnect lines effectively reduce losses in signal transmission and enhance signal integrity, which is especially important for high-frequency and high-speed circuits.<sup>12</sup> During copper electroplating, it is essential to adjust the metal deposition process in local microvias to avoid the formation of void defects caused by the edge effect, which can undermine the properties of the copper interconnect layer. The most common method is the addition of proper additives.<sup>13–15</sup>

The additives used in copper electroplating fall into three categories: accelerators, suppressors, and levelers.<sup>16</sup> The most commonly used accelerator, suppressor, and leveler is bis-(sodium sulfopropyl)- disulfide (SPS), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and Janus Green B (JGB).<sup>17</sup> During electroplating, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, in situ Raman spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) studies reveal that the disulfide bond of SPS will break up, with the sulfurcontaining side adsorbing on the copper base, while the other side (containing a sulfonic acid group) captures free $\operatorname { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ to accelerate reduction with adsorbed Cl<sup>-</sup> through the ‘‘bridging efect’’.<sup>18–20</sup> As for PEG, in situ Raman and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirm the formation of $\mathbf { P E G - C u ^ { 2 + } - C l ^ { - } }$ adsorbate complexes, which increase the energy barrier and suppress copper electrodeposition.<sup>21–23</sup> Mass spectrometry (MS) and DFT calculations demonstrate that the azo group of JGB competes with the reduction of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ to obtain electrons, leading to dissociation<sup>24,25</sup> into phenazine derivatives that can also adsorb on active sites to suppress copper growth.<sup>26,27</sup> Among these additives, levelers are key components for achieving defect-free filling in blind vias.<sup>28</sup> Nowadays, triphenylmethane derivatives are promising levelers and have been used in throughhole and blind-hole filling due to the unlocalized orbital distribution of the tertiary amine structure.<sup>29,30</sup>

In this work, a novel triphenylmethane derivative, Acid Blue 1 (AB1), was selected as a potential leveler, and the efects of diferent concentrations of AB1 on copper electroplating were investigated. The interactions among three diferent types of additives were studied using galvanostatic measurements. The influencing mechanism of AB1 on the copper cathode surface during electroplating was also studied theoretically and experimentally. The filling performance of AB1 in blind microvias was examined, and the electroplating process was optimized. Additionally, the surface morphology and roughness of the copper interconnect layer were analyzed, and finite element simulation was employed to study the high-frequency signal transmission losses influenced by AB1, while phase structure was investigated by XRD.

3.3.2 Filling mechanism. The difusion property of AB1 was studied using molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as shown in Fig. S8 (ESI†). Based on the Einstein equation (eqn (S2), ESI†), the difusion coeficient for AB1 $\left( D _ { \mathbf { A B 1 } } \right)$ is 2  $1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is close to the difusion coeficient for PEG $\left( D _ { \mathrm { P E G } } , 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } \right) ^ { 5 0 }$ and one order smaller than that for SPS $\big ( D _ { \mathrm { S P S } } , 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { ~ m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { ~ s } ^ { - 1 } \big ) . ^ { 5 1 }$ This illustrates that the leveler AB1 and suppressor PEG have slower difusion transport compared to the accelerator SPS. Coupled with the interactions among the three additives discussed in Section 3.1.3, namely the competition between AB1 and SPS, as well as cooperation between AB1 and PEG, gradient competitive adsorption superfilling was proposed to illustrate the AB1–SPS–PEG system, with a schematic diagram shown in Fig. 3d. At the initial stage (3d1), different additives are distributed uniformly within the microvias. As the filling process progresses (3d2), a concentration gradient for the additives forms due to their consumption and local diffusion transport limitations within the microvias. However, the concentration ratio of SPS to PEG and AB1 at the bottom increases compared to that at the opening area due to the differing diffusion properties among the three additives; specifically, $D _ { \mathrm { S P S } }$ is significantly larger than $D _ { \mathbf { A B 1 } }$ and $D _ { \mathbf { P E G } } .$ . As a result, the growth rate at the bottom is improved by the increased accelerating effect from the relatively amount of SPS, while growth at the opening area is effectively suppressed since AB1’s mass transport is not limited due to convection, leading to copper growth from the bottom to the top. At the final stage (3d3), the three additives redistribute uniformly at the opening area, resulting in the same growth rate across different areas. No momentum plating phenomena occur in the AB1–SPS–PEG system.<sup>52</sup>

A novel leveler, Acid Blue 1, was used to achieve void-free copper filling in blind microvias. Electrochemical tests (CV and EIS) confirm the suppressive efect on the reduction of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ . During copper electroplating, there is a synergistic suppression between AB1 and PEG, but competition between AB1 and SPS. DFT calculations and in situ infrared spectroscopy provide a deeper understanding of AB1 adsorption configuration on the copper substrate during electrodeposition, indicating that AB1 can reduce active sites and act as a barrier adsorption layer to increase cathodic polarization. After electroplating optimization, microvias with diameters of 125 mm and 150 mm can be filled with 20 mg $\mathrm { L } ^ { - 1 }$ AB1 at $1 . 5 \mathrm { A } \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 } ;$ the good stability of AB1 indicates its industrial potential. A gradient competitive adsorption superfilling mechanism was proposed to explain the filling process for the AB1–SPS–PEG system. The diffusion differences among the three additives and the competition between AB1 and SPS are key to achieving bottom-up growth in microvias. AB1 improves the copper layer quality, enhances surface flatness, refines the grains, and reduces signal losses during high-frequency transmission. Additionally, AB1 suppresses the formation of Cu(220) while promoting the formation of Cu(111) and Cu(200).
# Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes

ABSTRACT: Driven by the rapid development of 5G/6G communications, high-performance computing, and artificial intelligence, the metallization of high-aspect-ratio through-holes (THs) in printed circuit boards (PCBs) imposes stringent requirements on the thickness uniformity and interconnect reliability of electroplated copper layers. This study systematically investigates the application of a novel leveler, thiazolyl blue (MTT), for PCB THs’ electroplating, successfully realizing high-quality conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio (10:1) THs. Electrochemical analyses demonstrate that MTT significantly enhances the cathodic polarization and efectively inhibits the reduction of Cu<sup>2+</sup>. Meanwhile, microscopic morphological characterizations confirm

that MTT exhibits excellent leveling capability, reducing the surface roughness of the copper deposit to as low as 0.147 μm. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the high inhibitory eficiency of MTT originates from the dominant interfacial adsorption of MTT at the cathode. with the bulk cation-π interaction with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ contributing as a minor secondary effect at the microscopic level. Crystallographic and interfacial wettability analyses further indicate that MTT effectively refines the grain size and promotes the preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane while improving the wettability of the plating bath. In practical high-aspect-ratio through-hole plating tests, the introduction of MTT substantially increases the throwing power (TP) from 25.2% to 96.8%. Based on these results, a competitive interfacial polarization remodeling mechanism governed by multiphysics coupling is proposed to elucidate the intrinsic role of MTT in promoting conformal through-hole deposition. This work provides a solid theoretical foundation and practical engineering guidance for the fabrication of highly reliable, high-frequency 3D interconnected PCB structures.

Driven by the rapid advancement of 5G/6G communications, high-performance computing, and artificial intelligence (AI), printed circuit boards (PCBs)�the mother of electronic products�are undergoing profound technological revolutions.<sup>1−3</sup> As the fundamental carrier connecting electronic components, the PCB not only provides mechanical support for chips and passive devices but also functions as the neural network sustaining signal transmission and power delivery throughout the electronic system.<sup>4</sup> With the accelerated evolution of PCBs toward high integration, high interconnect density, and high-frequency/high-speed transmission, this trajectory poses two intertwined materials challenges. On the device side, the suppression of electromagnetic interference, interlayer crosstalk, and thermal accumulation in densely packed high-frequency boards has stimulated intensive research into advanced electromagnetic functional materials, with MXene-based two-dimensional absorbers and heterostructured composites emerging as a particularly promising family that delivers eficient GHz-to-THz electromagnetic wave absorption and integrated thermal management.<sup>5−8</sup> On the interconnect side, the multilayer copper network that mechanically and electrically links the chips must, in parallel, be reformulated to simultaneously sustain signal integrity, ensure robust interconnect reliability, and guarantee long-term service lifespan under increasingly aggressive high-frequency operation�demands that ultimately translate into unprece dentedly stringent requirements on the copper metallization of microvias with high aspect ratios. Copper electrodeposition in high-aspect-ratio through-holes (THs) is the core technology for achieving interlayer electrical interconnection in multilayer PCBs. The quality of this metallization directly dictates the signal integrity, current-carrying capacity, and long-term service lifespan of the electronic devices.<sup>9,10</sup>

However, during the practical electroplating of high-aspect ratio THs, the initial current distribution is highly nonuniform due to geometric constraints. The local current density at the via opening is significantly higher than that at the center, accompanied by severe mass transfer limitations of Cu<sup>2+</sup> within the hole. This multiphysics imbalance frequently triggers the “dog-bone” defect, characterized by excessive copper accumulation at the via opening and excessively thin deposits on the inner walls.<sup>11</sup> Such nonuniform deposition severely compromises the electrical and mechanical performance of the interconnected structures, constituting a universal bottleneck in the high-density interconnect (HDI) industry.<sup>12</sup> To overcome this challenge, it is imperative to introduce suppressors, accelerators, and levelers into the acidic copper sulfate bath.<sup>13</sup> The precise synergistic and competitive adsorption among these three additives dynamically modulates the deposition kinetics at diferent spatial locations within the TH, ultimately achieving high-quality conformal interconnection.

Typically, polyether macromolecules (e.g., polyethylene glycol, PEG) serve as suppressors; bridged by chloride ions, they profoundly enhance cathodic polarization and retard copper growth.<sup>14</sup> Sulfonate compounds bearing thiol or disulfide groups (e.g., bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide, SPS) act as accelerators: they capture Cu<sup>2+</sup> at the cathode interface and lower the activation barrier for its reduction.<sup>15</sup> Among the plating formulations, the leveler plays the most critica interfacial regulatory role. By preferentially adsorbing at strongly convected regions (e.g., the opening), the leveler establishes a localized high-impedance barrier that inhibits overplating,<sup>16−18</sup> thereby compelling the spatial electric field lines to redistribute deeper into TH.<sup>19−21</sup> To date, various commercial dyes have been reported as levelers (e.g., Janus Green B, tetrazolium blue chloride, PAN).<sup>22−24</sup> Meanwhile, some researchers have devoted eforts to the synthesis of nove polymeric levelers (e.g., VIBDGE, PBDGE, Sudan-QNL). 25−27 Nevertheless, each of the aforementioned levelers exhibits specific limitations. Polymeric levelers such as VIBDGE and PBDGE, despite their promising performance, typically require multistep synthesis and tedious purification procedures, which considerably increase the production cost and hinder their practical scalability. Commercial dye-based levelers (e.g., Janus Green B) are readily accessible and have been widely adopted in industry with proven efectiveness; however, as the aspec ratio of through-holes continues to increase, further enhance ment of throwing power remains highly desirable to ensure the thickness uniformity and long-term reliability of the copper interconnects. In this regard, MTT ofers a compelling combination of advantages: it is a commercially available, of the-shelf reagent that can be directly procured at low cost entirely eliminating the need for custom synthesis or purification, and as will be demonstrated in Section 3.5, it delivers a throwing power (TP = 96.8%) that markedly outperforms the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical bath composition and process conditions. Therefore, a systematic investigation of MTT as a tailored leveler for high aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating is of urgent practical significance.

It is worth noting that MTT has previously been explored in other copper electrodeposition contexts. Ogutu et al. first introduced MTT as a single additive for superconformal filling of through-glass vias (TGVs) with aspect ratios up to 10:1 in methanesulfonate-based electrolytes.<sup>28</sup> More recently, Yang et al. compared MTT with iodonitrotetrazolium chloride (INT) in a sulfate-based acidic electroplating system for blind via copper filling and reported that MTT exhibits a conformal type filling tendency rather than the bottom-up superfilling behavior required for microvia applications.<sup>29</sup> However, the performance of MTT in high-aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating�an application scenario in which conformal, uniform thickness distribution rather than bottom-up super filling is the primary objective�has not yet been systematically investigated. The present work therefore complements these prior studies by examining MTT as a leveler within a sulfate based acidic electroplating system specifically tailored for through-hole plating, thereby establishing the suitability of MTT for this distinct application scenario. It should also be noted that our group recently reported tetrazolium blue chloride (TB) as a leveler for copper through-hole electro plating. Although TB and MTT both belong to the tetrazolium family, their molecular architectures difer considerably: TB bears two methoxy-phenyl substituents on the tetrazolium ring, whereas MTT carries a 4,5-dimethylthiazole moiety together with two unsubstituted phenyl groups. Such substituent diferences lead to distinguishable electrochemical responses and leveling outcomes. At their respective optimized conditions, TB exhibits a relatively large convection-dependent polarization response with Δη ≈ 31 mV, yielding a TP value of 136.7% along with preferential Cu(111) growth, whereas MTT, as demonstrated in the present study, shows a smaller Δη ≈ 19.3 mV and afords a TP value of 96.8% accompanied by a preferential Cu(200) growth (see Sections 3.4 and 3.5). A recent comparative investigation by Yang et al. likewise reported that MTT exhibits filling characteristics distinct from those of its nitro-substituted tetrazolium analog INT, further supporting the notion that subtle substituent variations within the tetrazolium family can give rise to markedly diferent leveling behaviors.<sup>29</sup> These observations together underscore that MTT represents a distinct leveler within the tetrazolium family and warrants dedicated investigation for high-aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating applications.

This work systematically investigates the application performance of thiazolyl blue tetrazolium bromide (MTT) as a highly eficient leveler in PCB TH electroplating. Utilizing scanning electron microscopy and laser confocal microscopy, the exceptional microscopic leveling efect of MTT on the surface morphology of the electrodeposited copper layer is intuitively revealed. Furthermore, X-ray difraction and contact angle measurements are employed to deeply analyze its regulatory efects on crystallographic phase evolution and solid−liquid interfacial wettability. More importantly, this study establishes a multiscale analytical framework integrating macroscopic electrochemical analyses with microscopic quantum chemical calculations to comprehensively elucidate the TH filling mechanism of MTT under multiphysics coupling. Ultimately, through precise optimization of the additive concentration ratio and related processing parameters, high-quality conformal electrodeposition in high-aspect-ratio PCB THs is successfully realized.

All electrochemical measurements were performed in a standard three-electrode electrolysis cell, with test control and data collection accomplished using a Gamry Reference 3000 potentiostat/galvanostat (Gamry Instruments, USA). A 5 mm-diameter platinum disk rotating electrode (RDE) was selected as the working electrode (WE). A platinum sheet electrode $( 1 \ \times \ 2 \ \mathrm { ~ c m } ^ { 2 } )$ was used as the counter electrode, and a saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (SSE, Hg/ $\mathrm { H g } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } )$ served as the reference electrode (RE). Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were conducted over a potential window of −0.8 to 0.2 V (vs SSE). Prior to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) characterization, a copper layer was electrodeposited onto the RDE surface in the virgin makeup solution (VMS) at a constant current density of 1.5 A dm<sup>−2</sup> for 60 s, thus converting the Pt-RDE to a Cu-RDE. EIS measurements were executed at 1000 rpm with an alternating current (AC) amplitude of 10 mV, a direct current (DC) bias potential of −0.5 V (vs SSE), and a frequency sweep range of 10 to 10<sup>−2</sup> Hz. For chronopotentiometry (CP) tests, a constant current density of 2 A $\mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 }$ was applied to the electrode system. Under normal conditions, the rate of cathodic copper electrodeposition is positively correlated with the forced convection intensity of the plating bath because forced convection reduces the thickness of the $\dot { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ difusion boundary layer. However, the plating bath contains not only ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ but also various additives, which greatly complicate the mass transfer process at the cathode surface. According to the convection-dependent adsorption mechanism (CDA), a qualified plating bath system should exhibit the following behavior: a faster copper deposition rate under weakly forced convection and a relatively slower rate under strongly forced convection.<sup>30</sup>

The regulatory efect of the MTT additive on the surface morphology of the electrodeposited copper layers was systematically investigated utilizing a scanning electron microscope and a laser confocal microscope. As depicted in Figure $^ { \mathrm { 1 b , } }$ the copper coating electrodeposited in VMS (without MTT) exhibits a distinctly rough and uneven morphology, characterized by the presence of large and coarse crystalline particles on the surface. In sharp contrast, upon the introduction of MTT into the plating bath (Figure 1c−g), the surface flatness of the coatings shows a dramatic enhancement. With an incremental increase in MTT concentration, the crystalline morphology transitions progressively toward a highly compact and smooth state. This observation unambiguously indicates that MTT possesses excellent leveling capability at the microscopic scale, efectively refining the grain size and upgrading the surface quality. When the skin depth diminishes to a scale comparable to the surface roughness of the copper traces, the high-frequency current is forced to travel along the tortuous, rugged surface contour, thereby substantially elongating the actual conductive pathway. Consequently, a copper deposit with inherently low surface roughness can substantially reduce the transmission loss of high-frequency signals. In summary, functioning as a highly eficient leveler, MTT can significantly enhance the surface flatness and compactness of the electro plated copper layers, fulfilling the stringent physical requirements for high-frequency interconnects.

## 3.5. TH Electrodeposition Performance

To comprehensively evaluate the through-hole filling capability of MTT, the thickness uniformity of its electrodeposited copper layers within printed circuit board (PCB) throughholes was systematically characterized. In the PCB through hole electroplating process, Throwing Power (TP) serves as the pivotal quantitative index for evaluating the internal deposit thickness uniformity and evaluating the quality of the copper interconnects. The magnitude of the TP directly dictates the electrical reliability and long-term service lifespan of the 3D interconnected structures. Figures 5a,b, and S6 display high-resolution metallographic cross-sectional optical micrographs of the through-holes after electrodeposition under various MTT concentrations. At a constant current density of $2 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ,$ when VMS exclusively contains the accelerator SPS and the suppressor PEG (Figure 5a), the TP value of the through-hole is only 25.2%. At this juncture, a distinct geometric disparity exists between the deposit thickness at the opening and that in the central region, resulting in a severe “dog-bone” morphological defect that fundamentally fails to meet the electrical reliability requirements for high-density interconnects. Remarkably, with the introduction of MTT into the plating system, this geometric efect of uneven deposit distribution is efectively suppressed, and the overall coating morphology transits almost into a conformal deposition. As illustrated in Figure 5b, upon adding an optimal MTT concentration of 50 mg/L, the TP value increases to 96.8%. This visually dictates that MTT bridges the thickness gap between the surface opening and the deep interior, achieving high-quality conformal thickening of the copper layer within the through-hole.

To further benchmark the leveling performance of MTT against a well-established commercial leveler, a comparative through-hole electroplating experiment was conducted using 50 mg/L Janus Green B (JGB) under identical bath composition and process conditions. As illustrated in Figure S6d, the cross-sectional metallographic micrograph of the through-hole electroplated with JGB reveals a relatively uniform copper distribution along the hole wall, with no pronounced “dog-bone” defect observable at the orifice. Nevertheless, the overall copper deposit thickness within the through-hole remains noticeably thin compared to that achieved with MTT, yielding a TP value of approximately 84.5%. Although this TP value represents a substantial improvement over the additive-free system (TP = 25.2%), it remains significantly inferior to the 96.8% attained with 50 mg/L MTT. This performance disparity can be rationalized by the stronger cathodic polarization and more pronounced convection-dependent adsorption behavior of MTT, as demonstrated by the electrochemical analyses in Section 3.2. The higher inhibitory potency of MTT at the forcedconvection orifice region enables a more efective redistribution of the electric field lines toward the through-hole interior, thereby yielding superior thickness uniformity. These comparative results unequivocally corroborate the exceptional leveling eficacy of MTT and its marked advantage over the conventional JGB leveler in high-aspect-ratio through-hole electroplating applications.

Coupling the theoretical elucidation of the MTT inhibition mechanism in Section 3.3 with previous studies, competitive interfacial polarization remodeling driven by a multiphysics coupling mechanism was proposed to unveil the intrinsic influence of MTT. As portrayed in the schematic mechanism (Figure 5c), governed by the coupling of fluid dynamics (convective mass transfer) and electrochemical kinetics, MTT, PEG, and SPS undergo competitive adsorption at the solid− liquid interface within the through-hole. This induces a spatially diferentiated distribution of polarization resistance, reshaping the potential field across the inner surface of the through-hole. Specifically, propelled by the forced convection at the hole opening, MTT rapidly accumulates and adsorbs in this region via convection-dependent adsorption (CDA).<sup>54,55</sup> Concurrently, MTT interacts synergistically with the PEG polymer chains and the bridging chloride ions to form a dense ternary synergistic suppression film on the copper substrate. This compact adsorption layer triggers a notable increase in the local polarization resistance at the opening. The resulting elevated electrochemical reaction barrier efectively suppresses the electroreduction kinetics of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ in this vicinity. Consequently, the increased polarization resistance at the orifice compels the spatial electric field lines $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ the primary current distribution) to redistribute toward the deep interior of the through-hole, which is situated in a weak convection zone.<sup>56,57</sup> Through this polarization remodeling efect, the inherent Ohmic potential drop caused by the geometric aspect ratio of the through-hole is compensated. Simultaneously, a steady-state difusion flux of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ directed into the hole is sustained, ultimately driving the realization of a conformal through-hole deposition.

In summary, this study systematically investigated the application performance and multiphysics coupling mechanisms of MTT, acting as a leveler for copper electrodeposition in PCB through-holes. Electrochemical evaluations demon strate that MTT significantly enhances cathodic polarization via a convection-dependent interfacial adsorption. Meanwhile, microscopic morphological characterization confirms that MTT exhibits excellent leveling capability, significantly reducing the surface roughness of the copper deposit to 0.147 μm. Such a smooth surface topography is highly beneficial for mitigating the skin efect and lowering insertion loss during high-frequency signal transmission. Density functional theory analysis further elucidates that the microscopic origin of this robust inhibitory behavior lies primarily in the strong interfacial adsorption of MTT at the cathode, with the bulk cation−π interaction with ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ contributing as a minor secondary efect. Phase structure and interface analysis illustrate that an optimal MTT concentration (50 mg/L) not only efectively refines the crystalline grain size and promotes the preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane but also decreases the solid−liquid interfacial contact angle to ${ 5 4 . 6 } ^ { \circ } ,$ thereby fundamentally suppressing the generation of macroscopic morphological defects. Ultimately, in practical throughhole electroplating applications, the competitive adsorption among MTT, PEG, and SPS induces a spatially diferentiated remodeling of polarization resistance. By establishing a high impedance barrier at the forced-convection orifice region, the inherent Ohmic potential drop within the through-holes is efectively compensated. Driven by this multiphysical coupling mechanism, the TP value of through-holes is substantially elevated from 25.2% to 96.8%, markedly outperforming the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical conditions, successfully achieving high-quality conformal deposition and providing a theoretical and practical basis for the fabrication of highly reliable, high-frequency 3D interconnected PCB structures.
