BNS on the cobalt surface and enhanced cathodic polarization. BNS also transforms the nucleation of cobalt from instantaneous nucleation to progressive nucleation, result ing in a more uniform and dense cobalt film morphology. The selectivity and strong adsorption of BNS on the cobalt plane are the reasons for the preferential orientation growth of the (002) crystal plane. After annealing, the cobalt film prepared by BNS had obvious grain growth, obvious impurity difusion, and further improved electrical properties. Su et al.<sup>95</sup> showed that the hardness of nanocrystalline Co coatings increases with the decrease of grain size. Small average grain sizes and smooth surfaces contribute to the improvement of corrosion resistance of the coatings. A coating obtained by reverse pulse electrodeposition had the finest grains, the highest hardness, and the highest corrosion resistance, followed by bipolar pulse electrodeposition. Hardness, surface roughness, morphology, and phase structure have significant efects on the tribological properties and wear mechanism of nanocrystalline Co coatings, with those prepared by dual pulse electrodeposition showing the highest wear resistance and the lowest friction due to their higher hardness and smoothness. Nanocrystalline Co coatings prepared by reverse pulse electrodeposition showed the highest friction and the lowest wear resistance due to their higher surface roughness, the absence of an hcp(110) peak, and the weakening of the hcp(100) peak.

At present, the study of cobalt electroplating often obtains average information of various thermodynamics and kinetics of the electrode/solution interface and electrode surface processes at the macrolevel by using classical electrochemical research methods and theoretical calculations. However, classical electrochemical research methods find it dificult to identify the characteristics of electrode reaction intermediates and products, and cannot provide mechanism information at the microscopic and molecular levels. Some advanced in situ characterization methods are used in copper electroplating .<sup>96–99</sup> Therefore, advanced electrochemical in situ research methods should be used in the future. In addition, annealing treatment of cobalt coatings is also a future research direction.

The nucleation and growth process of cobalt electrocrystallization determines the quality and performance of the cobalt coating.<sup>108</sup> Since the cobalt nucleation and growth process is very rapid, the crystal nuclei grown at the solid/liquid interface are submicron/nanoscale, which brings certain difficulties to in  situ research. In situ transmission electron microscopy or in situ scanning electron microscopy) has high spatial resolution and are the most intuitive and eficient research method for studying nucleation and growth.<sup>109–111</sup> In situ observation, recording the nucleation and growth behavior of the initial stage of metal deposition, and studying the influence of additives on the cobalt nucleation process and growth, can provide theoretical guidance and technical support for electroplating, especially chip electroplating.

The introduction of impurity atoms afects the grain structure and preferred orientation of cobalt, and its redistribution and segregation in the coating will also afect the change of resistance.<sup>114,115</sup> Like copper electroplating, the electroplated cobalt also needs to be annealed and recrystallized to allow the impurities in the coating to escape and thus improve its conductivity.

Electroplating is a critical technology in high-end electronic manufacturing, including integrated circuits. As interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, copper electroplating is increasingly unable to meet the required performance and safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt electroplating, current research has primarily focused on the electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias, along with proposed filling mechanisms. However, several key aspects remain insuficiently explored. These include the specific actions and synergistic/antagonistic interactions of components such as boric acid and additives in the plating bath, the mechanisms by which pH, temperature, and individual bath components influence cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Future research directions should prioritize the development and application of advanced in situ techniques, including morphological, spectroscopic, and energy spectroscopic, to address these challenges. Clarifying these mechanisms will be essential for advancing cobalt electroplating as a viable interconnect technology in next-generation chip fabrication.

The metal cobalt is expected to be the next generation of interconnect materials due to its shorter average free path of electrons and greater resistance to electromigration. Additives especially the leveling agents are key regulatory factors for achieving a bottom-up dense superfilling of interconnect metals in the electroplating process. Here the hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) with methylene structure was chosen as a leveling agent to study the deposition behavior and the blind hole filling behavior of cobalt. The electrochemical analysis showed that the HMTA exhibits an evident inhibition ability on the deposition of cobalt. Moreover, this inhibitory ability has a significant dependence on the rotational speed of the solution and a greater inhibitory effect on the deposition of cobalt occurs at high rotational speeds.The simulation indicates that such a strong inhibition ability on the deposition of cobalt sourced from the preferred adsorption of the leveling agent on the cobalt surface by the nucleophilic active site provided by the methylene structure of HMTA. Such preferential adsorption behavior was further confirmed by the captured vibration peaks of C–N and C–H bonds associated with the HMTA from the in-situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy. Under the action of this leveling agent, the metal cobalt exhibits the expected bottom-up growth behavior in blind holes of Printed circuit board (PCB) The addition of HMTA is also beneficial for obtaining a flat and dense coating with preferred growth of (100) crystal planes. These results indicate that the HMTA is a potential effective leveling agent for the cobalt interconnects processes.

Cu interconnect has become a typical interconnect technology for large-scale and ultra large scale integrated circuits due to its excellent conductivity, high reliability, and resistance to electromigration [1]. However, as the feature size of the chip process decreases to below 10 nm, the resistance of Cu interconnect will significantly increase [2], which will seriously affect the reliability and communication speed improvement of the chip [3]. Therefore, finding more suitable conductive materials for filling nanoscale interconnect has become the key to chip micro integration along Moore’s Law. Metal cobalt is expected to replace copper interconnect as the next generation of interconnect materials in chip processes due to its lower average free path of electrons, smaller size effect, and better resistance to electromigration compared to copper [4]. Therefore, cobalt interconnect have become one of the research hotspots in the field of chip processes in recent years. The current chip copper interconnect mainly adopts the damascus electrodeposition process. In the damascus electrodeposition process, the application of two typical additives, namely inhibitors and accelerators, is necessary to obtain high-quality electroplating filling layers [5]. Inhibitors and accelerators are selectively adsorbed in the chip groove hole area to suppress copper deposition and at the bottom of the groove to accelerate copper deposition. With the synergistic effect of these two types of additives, copper can achieve dense filling from bottom to top from the groove hole bottom [6]. Given the filling copper process of electroplating copper in damascene, recent research on cobalt interconnect has mainly focused on seeking suitable accelerators and inhibitors to achieve bottom-up cobalt super filling in trenches and some suitable additives for cobalt super filling have been proposed.

In the research on cobalt interconnect electroplating accelerators, recent researchers have mainly attempted to use accelerators used in the damascus copper interconnect electroplating process as accelerators for cobalt interconnect electroplating to explore their effects on cobalt deposition behavior and filling ability.These accelerators typically contain specific functional groups such as (-S-S-), thiols (-SH), and sul fonic acids $\left( - S 0 _ { 3 } \right)$ [7]. The result indicate that the adsorption sites during cobalt electrodeposition ar provided by functional groups such as the imine group of DMG, the sulfonic acid group of SPS, and the imidazole group of HIS. However, th actual effects of these three additives need further research. Recently, some studies indicated that the nitrogen-containing com pounds can form coordination bonds with the cobalt surface or ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ [17–20] by utilizing the lone pair electrons of nitrogen and thereby produce effectively suppress the reduction of cobalt. The HMTA is a kind of nitrogen-containing small molecule compounds containing methylene structures, which indicates that the HMTA is a potential inhibitor for cobalt deposition. Meanwhile, this HMTA is a stable compound that is not easily decomposed at high temperatures. Therefore, in this work, the HMTA molecules was selected to be as leveling agents for cobalt interconnect electrodeposition. ## 2.4. Electrodeposition

The blind hole filling experiment was carried out in acidic cobalt sulfate plating bath and DC electrodeposition process at room temperature with current density of $\mathrm { 1 . 0 A / d m } ^ { \bar { 2 } } .$ The acidic cobalt sulfate plating solution was composed of 75 $g / \mathrm { L }$ $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } 0$ , 35 $g / \mathrm { L }$ boric acid $\mathrm { ( H _ { 3 } B O _ { 3 } ) }$ , 50 ppm $\mathrm { C I } ^ { - } ( \mathrm { C o C l } _ { 2 } ) ;$ , 14 ppm 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate sodium salt (MPS), 0.005 g/L Sodium lauryl sulfate $\left( \mathrm { C _ { 1 2 } H _ { 2 5 } S O _ { 4 } N a } \right)$ and 9-15 ppm HMTA $\mathrm { ( C _ { 6 } H _ { 1 2 } N _ { 4 } ) }$ . During electroplating filling experi ment, a pure cobalt plate acted as the anode and the PCB plate with the blind hole acts as the cathode and the pH of electroplating solution was adjusted between 3.5 and 4.5 by using $\mathrm { H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } }$ and NaOH. Here, two types of PCB with different blind hole size (hole diameter and depth of $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $1 2 5 \mu \mathrm { m } \times 1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } ,$ , respectively) were used in the filling experiments. In order to analyze the filling behavior of cobalt in blind holes, blind hole filling experiments were conducted at 1 hour, 2 h, and 5 h to capture the phased state of cobalt blind hole filling. Pretreatment is required before electroplating.The cathode PCB should be washed with ethanol, then immersed in 1 mol/L sulfuric acid solution for 3 min to remove surface oxides, and then rinsed thoroughly with deionized water. Then, the PCB and the stainless steel surface are connected with conductive adhesive, and the other stainless steel surfaces were coatedwith insulating adhesive, transparent adhesive, etc. to ensure that only the PCB can touch the plating solution. The pure cobalt anode plate was activated by immersion in 1 mol/L sulfuric acid for 3 min before electroplating and then washed with deionized water. When conducting electroplating filling experiments, the current density is controlled at $1 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ;$ , and good mass transfer is ensured by a DC regulated power supply and magnetic stirrer. For a more detailed pretreatment process, see the literature [25,26].

CV was used to analyze the inhibitory effect of HMTA molecule concentration on cobalt metal deposition at two different rotational speeds where the 100 rpm is used to simulate the weak convection at the bottom of the blind hole and the 1600 rpm is used to simulate the strong convection at the orifice area of the blind hole to evaluate the suppression efficiency under different mass transfer conditions and the CV results are shown in Fig. 1 and the corresponding absolute areas of dissolution peaks obtained from the CV curves is summarized. It can be seen Fig. 1 that the addition of HMTA leads to a decrease in the dissolution peak of cobalt at the low and high speeds, indicating that HMTA has an inhibitory effect on cobalt electrodeposition. Furthermore, as the concentration of HMTA increases from 1 ppm to 13 ppm, the dissolution peak of cobalt continues to decrease, indicating that the inhibitory ability of adding high concentrations of HMTA on cobalt deposition will become greater. But it is worth emphasizing that although the CV results indicate that the inhibitory ability of HMTA on cobalt deposition continues to increase with increasing concentration, it was found through the Hall cell experiments that the quality of the cobalt coating decreases when the concentration exceeds 13 ppm. # Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects

In advanced electronic manufacturing, additives play a pivotal role in achieving high-quality metal interconnect by enabling precise pattern filling during electrodeposition. Currently, due to complex mechanisms, vast molecular spaces and lack of predictive models, the development of additives still relies on inefficient trial-and-error methods. In this work, a machine learning (ML)-based data-driven framework is developed to accelerate the discovery of cobalt electrodeposition additives. Focusing on molecular adsorption dynamics at the cobalt elec trolyte interface during electrodeposition, this work employs quantum chemical properties to guide the construction of machine learning models for identifying molecules with ideal adsorption potential. Bayesian optimization is employed to optimize model accuracy by tuning hyperparameters, and SHAP analysis provides interpretable chemical insights. Three novel additives are identified, which are 2-aminopyrazine (APZ), 1-methylimidazole-4,5-dicarbonitrile (MIDCN), and 2-amino-4-ethylpyridine (AEP). Electrochemical and electroplating validation confirms that all additives exhibit strong inhibition effects, enabling grain refinement that reduces cobalt film surface roughness below 10 nm $R _ { \mathrm { a } } ,$ with the optimal performer achieving 4.58 nm $R _ { \mathbf { a } } .$ . Furthermore, superconformal filling of through‑silicon vias (TSVs) with aspect ratios >5 is achieved. This work establishes a machine learning-based data-driven strategy as an effective tool for accelerating the discovery of highperformance electrodeposition additives. The identified additives provide new insights into industrial metalli zation solutions for scaled-down nodes.

As advanced chip manufacturing technologies trend toward miniaturization in the post-Moore's Law era, cobalt (Co) has been proposed as a promising alternative to replace copper (Cu) in advanced semiconductor applications [1–4] due to its superior electrical performance [5,6] and interconnect reliability at the nanoscale [7]. Electrodeposition is the predominant technique for Co interconnects [8,9]. Organic additives are decisive for modulating deposition kinetics and achieving high quality Co interconnects, such as surface planarization [10] and defectfree superfilling in submicron patterns.

In recent years, many studies have focused on the development of additives for cobalt superconformal electrodeposition and the underlying superfilling mechanisms [11–16]. It has been found that molecules influence the electrode process through their adsorption and interactions with the metal surface [17]. These interactions can be eluci dated by Frontier Molecular Orbital (FMO) theory [18], where a higher highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy indicates a stronger electron donation capability, while a lower lowest unoccupied molec ular orbital (LUMO) energy suggests a greater tendency to accept electrons. Additionally, within the framework of the Hard-Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) principle [19], metallic cobalt $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 0 } )$ is classified as a ‘soft acid and therefore exhibits a preferential affinity for ‘soft bases’ — molecules characterized by a narrow HOMO-LUMO gap (ΔE), as chemical hardness $\boldsymbol \eta \approx \varDelta \mathrm { E } / 2$ . Consequently, in the electrodeposition field, ΔE has been considered as a practical criterion for identifying promising additives [20], as molecules with smaller ΔE values generally exhibit stronger adsorption affinity toward the metal surface and thus exert more significant regulatory effects on the electrodeposition process [21–24]. An et al. [25] demonstrated a strong correlation between ΔE and both calculated adsorption energies and electrochemically measured inhibition ability, successfully applying this metric to identify Methylene Blue as a promising candidate for Cu electroplating.

Organic additives for cobalt electrodeposition typically feature nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), or sulfur (S) heteroatoms. Studies have shown that S-containing molecules functionalized with disulfide (-S-S-), thiol (-SH), or sulfonate (-SO₃H) groups generally exhibit an accelerating effect in cobalt electroplating (e.g. MPS [21] and thiourea [26]). O-containing additives mainly affect metal-ion solvation and complexation [12], rather than functioning through strong interfacial adsorption where ΔE serves as a key predictor. Notably, inhibitory additives play a particularly critical role in cobalt interconnects, as cobalt superfilling can be accomplished with one-component suppressors [27,28]. Nitrogen-containing molecules, which can interact with the electrode surface through π-bonds and the lone pair electrons of nitrogen, and often exhibit suppressive behavior during the deposition process [29], are preferable to S- and O-containing additives for screening strategies targeting interfacial adsorption–dominated suppression. Furthermore, they present enhanced environmental and economic advantages [30].

Finding effective additives is a challenge in the field of electrode position. Due to the absence of established screening criteria and the vastness of the chemical space of organic compounds, the process of discovering additives through traditional experimental trial-and-error methods resembles searching for a needle in a haystack and is both time-consuming and resource-intensive [31]. Quantum chemical prop erties enable the prediction of adsorption propensity, thereby accelerating additive screening [13]. However, DFT calculations for numerous molecules often require substantial computational resources and time. Therefore, a much more effective and cost-friendly screening method is essential for achieving high-efficiency screening of additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition. With the accumulation of databases in materials science, machine learning and data-driven strategies have made significant progress in materials discovery [32], property prediction and experiment optimization [33] by uncovering the statistical patterns embedded within extensive datasets and constructing quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) models [34–36]. The combination of first-principles calculations with machine learning is anticipated to enhance the prediction of material properties, thereby expediting the design and discovery of new materials [37] and has been successfully applied to the screening of electrolyte additives of Zn-ion batteries recently [38].

This consistent and homogeneous distribution of Co demonstrates the effectiveness of these candidates as additives in achieving uniform and void-free Co deposition in high-aspect-ratio microstructures. The underlying bottom-up filling mechanism can be described as follows (Fig. 8b). In the initial stage of electrodeposition, additives uniformly adsorb onto the cobalt surface. As the deposition proceeds, the additive molecules within the TSV trenches are gradually depleted. Owing to mass transport constraints, the replenishment of additives inside the deep vias occurs at a slower rate than on the upper surface, resulting in a reduced inhibitor concentration within the trenches compared to the via opening. This concentration gradient leads to weaker suppression at the bottom of the via relative to its top. Consequently, the deposition rate is elevated at the bottom in comparison to the top, facilitating bottom-up filling and thereby enabling the formation of void-free interconnect structures.

In summary, this study established a data-driven framework that integrates machine learning with experimental validation to efficiently identify novel, high-efficiency, and low-toxicity nitrogen-containing additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition. A comprehensive description of the molecules' physical properties was obtained using RDKit descriptors, and the key feature set was subsequently identified by integrating three feature selection strategies. Among the six evaluated ML models, XGBoost achieved the best predictive performance for ΔE prediction $( \mathrm { R } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 9 4 5 )$ . SHAP analysis revealed that descriptors associated with van der Waals surface area (SMR\_VSA7) and molecular topology (HallKierAlpha) significantly influence ΔE. These findings provide interpretable insights that can guide the design of additive molecules. The trained model was applied to a commercial molecular database, successfully identifying APZ, MIDCN, and AEP as three promising candidate molecules. Experimental validation demonstrated that the three additives effectively induce cathodic polarization and exhibit significant inhibitory effects even at low concentrations. In terms of coating quality, the introduction of these additives reduced the surface roughness (R ) of the cobalt film from 69.4 nm to below 10 nm, with MIDCN achieving a remarkably low roughness of 4.58 nm. Moreover, all three additives successfully facilitated defect-free superfilling of highaspect-ratio through‑silicon vias (TSVs), thereby confirming their excellent capability for three-dimensional structural filling. This study proposes an effective approach for the development of environmentally friendly and cost-efficient advanced interconnect additives.

Conventional damascene electroplating utilizes a combination of organic additives, namely, a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler, to achieve superconformal fill of interconnects. An alternative mechanism for superconformal cobalt fill is proposed here. This mechanism, the Differential Current Efficiency Fill (DCEF) mechanism, utilizes sacrificial oxidants to achieve voidfree superconformal fill. In the DCEF mechanism, the presence of a sacrificial oxidant, such as H<sup>+</sup>, O<sub>2</sub>, or an organic additive, promotes a difference in metal deposition rate between the field and the feature bottom. Addition of a single suppressor-type additive assists in driving the plating rate differential. By appropriately selecting the sacrificial oxidants, organic additives, the waveform, and the mass transport conditions, void-free superconformal cobalt fill can be achieved in a variety of features.

As interconnect dimensions continue to decrease, the extendibility of conventional copper damascene processing becomes increasingly problematic, in terms of yield and reliability. Small feature openings require thin seed to avoid having them close before the features can be filled (pinch-off) due to large overhang formation during seed deposition. The thin seed is susceptible to agglomeration, which leads to discontinuities and poor nucleation during the electrodeposition process. Reliability is also impacted by the decreasing line dimensions (1-2). Due to the higher current density in smaller lines, void formation occurs more readily, leading to decreasing electromigration lifetime as critical dimensions scale down. A third issue with decreasing dimensions is increasing RC delay and IR drop due to the exponential increase in resistivity with decreasing line crosssection (1-2). As such, the space occupied by the barrier layer within the feature becomes much more valuable.

# Induction-Diffusion-Adsorption Process of Malachite Green for Cobalt Superconformal Electrodeposition

Since the copper plating process, namely Damascus Copper Plating process, has been proposed by IBM in order to achieve metal interconnect integrated circuits (IC), it has attracted a great deal of attention in terms of electroplating technology in electronic devices with metal deposition of copper interconnect line.<sup>1</sup> Up to now, the damascene plating technology is still leading technology for the production of large scale integration (LSI) devices.

Applying electrodeposition method to prepare Co thin films is a cost-friendly, fast, and easy-operating method, and has been applied in many fields.<sup>14–17</sup> Achieving bottom-up growth of cobalt is the key to manufacturing the interconnect line, while the superconformal electrodeposition of cobalt can be obtained by exploring additive,<sup>18</sup> and optimizing the electrodeposition parameters, including the composition of bath solution,<sup>19</sup> current density,<sup>20</sup> pH<sup>21</sup> and so on. Besides, Co film with different structure and crystal phase can be obtained by changing electrodeposition parameters.<sup>22</sup> Generally, the Watts-based electrolyte or buffered sulfate electrolyte can be used to deposit Co film, in which boric acid has been added to stabilize the increasing pH in plating bath caused by polyborates and primarily triborate and occupy block surface sites to inhibit HER as well as facilitate cobalt deposition by the surface complex with cobalt.<sup>23–25</sup> In order to achieve bottom-up growth of cobalt deposit, appropriate additives should be introduced into plating bath to achieve growth rate difference in the blind vias.<sup>26–28</sup> And, this difference is consistent with the diffusion-adsorption mechanism.<sup>29–32</sup>

Josell et al.<sup>28</sup> realized the superconformation filling of TSVs with high aspect ratio by adding polyethyleneimine (PEI) as suppressor into the plating solution, which is composed of cobalt sulfate, cobalt chloride and boric acid. The deposition mechanism is due to the occurrence of S-NDR characteristics after the breakdown of the adsorption of PEI on the cathode surface, in which active-passive transitions are formed in TSVs with the applied voltage. Hydrogen induction deactivation mechanism was proposed to explain the influence of additive XF on superfilling of cobalt by Wu et al.<sup>33</sup> The growth rate different within blind vias was ascribed to the fact that the deactivation rate of additive is higher than the compensatory rate by mass transport. Huang et al.<sup>34</sup> added the dioxime additive as suppressor to achieve Co defect-free filling. Co(DMG) complex can be formed between dioxime and cobalt ions so as to inhibit the Co reduction. When the voltage rises to the breakdown threshold, Co begins to deposit on the cathode surface. Under the influence of convection, an obvious inhibition gradient was formed during the deposition process, which is consistent with S-NDR mechanism.

In this study, Malachite Green (MG), was selected as a suppressor for cobalt electrodeposition. It has been verified that MG adsorbed on the cathode surface to inhibit the reduction of copper and titanium.<sup>35</sup> And the influence of MG on Co metal deposition process have also been discussed before,<sup>36</sup> so this paper mainly studies the influence of MG adsorption on the hydrogen evolution process. The electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV), were applied to research the inhibition ability of MG on the deposition process of cobalt, while the influence of MG on HER was also studied by EQCM tests. Superconformal electrodeposition of cobalt was achieved and induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism was proposed to illustrate the synergistic effect of MG and pH.

Electroplating.—The electroplating bath contained 0.4 mol $1 ^ { - 1 }$ $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } , 0 . 5$ mol $\overline { { 1 } } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ , 10 mM Cl<sup>−</sup>, 20 ppm MPS and 10 ppm MG, and pH was adjusted to 4.0 at 298 K with the stirring rate of 500 rpm. A three-electrode cell was used for cobalt deposition process with Co-coated blind via as cathode, 99.99% Co foils as anode and MSE as the reference electrode. The depth of microvias used in this work is 100 $\mu \mathrm { m }$ , while the diameter is $5 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m } .$ , 100 μm, 150 μm. The blind via was pre-plating $\mathrm { a t } - 1 . 2 5 \ : \mathrm { V }$ for 5 min, after which nitrogen was used to dry blind vias. The blind vias were immersed into 10% $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ solution, and then the vias were rinsed with large amounts of deionized water (with a resistivity of 18.2 MOhm-cm). Pre-wetting with ethanol was carried out before being immersed in the bath. The morphology of cobalt coating was obtained with a Helios (Nanolab 600i) scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an Olympus (DSX 510) optical microscope.

The effect of MG on cobalt reduction process.—The electrochemical behaviors of MG were obtained from CV in order to study the influence of MG on cobalt reduction process. The influence of MPS on electrochemical behavior can be regarded as an accelerator for the electrodeposition of cobalt with a depolarization effect according to LSV analysis in Fig. S1. Figure 1 shows the CV curves of 10ppm MG in the bath with the different rotation rate so as to study the influence of mass transport. It can be seen that the current density begins to increase sharply when potential reaches to $- 1 . 2 4 \mathrm { V }$ (vs MSE) without rotating. When the rotation rate increased from 0 rpm to 800 rpm, the threshold potential of Co ion reduction shifted negatively from −1.24 V to −1.31 V (vs MSE) on the negative-going sweep, which can be attributed to the adsorption of the $\mathrm { \overline { { M } } G } ^ { 3 8 }$ and the change of surface coverage. The adsorption MG can be used as site-blocking by decreasing the active surface area for cobalt ions reduction. And the current density of the reduction process gradually decreases with the increasing rotation rate, due to the faster replenishment of MG from the bath to the cathode surface. In addition, the current loop at around −1.26 V was observed, demonstrated that the overpotential of cobalt nucleation is large. The slightly increase of current at about −1.15 V to −1.24 V was mainly attributed to the reduction of hydrogen ion and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } . ^ { 3 9 , 4 0 }$ No metal deposits were found on the cathode surface (not shown here). In this case, the total current density vs potential curve exhibits S-shape negative diffierential resistance (S-NDR) behavior,<sup>28,41,42</sup> which attributes to the breakdown of the blocking inhibitor layer (MG layer).

The CV curves of different concentrations of MG on electrochemical behavior were tested, as shown in Fig. 2. It can be seen that the significant hysteretic voltammetric curves appeared after MG was introduced into the electroplating bath even though the concentration is quite low (2 ppm), demonstrating that the additive MG is of excellent inhibition ability for the reduction of cobalt. It should be noted that the strong inhibition effect might be caused by strong adsorption and coordination between MG and cobalt ions studied in our previous work.<sup>45</sup> Besides, the breakdown potential shifted negatively from about $- 1 . 2 5 \mathrm { V }$ to lower than −1.40 V with the MG concentration increasing from 2 ppm to 20 ppm, while there is a relationship between the increase of threshold potential and the concentration of $\mathbf { M G } ,$ illustrating that the threshold value is related to the adsorption and transport of MG. Meanwhile, the S-shape negative differential resistance (S-NDR) can be observed when the MG concentration is higher than 10 ppm since the current density rises sharply when the cathode potential is lower than the breakdown potential. Furthermore, the current density of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ reduction was also accelerated with the increase of MG.

EQCM was used to separate the Co deposition current and HER current respectively, as shown in Fig. 3. It can be seen that under the condition of none convection, the total current density began to increase when the potential scanning $\mathrm { ~ t o ~ } - 1 . 1 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ after MG was added into the plating bath, lower than that obtained without MG. Likewise, there is a similar trend for the current density of the Co reduction at about −1.14 V, which was attributed to the absorption of suppressor MG and the CoMG complexes. The decreased current density of HER with a potential range from $- 1 . 1 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ t o ~ } - 1 . 3 0 \mathrm { ~ V } .$ shown in the inset, was mainly due to the reduction current of $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ or $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ . At lower overpotential, the current density of the proton reduction is higher than that of Co reduction, which means that the main electrochemical reaction is hydrogen evolution process, consistent with the thermodynamic result. In other words, the current density of HER was boosted with the existence of MG. So, it can be concluded that MG can suppress the reduction of ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ ions but boost the HER.

What’s more, voltammetry curves were used to further study the influence of MG on HER without Co ion in the bath. The solution contains of the same composition of plating bath except that the $\mathrm { C o S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ was replaced by $\mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ in order to match the conductivity of electrolyte. Co-seeded platinum electrode was selected as the cathode was shown in the Fig. 4. It can be seen that the current density increases with the increase of additive concentration at about −1.0 V. The process of hydrogen evolution was significantly accelerated even though 2 ppm MG added into plating bath. The accelerating effect on HER can be enhanced with the increase of MG concentration. The MG could absorb on the cathode surface as active sites to promote the HER, which is consistent with EQCM analysis (Fig. 3). It should be noted that the current density obtained in EQCM analysis is slightly different from that of cyclic voltammetry analysis, which is due to the fact that rotation electrode was applied in cyclic voltammetry tests while there was none convection in EQCM test.

Electroplating.—The electroplating test was carried out in order to observe the influence of MG and pH on the bottom-up growth of cobalt. The test condition in filling experiments was the same as that in electroanalytical experiments except for stirring way. The ohmic losses difference caused by different stirring way can be neglected (Fig. S8). Electroplating test were investigated at the potential range of −1.19 V and −1.22 V since superconformal electrodeposition could be achieved due to intense pH and strong inhibition of MG. As shown in Fig. 7, there is almost no cobalt reduced when the cathode potential is −1.19 V. Referring to the previous voltammetry curve, when the external potential at −1.19 V, the main electrochemical reaction in the via is hydrogen ion reduction. When the deposition potential is −1.20 V, it can be seen that the deposition layer begins to appear at the bottom and side wall. According to Moffat’s description of the metal filling process in TSV,<sup>28,50,51</sup> the blocking effect caused by the coverage of inhibitors on the electrode makes the deposition efficiency of metal on the sidewall higher than that on the surface, which can form a passive-active transition. From the Fig. 7(b), it can be seen that the rapid deposition rates take place in the lower portion of the via, while the sidewall and outside surface remain in the passive state. What’s more, the boundary of the passive-active transition gradually rises at more positive potential in Fig. 7(c). The transition forms mainly due to the difference of the vias coverage caused by the breakdown and diffusion-limited process of the MG.<sup>28,52</sup>

According to the deposition process provided above, the superfilling growth of cobalt in PCB board is realized in the Fig. 10(a). The schematic diagram of the filling process was exhibited in the Fig. 10(b) and induction-diffusion-adsorption filling mechanism was proposed, which consists of the induction effect of MG on HER as well as the diffusion-adsorption effect<sup>55</sup> caused by the MG concentration gradient and pH gradient within the blind vias.

At the initial state, the cathode surface covered with inhibitor MG which suppress the Co reduction and promote the HER. During the electrodeposition, the deposit suppression gradient was formed because of the diffusion-limited of MG. The passive-active transition zone come into being, and then the zone grows until it covers the entire trench due to the induction HER of MG. Meantime, the effective pH gradient is also established due to the mass transport limitation of hydrogen ion, resulting that the current efficiency at the bottom is higher, as shown in stage b in Fig. 10. Compared with the formation of inhibition gradient, the disruption of MG caused by HER is weaker, which is more conducive to the bottom-up superfilling process. In summary, the induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism, namely diffusion-adsorption effect caused by MG gradient and pH gradient as well as induction effect of MG on HER, was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt.

The formation of hydroxide ions at the electrode surface caused by the HER which leaded to the formation of $\mathrm { C o O H } ^ { + } \mathrm { ( a d s ) } .$ The induction-diffusionadsorption mechanism was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt. When adsorbed onto the deposit surface, W (VI) ions tend to become an inhibiting component that blocks the self-catalytic sites of Co [25]. Thus, the W (VI) ions depress Co deposition and their reduction reaction into metallic W being incorporated to the main Co deposit is interde pendent upon the main reduction reaction of the cobaltous ions. Specifically, previous studies have shown that adding high contents of tungstate $( \mathrm { W O _ { 3 } ^ { 4 + } } )$ to the cobalt sulfate $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + } )$ aqueous solutions with $\mathrm { W O } _ { 3 } ^ { 4 + } \mathrm { - t o - C O } ^ { 2 + }$ molarity ratios exceeding 0.3 or even greater than 2, using a given chemical reductant such as hypophosphite or dimethylamine borane, results in a decrease in the deposition rates of Co [25–28]. Here, the pure Co film was deposited by a sulfate-citrate-hydrazine bath. It should be noted that the concentration of the sulfate in this bath was 0.2 M. The $\mathrm { C o W _ { l } , C o W _ { m } }$ and $\mathrm { C o W _ { h } }$ films were deposited by otherwise this same bath except including quite low tungstate concentrations of about $2 . 5 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } , 1 . 0 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ and $5 . 3 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { M }$ , respectively. The $\mathrm { W O _ { 3 } ^ { 4 + } - t o { - } C O ^ { 2 + } }$ molarity ratios of the three CoW electroless-plating baths were very low, only $1 . 2 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } , 5 . 3 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ and $2 . 6 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 }$ However, they do cause the Co deposits to yield gradually decreased deposition rates. These results suggest that the tungstate in the tungstate-diluted Co-plating baths also depresses Co deposition as it does in the tungstate-concentrated baths.

It is significantly important to develop novel suppressor to achieve cobalt superconformal filling. Linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and impedance spectra (EIS) were coupled together to study the effect of novel dye suppressor nitrotetrazolium blue chloride (NBT) on cobalt electrodeposition. The adsorption behavior of NBT on cobalt substrate was investigated by applying density functional theory (DFT) calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra, while the interaction between NBT and cobalt ions $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + } )$ is analyzed based on topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis. Synergistic suppressing mechanism, namely adsorption effect and coordination effect, was proposed to explain the suppressing effect of NBT during cobalt electrodeposition. The cobalt surface morphology analysis under the influence of NBT demonstrates that NBT is of grain refinement, while XRD analysis indicates that the formation of Co hcp (100) is formed preferentially. The superconformal filling of cobalt is achieved in microvias with different diameters. The cobalt layer is of excellent quality due to low surface deposit thickness (SDT). The SDT values are 15.9 μm, 8.8 μm and 4.9 μm for 150 m, 100 m and 50 m.

With semiconductor technology evolving continuously along the way based on Moore’s Law, the traditional copper damascene process is facing enormous challenges in terms of yield and reliability [1,2]. On one hand, when trench size is decreased to lower than Mean electron free path of copper, the intensified electron scattering at external surfaces and grain boundaries leads to the exponential growth of resistivity of copper interconnect, resulting in severely increased RC delay and IR drop [3,4]. On the other hand, the seed layer and barrier layer increase the proportion of non-conductive material within copper interconnect, further increasing the resistivity [5]. Meanwhile, it is hard to achieve void-defect filling of copper in downscaling interconnect line width since the current density at the opening is increased due to edge effect, which has a negative effect on reliability [6,7]. Among alternative metals, cobalt [8] is regarded as candidate interconnect metal as a result of low line resistivity at advanced node and compatibility to electroplating process compared with Ni [9,10], Ru [11], Au [12], graphene [13,14] etc.

Electroplating technology is key fabrication process to obtain cobalt interconnect [14]. It is essentially important to introduce proper additives to achieve superconformal growth of cobalt [15,16] since the growth rate at the plane and opening of vias is higher than that in the bottom and sidewalls as a result of mass transfer limitation within vias and edge effect at the opening [17,18]. Several additives used for cobalt superconformal filling has been reported in the literature. Josell et al. investigated branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) as suppressor and proposed S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) model to predict bottowm-up filling of cobalt [19], while Huang et al. studied the effect of oxime additive and believed that amine groups could coordinate with ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ to suppress the cobalt electrodeposition [20–22]. He et al. studied the influence of inhibitor polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) on cobalt electrodeposition as well as cobalt superconformal electrodeposition was achieved at trench with high aspect ratio [23]. In contrast, Ma et al. proposed adsorption-coordination inhibition mechanism to explain the suppressing effect of malachite green (MG) during cobalt electrodeposition and achieve superconformal filling [24].

In this work, a kind of dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT), was used as novel suppressor on cobalt electrodeposition. Electrochemical methods including linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were used together to study the influence of NBT on kinetics of ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation was accepted to obtain the quantum chemical parameters of NBT. Besides, theoretical calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra were used to study the adsorption of NBT on cobalt substrate. Topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis were accepted to study the coordination between NBT and cobalt ions $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + } )$ . The suppressing mechanism of NBT is explained by proposing synergistic suppressing mechanism. The influence of NBT on morphology and crystal orientation is investi gated by SEM and XRD, respectively. Cobalt superconformal growth is achieved at microvias with different diameters.

Fig. 1 (a) shows the effect of NBT on electrochemical reaction. Generally, the increased cathodic polarization indicates that the metal electrodeposition is suppressed. In order to exclude the influence of NBT on hydrogen evolution reaction, LSV curves were measured without the existence of cobalt ions, as shown in Fig. S1. It can be seen that NBT can improve HER at a limited extent. As a result, the strengthened cathodic polarization will reflect the suppressing effect of NBT on cobalt deposition. The cathodic polarization is −1.180 V when NBT concentration is 0 mg/L. After the introduction of NBT, it can be found that even trace NBT can effectively increase the overpotential (more than 35 mV for 5 mg/L). Besides, the cathodic polarization sees an increase from −1.215 V to lower than −1.250 V with NBT increasing from 5 mg/L to 20 mg/L, which illustrates that suppressing effect for the electrodeposition of cobalt is intensified with the increase of NBT concentration and NBT is an effective suppressor for cobalt electrodeposition.

Electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) are also used to confirm the suppressing effect of NBT on ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction, as shown in Fig. 1 (b) and Figs. S1 to S3. Generally, the reaction energy barrier increases with impedance ring diameters [40]. As a result, the phenomenon of increasing impedance ring diameters with NBT illustrates that the suppressing effect is intensified by NBT regardless of applied measuring potential, consistent with the analysis from Fig. 1 (a). Besides, the equivalent circuit is established to calculate the charge transfer impedance (Rct) and solution impedance (Rs) by fitting parameters. The calculated results are shown in Fig. 1(c). Rs range from 30.1 to 30.8 Ω, indicating that NBT almost has no influence on solution impedance. The impedance with 5 mg/L is 596.6 Ω, far higher than that of VMS (400.5 Ω), which confirms that trace NBT can lead to strong cathodic polarization. When NBT is higher than 15 mg/L, the increased impedance become larger than 1250 Ω, which is two times higher than VMS, illustrating that NBT is of excellent suppressing effect during cobalt electrodeposition.

The energy of HOMO and LUMO indicates the electron donating ability and electron accepting ability according to the frontier molecular orbital theory. The relatively low ΔE $( E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } ^ { - } } E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } )$ illustrates that it is easier for the additive molecule to accept and donate electrons at the electrode surface. As a result, there is relationship between the value of ΔE (E<sub>LUMO</sub>-E<sub>HOMO</sub>) and the adsorption intensity of additives [43]. Generally, less ΔE means stronger adsorption [44]. E<sub>LUMO</sub> and E<sub>HOMO</sub> is - 0.15179 Ha and - 0.26626 Ha, respectively. And the ΔE is 0.11447 Ha, demonstrating that NBT is of potential to adsorb on the cobalt surface during electrodeposition.

Electrostatic potential (ESP) distribution and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation were applied to study NBT adsorption behavior. $\mathrm { F i g . 2 }$ (c) shows the ESP distribution histogram and the average potential is 101.15 kcal/mol. Besides, the ESP ranges from 30 kcal/mol to 160 kcal/ mol, indicating that the positively charged NBT is of adsorption potential on cathodic surface due to electrostatic interaction between NBT and cobalt substrate during electrodeposition.

In order to verify the calculated results, in situ Raman spectra is carried out, as shown in Fig. 4. The typical peaks of NBT appears at 991, 1126, 1186, 1222, 1316, 1364, 1435, 1502, 1597 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively, when cathodic potential changes from open circuit potential (OCP) to $- 2 . 2 \mathrm { V } .$ It can be seen from Table 2 that characteristic peaks appeared at 991 and 1316 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ attribute to stretching vibration of tetrazole ring $\mathsf { N { - N } } [ 4 5 , 4 6 ]$ , while 1222 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and 1364 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ are due to tetrazole ring $\mathrm { N - N }$ bending vibration and -tetrazole bending vibration [47,48]. The characteristic peaks of 1126 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and $1 1 8 6 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ is aromatic $\mathrm { C - H }$ bending vibration [49,50] as well as 1435 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ is aromatic $\mathrm { C - H }$ stretching vibration [51]. In contrast, C–N stretching vibration and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 2 }$ stretching vibration appear at $1 5 0 2 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ and 1597 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ separately $[ 4 8 , 5 1 ]$ . Overall, the theoretical calculation analysis and in situ Raman spectra analysis illustrate that NBT can absorb well on cobalt surface to reduce active sites and suppress the cobalt electrodeposition.

During the electrodeposition, the nitrogenous heterocyclic ring of the adsorbed NBT will accept electrons from cathodic surface due to the local minima appear at nitrogenous heterocyclic ring, as shown in Fig. 5 (a), and later the nitrogenous heterocyclic ring is opened [52,53]. When cobalt ions move toward the cathode surface, a possible coordination interaction would be formed between cobalt ions and opened nitrogenous heterocyclic ring.

In summary, synergistic suppressing mechanism was proposed to illustrate the excellent suppressing ability of NBT during cobalt electrodeposition. On one hand, NBT is of excellent adsorption ability on cathodic surface since it is positively charged and is full of $\mathfrak { p i }$ electron cloud of benzene and nitrogenous heterocyclic ring, which can reduce the active sites for reduction of ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ (Adsorption effect). On the other hand, the nitrogenous heterocyclic ring opening due to accepting electrons from cathodic surface leads to that NBT can coordinate with ${ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ when ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ go through the NBT adsorption layer, which further increase the energy barrier (Coordination effect).

## 3.7. Electroplating

The superconformal growth of cobalt within microvias is achieved to confirm the effect of NBT, as shown in Fig. 8. The current transients are provided in supplementary (Fig. S5) and the current density is about 1.6 mA/cm<sup>2</sup> while calculated current efficiency is 40 %. Fig. 8 (a) shows the shape evolution in microvias of 150 μm during cobalt electrodeposition. The cobalt electrodeposition at the opening of microvias is effectively suppressed due to fast mass transfer of NBT near the plane and opening. In contrast, the supplementary rate of NBT at the bottom is lowered than consuming rate as a result of relatively slow mass transfer of NBT from bulk solution into microvias. Cobalt layer began to grow from the bottom to the top of the microvias, as shown in a2 (8h) in Fig. 8 (a). After being electrodeposited for 16 h, cobalt layer grows near the opening of microvias while the surface deposit thickness (SDT) is lowered than 16 μm, indicating that NBT is of excellent selectivity.

Likewise, the superconformal electrodeposition of cobalt is achieved at microvias with 100 μm and 50 μm, as shown in Fig. 8 (b) and (c). This comprehensive review explores electroless cobalt deposition, an appealing surface modification technique that offers advantages such as uniform coverage on complex geometries and compatibility with diverse substrate materials without external power. The article systematically examines the critical impact of various bath constituents and operational variables on the characteristics of deposited films. It details the roles of the cobalt source, different reducing agents, complexing agents, pH regulators, and stabilizers. Additionally, the article scrutinizes the influence of deposition parameters like temperature, solution pH, agitation methods, and bath aging. The formation of numerous cobalt-based alloys and composite materials are also discussed. This review aims to guide the development of optimized electroless cobalt plating solutions, highlighting their wide-ranging utility in fields such as microelectronics, data storage, protective coatings, electrolytic green H₂ generation metal matrix composites, and electromagnetic shielding, thereby fostering advancements in intricate material fabrication

Electroless cobalt plating stands out as a versatile and efficient method for depositing a thin layer of cobalt metal on any surface. Unlike traditional electroplating, which relies on external electrical current, electroless cobalt utilizes a chemical reduction process. This eliminates the need for exclusively conducting substrates, complex electrical setup and allows for more uniform deposition on intricate surfaces. The process is steadily gaining traction since its inception by Brenner and Riddell [1] in 1947 due to simplicity of the technique and lower cost of instrumentation. Electroless coating or autocatalytic coating is a category of chemical process that deposits one or more metal layers by autocatalytic reduction of metal cations in a liquid chemical bath. One of the significant advantages of electroless plating is its ability to achieve a more even and conformal coating compared to electroplating. Unlike electroplating, homogeneity of deposit thickness is maintained even in the sharp corners or intricate recesses of the substrate surface [2, 3]. This characteristic makes it ideal for applications where uniform coverage is crucial, such as in microelectronics and the fabrication of magnetic thin films. The composition of the electroless plating solution can be tailored to control the properties of the deposited cobalt layer. Electroless cobalt alloy finds applications in various fields. In the microelectronics industry, it is used to create diffusion barriers [4, 5] and seed layers [6, 7] for subsequent electroplating processes. The magnetic properties ofcobalt make it a valuable material for data storage devices and magnetic sensors [8, 9]. Since US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) categorized Cr<sup>6+</sup> containing baths (essential for hard chrome plating) as unsuitable for environment and stressed on alternative approaches [10], cobalt-based plating has also been explored and employed for wear [11–13] and corrosion [14, 15] protection of metallic components. While electroless plating excels at creating thin films, its potential extends far beyond simple flat surfaces. Deposition of 3D structures like cobalt microspheres [16, 17] and 1D structures like nanowires [18] or nanotubes [19] has been successfully demonstrated, paving the way for a new generation of micro and nanostructured materials with enhanced functionalities in various fields.

As research in this area continues, advancements are being made to optimize electroless cobalt plating solutions for specific applications. Although a large volume of research work is available, comprehensive review article on this area is scarce. Shen et al. [20] in 2022 provided a summary on the progress of electroless cobalt deposition narrowly focusing on semiconductor-based electronics application. The main aim of the current article is to discuss and summarize past works on the influence of bath composition and coating parameters on autocatalytic cobalt deposition. The article also includes brief discussion on the development of Co-based alloys and composites structures obtained via electroless path and their intended applications.

The manufacture process of cobalt interconnects is similar to that of copper interconnects and is compatible with existing electrodeposition processes for copper damascene interconnects. The electrodeposition process for cobalt interconnection is an advanced interconnect technology for integrated circuits that utilizes a wet electrochemical deposition method to bottom-up fill the interconnect structures of semiconductor chips with cobalt metal. Electrodeposition has the advantages of simple operation, easy control of process parameters, and low cost and is considered to be the main technology for cobalt filling at present.<sup>16−18</sup> In recent years, the process of copper electrodeposition has been thoroughly studied, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the bottom-up electro deposition (superfilling) mechanism, which is also applied to cobalt electrodeposition to achieve defect-free interconnect structures.<sup>19,20</sup>

The search for suitable additives is the core to fulfill the bottom-up electrodeposition mechanism. Generally, the electrodeposition rate of cobalt changes in diferent positions of the hole due to changing thermodynamics across the additive concentration gradient.<sup>21,22</sup> When the deposition rate at the bottom of the hole is higher than that at the upper part of the hole, it can obtain the void-free superfilling deposition of cobalt in the microvias, holes, or trenches from bottom to to p.<sup>23−25</sup> These additives have efects on controlling the deposition process and have influence on the surface morphology, crystal structure, and electrical properties of the cobalt films.<sup>26−29</sup> The research on cobalt electroplating additives has focused on finding compounds that can achieve superfilling while improving plating properties. However, there are few reports and research studies in this field, particularly for the superfilling processes at present.

In this work, we propose a cobalt electrodeposition additive which can be used for superfilling. The inhibition efect of alkyne-PEG4-amine (AP4A) was investigated by electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry and chronopotentiometry. Quantum chemical calculations were applied to confirm the inhibition efect of the AP4A molecule on electrodeposition. The results of the cobalt electrodeposition experiment showed that AP4A has significant influence on electrical properties, surface morphology, and crystal structure. In superfilling of nanometer scale structures with high aspect ratios, the additive AP4A was used to achieve bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition successfully. This study provides a targeted solution for superfilled cobalt plating, which has a good role in promoting the development of electroplating in the future.

# Superconformal Electrodeposition of Cobalt into Micron-Scale Trench with Alkynol Derivatives

Abstract: Copper interconnect technology faces limitations due to the electron’s mean free path and electromigration, driving the adoption of cobalt alternatives. This study proposes a novel mechanism to achieve superfilling by tuning the adsorption energy of additive molecules on cobalt surfaces. The adsorption energies of additives are tailored by changing molecular structures with different functional groups. Computational results reveal that carbon–carbon triple bonds critically strengthen adsorption, while ether bonds further enhance binding on distinct cobalt crystallographic planes. Specifically, 1,4-bis(2- hydroxyethoxy)-2-butyne (BEO) containing both triple bonds and ether groups exhibits the highest adsorption energy (−22.62 eV). Replacing ether with hydroxyl groups in 2- butyne-1,4-diol (BOZ) reduces the adsorption energy to −10.39 eV, while eliminating triple bonds in 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDE) further decreases it to −8.43 eV. Experimental studies demonstrate that BOZ and BEO preferentially adsorb on the (101) and (110) planes of hexagonal close-packed cobalt (HCP-Co) due to their differential adsorption energies. This selective suppression promotes preferential growth along the densely packed (002) orientation. This leads to a trench-filling process dominated by the most densely packed plane, resulting in better electrical performance. Superfilling is achieved when molecular adsorption energies are in the range of 5–8 eV. The work establishes a functional group design strategy to regulate additive adsorption, enabling crystallographic control for advanced cobalt electrodeposition processes.

Thin film deposition technology is critical to realize high-quality cobalt interconnects. Physical vapor deposition [12,13] (PVD), chemical vapor deposition [14,15] (CVD), atomic layer deposition [16–18] (ALD), and electrodeposition [19–21] are the primary synthesis methods reported to date. PVD is a widely used film deposition technique, yet its filling efficiency and step coverage remain inadequate, primarily due to one-direction linear de position characteristics. This results in particles with large incidence angles failing to enter the trenches and instead depositing at the trench openings [22]. Consequently, the opening closes before the trench is fully filled [23]. To solve this problem, the industrial sector has de veloped specific PVD technologies, such as ionized PVD and collimated sputtering [24,25]. Nevertheless, the hole problem in small-sized channels still exists. In addition, CVD tech nologies have better filling capabilities, especially when trench widths are around several hundred nanometers, such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition [26]. ALD possesses the unique characteristic of layer-by-layer self-limiting growth, providing exceptional step coverage and film uniformity. However, its deposition rate is exceedingly low, making it particularly suitable for applications such as barrier layers and seed layers [27]. In contrast, electroplating technology is extensively utilized in damascene copper interconnect processes, where it enables bottom-up film growth and demonstrates remarkable filling capabilities [28,29]. During the electroplating process, precise control over parameters such as applied current, anode material, accelerants, inhibitors, planarization agents, and mass transport allows for the fine-tuning of deposition rate, grain size, morphology, impurity content, and stress [30]. This level of control highlights the considerable potential for further advancement of metal-interconnect trench-filling techniques.

Cobalt electroplating is an efficient and cost-effective method for achieving highquality cobalt interconnects [31,32]. By introducing certain organic additives into the plating solution, bottom-up cobalt superfilling can be realized. Superfilling refers to the phenomenon where the metal deposition rate at the bottom of a trench exceeds that in the side wall. This technique is particularly crucial for the fabrication of interconnects with high aspect ratios, as it effectively prevents the formation of voids, ensuring the integrity and reliability of the interconnects. To date, multiple super-conformal filling mechanisms have been proposed by different research groups. The S-shaped negative differential resistance [33,34] has been extensively applied to the overfilling processes of various metals, including copper [35], gold [36], nickel [37], cobalt [38], and zinc [39]. This model suggests that the adsorption and desorption behavior of inhibitors on the electrode surface leads to a nonlinear variation in current density within a specific potential range, resulting in an “S”-shaped curve. By optimizing inhibitor concentration and potential control, this model enables the realization of the bottom-up overfilling of metals in high-aspect-ratio structures. Rigsby et al. [40,41] introduced the differential current efficiency fill mechanism, emphasizing the critical role of the H<sup>+</sup> concentration gradient in overfilling processes. They observed that during the electrodeposition of cobalt, the pH gradient rapidly formed within the trenches due to proton transfer, resulting in a disparity between the current efficiency and deposition rate at the trench interior and the opening. This differential effect facilitated the bottom-up filling of cobalt. In parallel, Wu et al. [42] introduced the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation mechanism, which elaborates on how changes in pH and H<sup>+</sup> concentration affect the inhibitory efficacy of additives, thereby triggering a bottom-up filling mechanism. That model showed that the self-initiated bottom-up filling of cobalt was driven by the reduction in and deactivation of inhibitors at the bottom of the trench, caused by hydrogen gas evolution, leading to a diminished inhibitory effect and subsequently promoting the deposition rate at the bottom. The adsorption energy determines the conformality of deposited cobalt layers, especially in complex geometries structures, but its role in achieving superconformal filling has been largely overlooked. Addressing this gap is essential for improving the precision and reliability of coating processes in advanced applications.

In this paper, we propose a mechanism to achieve superfilling by regulating the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. By rationally designing the chemical structure of the additive molecules (such as introducing specific functional groups or adjusting the molecular size), the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface can be regulated. It is worth noting that alkynol additives [43–46] (such as 2-butyne-1,4-diol) exhibit a strong adsorption effect on the (100) and (101) crystal planes of hexagonal close packed (HCP) cobalt, which provides a potential way to regulate the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. However, at present, there is still a lack of in-depth research on the filling effect of alkynols in cobalt interconnect trenches and the regulation mechanism of specific groups on the adsorption energy of molecules. We investigate the effects of three organic additives—2-butyne-1,4-diol (BOZ), 1,4-bis(2-hydroxyethoxy)-2- butyne $( \mathrm { B E O } ) ,$ and $^ { 1 , 4 }$ -butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDE)—on the morphology, structure, and electrical properties of cobalt electroplating. BEO, which adds two ether groups compared to BOZ, and BDE, which lacks the triple bond and hydroxyl group found in BOZ and BEO, to highlight the role of the alkyne–ether functionality and clarify the influence of the unsaturated triple bond. Through electrochemical experiments, we compare the polarization capabilities of these additives and analyze their behavior during the electroplating process. By calculating the surface energies of different crystal planes, we uncover the mechanism behind selective crystal facet adsorption. Using quantum chemical methods, we further examine the adsorption and desorption behaviors of organic molecules during the electroplating process.

The electrochemical experimental setup used was a multi-channel electrochemical workstation (Model M204) manufactured by Metrohm (Herisau, Switzerland). A standard three-electrode system was employed, with a Pt electrode (Tianjin Aida Hengsheng Technology Development ${ \mathrm { C o . , L t d . } }$ , Tianjin, China) as the counter electrode, a saturated $\mathrm { A g / A g C l }$ electrode (Tianjin Aida Hengsheng Technology Development $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { C } } \mathbf { \boldsymbol { o } } .$ ., Ltd., Tianjin, China) as the reference electrode, and a $\mathrm { C o } / \mathrm { T i N } / \mathrm { S i }$ patterned wafer (Prepared by magnetron sputtering) as the working electrode. The patterned wafer had a line width of 3 µm and a trench depth of 1 µm. Cobalt electrodeposition was performed using the constant current chronopotentiometry method. During deposition, only one square surface was exposed, while the remaining area was tightly clamped with the Pt electrode, deposited at a current density of $3 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for 56.5 min. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed from 0 to −1.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl using a negative potential scan at a rate of $2 \mathrm { m V } { \cdot } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The stability of the additives during electrodeposition was evaluated in an acidic solution (pH 4.00) of $3 0 \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { L } \mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ (See Figure S1 for details).

The electrochemical behavior during cobalt electrodeposition was analyzed using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and the electrochemical deposition method with constant current. The LSV test involved a negative sweep starting from 0 V to −1 V vs. $\mathrm { A g / A g C l }$ with a scan rate of $2 \mathrm { m V } { \cdot } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , as shown in Figure 2a. The results indicated that after adding BOZ and BEO, the onset potential for the increase in current density shifted negatively (the potentials of the control group at −0.795 V shifted negatively to −0.838 V and −0.862 V, as shown in Figure 2c). This implies that cobalt deposition was suppressed at the same applied potential, with BEO exhibiting a stronger inhibitory effect than BOZ. The inhibition of cobalt deposition is attributed to the formation of an adsorption layer on the electrode surface by the additives, which alters the electrode properties and increases the energy barrier for cobalt deposition on the substrate [50]. In contrast, no negative shift was observed in the presence of BDE, indicating that the adsorption capability of BDE on the substrate was weaker than that of BOZ and BEO. This highlighted the significant contribution of the carbon–carbon triple bond to enhance the adsorption energy of the additives, which was consistent with the DFT analysis results discussed in Section 3.1.

To investigate the effect of additives on crystal morphology, SEM characterization was performed on the surface and cross-sectional morphology of cobalt films after electrodeposition. As shown in Figure 3, the surface and cross-sectional morphologies of the cobalt films are presented. The super-conformal filling was achieved in the electrolyte with BDE in micro-scale trend. The cross-sectional of Co deposited with the addition of BOZ and BEO showed a gap, although the gap already shrunk compared to the one without additives. It is evident that prolonged electrodeposition allowed sufficient time for the cobalt grains to grow, and the addition of additives significantly altered the morphology of the deposited Co. When Co was deposited in the solution without additives (as shown in Figure 3a), the presence of cobalt dendrites [55] was observed. Under the influence of the tip effect, these cobalt dendrites may lead to the premature narrowing of openings. The addition of organic additives effectively suppressed the formation of dendrites. The cobalt grains became larger and more uniform with the presence of BOZ, BEO, and BDE. Specifically, BEO also made the surface of the cobalt film more compact, but the grain contours became more blurred. This might be owing to the effect of the ether bonds. In the cross sections shown in Figure 3e–h, no significant filling defects were observed. However, the cleavage planes of the BOZ-treated sample (Figure 3f) and the BEO-treated sample (Figure 3g) appeared much smoother compared to the control group (Figure 3e) and the BDE-treated sample (Figure 3h).

The effect of organic additives on the crystal structure was further investigated by XRD. Figure 4a reveals that cobalt growth in the trench covered with PVD Co as a seed layer was well crystallized. During cobalt electrodeposition, cobalt preferentially grew along the (100) direction with strong crystallinity in the electrolyte without additives and with BDE. Additionally, the (002) crystal orientation of Co deposited with BEO was also observed in the TEM image (Figure 4d). The change in the Co preferential orientation may be related to the specific adsorption of additives on certain crystal planes. This adsorption inhibits the growth of the adsorbed planes, causing the crystal to preferentially grow along the non-adsorbed surfaces.
